## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Foam-Volume-Dominated Space — Lowest Composite Density of the Audience Seating Category:**
- Very low composite density (200 kg/m³) — slightly lower than the large-format auditorium (219 kg/m³); results from lower seat density per floor area (1.40 vs. 1.50 seats/m²) combined with thicker premium foam cushions (55 mm/45 mm vs. 50 mm/40 mm); foam at 35–50 kg/m³ occupies 92.2% of composite volume
- Moderate SA ratio (2.06 m²/m²) — slightly lower than the auditorium (2.11 m²/m²) primarily due to fewer seats per m²; the performing arts theater's more generous seating pitch (0.95 m vs. 0.90 m) and slightly lower seat density are typical of regional theater programming priorities (sight lines, legroom, and patron comfort over raw capacity)
- Moderate specific heat (879 J/kg·K) — higher than the auditorium (859 J/kg·K) because the larger foam mass fraction (16.1% vs. 14.6%) pulls the composite specific heat upward; foam's high c_p (1,700 J/kg·K) offsets steel's low value (460 J/kg·K)
- Lower conductivity (0.863 W/m·K) than the auditorium (0.966 W/m·K) — fewer steel pedestals per m² (lower seat density) reduces the thermal bridge pathway count; foam dominance at 92.2% of volume is more complete

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Low thermal capacitance per unit volume (175,800 J/m³·K) — the lowest of the audience seating space types; foam-dominated composite responds relatively quickly to zone air temperature changes; pre-conditioning the seating zone from setback requires less energy than a masonry-heavy space
- Moderate total thermal mass (15.63 kg/m²) — comparable to the auditorium (15.36 kg/m²) despite lower seat density; the premium seat construction (heavier per-seat mass: 9.45 kg vs. 9.00 kg) largely compensates for the reduced seat count per m²
- The orchestra pit barrier rail (0.094 kg/m², 0.6% of total mass) is thermally minor but represents an actively convective surface — positioned at the front edge of the seating deck, exposed to the temperature differential between the seating zone and the cooler pit cavity below
- The sound mixing console (0.400 kg/m², 2.6% of mass, 0.013 m²/m² SA) generates both waste heat (amplifiers, signal processors) and provides additional internal thermal mass at the rear of the house; its contribution is modest in mass terms but non-trivial as a localized heat source during events

### Design Appropriateness

**Performing Arts Theater Seating — Distinctive Thermal Profile vs. General Auditorium:**
- **Seating density is the primary differentiator** — the performing arts theater's seating density (1.40 seats/m²) is lower than a large-format auditorium's (1.50 seats/m²); this modest difference has cascading effects on composite density, SA ratio, and conductivity; all other per-seat properties are similar between the two types
- **Premium foam specification is characteristic** — performing arts theaters, especially regional companies and university performing arts centers, specify thicker, denser foam for patron comfort and long-term durability under intensive use schedules; the 55 mm/45 mm specification used here is representative of mid-grade to premium commercial theater seating
- **The orchestra pit barrier rail is a distinguishing element** absent from the general auditorium configuration; it contributes negligibly to thermal mass (0.094 kg/m²) but is architecturally diagnostic of the space type and is included for completeness
- **The fixed sound mixing console** (0.400 kg/m²) is present in performing arts theaters as a permanently installed house system; in large concert halls this position is typically more elaborate (larger console, more equipment), which would increase this component's mass and SA contribution modestly

### Comparison to Related Audience Seating Space Types

| Parameter | Performing Arts Theater | Auditorium | Convention Center | Exercise Center |
|-----------|------------------------|------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 2.06 | 2.11 | — | — |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 15.63 | 15.36 | — | — |
| Density (kg/m³) | 200 | 219 | — | — |
| Conductivity (W/m·K) | 0.863 | 0.966 | — | — |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 879 | 859 | — | — |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 175,800 | 188,121 | — | — |
| Seats/m² | 1.40 | 1.50 | — | — |
| Distinctive component | Pit barrier rail + console | Aisle handrails | — | — |

> The performing arts theater and auditorium are the most closely related seating space types in the taxonomy. Their thermal mass profiles are nearly identical by mass per floor area (~15.4–15.6 kg/m²), with the primary differences driven by seat density (1.40 vs. 1.50 seats/m²). The lower seat density reduces SA ratio and steel pedestals per m², bringing the composite density (200 vs. 219 kg/m³) and conductivity (0.863 vs. 0.966 W/m·K) both slightly lower. The higher per-seat foam mass in the theater type partially offsets the capacity reduction, resulting in nearly identical total mass per floor area. Both spaces are fundamentally foam-dominated composites with steel structural elements acting as thermal bridges through the insulating foam body.

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- Performing arts theaters operate on the same extreme bimodal occupancy schedule as auditoriums: full occupancy during events (490 persons in 350 m² = 1.40 p/m²) versus near-zero between events; the HVAC system must recover the seating zone from setback to full comfort within a 1–2 hour pre-event window
- High latent loads during events from dense audience occupancy (490 people × ~90 W sensible + ~60 W latent = 44.1 kW sensible + 29.4 kW latent in 350 m²); transient occupancy loads dominate over internal mass thermal storage effects during active programming
- Under-seat supply air (displacement ventilation) is standard in performing arts theaters — low-velocity delivery at seat level directly conditions the occupied zone; the internal mass of the foam-bodied seats moderates temperature gradients between supply pulses
- The sound mixing console at the rear of the house generates continuous waste heat during events (typical: 300–800 W total); this localized heat source at the rear of the seating deck should be accounted for in zone load calculations, particularly in smaller theaters where the console-to-floor area ratio is high

**Operational Patterns:**
- Event schedule: 4–8 performances per week for active regional companies; dark nights create full setback opportunities
- Pre-event conditioning: 1.5–2 hours before curtain; foam-dominated thermal mass responds relatively quickly — the 175,800 J/m³·K capacitance is lower than most hard-finish commercial spaces, supporting faster pre-conditioning
- Event duration: 1.5–3 hours (plays and musicals); intermission (15–20 min) provides a brief occupancy reduction at the seating deck level
- Technical rehearsals and load-in days may have extended periods of partial occupancy (crew only) with HVAC at reduced capacity

**Special Considerations:**
- **Balcony seating** in multi-level performing arts theaters should be modeled as a separate thermal zone; the internal mass definition (`AudienceSeating_PerformingArtsTheater_IntMass`) is applicable to balcony zones with the same per-seat properties, but balcony zones have different HVAC connectivity, solar exposure, and potentially higher ceiling heights
- **Orchestra pit thermal interface**: the orchestra pit is a separate HVAC zone (pit musicians have different conditioning requirements than audience); the barrier rail at the front of the seating deck represents the thermal boundary between the seating zone and the cooler, separately conditioned pit zone; this boundary effect is minor but may be relevant in detailed zone coupling models
- **Sound console heat generation**: the mixing console waste heat (0.3–0.8 kW typical) should be assigned to the ElecEquip object for the space type rather than to the InternalMass object; the InternalMass object captures the thermal storage capacity of the console chassis, not its heat generation
- **Acoustic absorptivity**: the upholstered theater seats provide primary acoustic absorption in the unoccupied hall, consistent with the auditorium type; the performing arts theater's typical use of thicker foam (55 mm) provides slightly higher acoustic absorption per seat, which is consistent with the acoustically drier sound desired for speech-forward theatrical productions (as opposed to music-optimized concert halls that may prefer less absorption)

---

*End of Calculation Report*

## CS Audience Seating Area - Religious Building

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 50–400 attendees (highly variable; peak during services and special events)
**Floor Area:** 150–500 m² (dedicated audience seating room, separate from the primary nave or sanctuary); reference area: **300 m²**
**Ceiling Height:** 4.5–7.0 m (flat or low-pitched ceiling; lower than main sanctuary); reference height: **5.0 m**
**Function:** Secondary audience seating space within a religious building complex — typically a fellowship hall, overflow room, satellite chapel, or multipurpose teaching room configured with rows of portable padded stackable chairs for lectures, auxiliary services, large-group bible study, visiting speakers, or overflow broadcast seating. The space is distinct from the primary pew-seated nave or sanctuary (modeled separately under SS Religious Building - Worship/Pulpit/Choir). The defining furnishing is the padded stackable chair arranged in ganged rows; the space is reconfigurable and the chairs are stored on carts when not in use for audience seating.

**Key Features:**
- Padded stackable chairs in ganged rows (the dominant thermal mass element)
- Steel gang-lock row connectors linking adjacent chairs (minor)
- Portable folding tables along room perimeter (bulletins, sound equipment, refreshments)
- Portable podium or lectern at front (usually lightweight, excluded as negligible)
- Chair transport dollies (stored in adjacent closet or storeroom; excluded)
- Portable aisle safety stanchions (lightweight plastic; excluded as negligible)
- AV equipment (projector, screen; excluded — modeled under plug loads)
- Highly intermittent use pattern — irregular peak events; otherwise unoccupied

### Reference Configuration

**300 m² religious building multipurpose audience room:**
- 330 padded stackable chairs
- Row pitch: 0.81 m (back of one chair to back of next row)
- Chair width: 0.46 m; center-to-center spacing: 0.50 m
- ~41 rows; ~8 chairs per row average
- Seating density: 1.10 seats/m² (including aisle share)
- Gang-lock connectors: 280 (7 per row × 41 rows, approximate)
- Portable folding tables: 4 (one each at front and three along back/side walls)

## Material Property Calculations

### Mass-Weighted Composite Properties

**Material Breakdown by Mass:**

*Steel (chair frames + ganging hardware + gang-lock connectors + table leg frames):*
- Chair steel frames (3.25 kg/chair): 3.25 × 330 / 300 = 3.575 kg/m²
- Gang-lock connectors: 0.140 kg/m²
- Table steel leg frames: 7.00 × 4 / 300 = 0.093 kg/m²
- **Total steel: 3.808 kg/m²** (70.0%)

*Polyurethane foam (seat and back cushioning in chairs):*
- 0.61 × 330 / 300 = **0.671 kg/m²** (12.3%)

*Commercial polyester fabric (chair upholstery + table vinyl laminate):*
- Chair fabric: 0.64 × 330 / 300 = 0.704 kg/m²
- Table vinyl laminate: 0.50 × 4 / 300 = 0.007 kg/m²
- **Total fabric/vinyl: 0.711 kg/m²** (13.1%)

*MDF/particleboard (table tops):*
- 18.52 × 4 / 300 = **0.247 kg/m²** (4.5%)

**Total: 3.808 + 0.671 + 0.711 + 0.247 = 5.437 kg/m²** ✓

### Volume Fractions (for Conductivity Weighting)

```
V_i = mass_i / density_i  [m³ per m² of floor area]

Steel:    3.808 / 7,800  = 4.882 × 10⁻⁴ m³/m²
Foam:     0.671 /    35  = 0.019171 m³/m²
Fabric:   0.711 /   550  = 1.293 × 10⁻³ m³/m²
MDF:      0.247 /   700  = 3.529 × 10⁻⁴ m³/m²

V_total = 0.000488 + 0.019171 + 0.001293 + 0.000353 = 0.021305 m³/m²

Volume fractions:
  Steel:   0.000488 / 0.021305 = 2.29%
  Foam:    0.019171 / 0.021305 = 89.97%
  Fabric:  0.001293 / 0.021305 = 6.07%
  MDF:     0.000353 / 0.021305 = 1.66%
```

> Polyurethane foam occupies 90.0% of composite volume despite representing only 12.3% of composite mass. This mirrors the foam-volume dominance seen in the theater seating (Auditorium) space type, and reflects the fundamental nature of padded chair thermal mass: the cushioning volume dwarfs all structural material volumes. Steel, at 70.0% of mass, occupies only 2.29% of volume.

### Weighted Average Density

```
rho_composite = Total mass / Total volume
              = 5.437 / 0.021305
              = 255.2 kg/m³  -->  255 kg/m³
```

> The composite density of 255 kg/m³ is moderately low — higher than the performing arts auditorium (219 kg/m³) because the padded stackable chair carries proportionally more steel frame mass per unit of foam volume than the deep-cushioned fixed theater seat: the stackable chair's 0.61 kg of foam supports a 3.25 kg steel frame (ratio 5.3:1 steel-to-foam by mass), while the theater seat's 1.50 kg of foam carries a 4.50 kg frame (ratio 3.0:1). The overall composite volume is dominated by foam in both cases, but the religious building chair is more mass-efficient (more steel per unit volume), raising its composite density modestly above the auditorium value.

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Sum(m_i x c_p,i) / Sum(m_i)

Material properties:
  Steel:   460 J/kg·K   (carbon steel)
  Foam:  1,700 J/kg·K   (polyurethane foam, open/semi-open cell)
  Fabric: 1,340 J/kg·K   (commercial polyester textile)
  MDF:   1,700 J/kg·K   (MDF/particleboard, cellulose-based)

Steel:   3.808 x 460   = 1,752
Foam:    0.671 x 1,700 = 1,141
Fabric:  0.711 x 1,340 =   953
MDF:     0.247 x 1,700 =   420

c_p,composite = (1,752 + 1,141 + 953 + 420) / 5.437
              = 4,266 / 5.437
              = 784.7 J/kg·K  -->  785 J/kg·K
```

### Weighted Average Conductivity (Volume-Weighted)

```
k_composite = Sum(V_frac_i x k_i)

Material conductivities:
  Steel:  50.0 W/m·K   (carbon steel)
  Foam:   0.038 W/m·K  (polyurethane foam, typical)
  Fabric: 0.06 W/m·K   (commercial textile)
  MDF:    0.12 W/m·K   (MDF, across board)

Steel:   0.02290 x 50.0  = 1.145
Foam:    0.89970 x 0.038 = 0.034
Fabric:  0.06070 x 0.06  = 0.004
MDF:     0.01660 x 0.12  = 0.002

k_composite = 1.145 + 0.034 + 0.004 + 0.002
            = 1.185 W/m·K  -->  1.19 W/m·K
```

> Steel at 2.29% of total volume contributes 1.145 W/m·K — 96.6% of composite conductivity, despite representing less than 2.3% of total volume. This is the same phenomenon seen in the auditorium seating composite: steel's conductivity (50.0 W/m·K) is over 1,300× that of foam (0.038 W/m·K), so even trace volumetric fractions dominate the conductivity result. The religious building audience seating composite (1.19 W/m·K) is slightly higher than the auditorium seating (0.966 W/m·K) because the stackable chair carries a higher steel-to-foam mass ratio, yielding a slightly larger steel volume fraction (2.29% vs. 1.85%), with corresponding conductivity increase.

### Effective Thickness

```
t_eff = Total mass per m² / (SA_ratio x composite density)
      = 5.437 / (1.17 x 255)
      = 5.437 / 298.35
      = 0.01822 m  ~  0.018 m  (18 mm)
```

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = rho x c_p
    = 255 x 785
    = 200,175 J/m³·K
```

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Foam-Dominated but Steel-Framed — Intermediate Composite Profile:**
- Moderate-low composite density (255 kg/m³) — driven by foam volume dominance (90% of composite volume at 35 kg/m³); higher than the performing arts auditorium (219 kg/m³) because the stackable chair carries proportionally more steel frame mass per unit of foam volume than the deep-cushioned fixed theater seat
- Moderate SA ratio (1.17 m²/m²) — the stackable chair generates approximately 1.022 m² per unit; at 1.10 seats/m², this yields 1.124 m²/m² from chairs alone; the folding tables add a small increment; the result is substantially below the performing arts auditorium (2.11 m²/m²) because the fixed theater seat's folding mechanism, side panels, and steel pedestals contribute significant additional SA not present in the simpler stackable chair geometry
- Moderate specific heat (785 J/kg·K) — the steel-heavy composition (70% of mass at 460 J/kg·K) depresses the composite specific heat compared to the auditorium (859 J/kg·K); the religious building chair's higher steel-to-foam mass ratio (5.3:1) vs. the theater seat's (3.0:1) increases the low-cp steel fraction, pulling the composite cp downward
- Moderate conductivity (1.19 W/m·K) — the highest of any seating-category space type; the slightly elevated steel volume fraction (2.29% vs. 1.85% for the auditorium) is enough to increase composite conductivity by 23%; the steel frame tube-and-channel construction of stackable chairs concentrates more metal per unit foam volume than the theater seat's thin-wall pedestal design

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Moderate total thermal mass (5.44 kg/m²) — substantially lower than both the performing arts auditorium (15.36 kg/m²) and the primary worship space (13.17 kg/m²); the difference from the auditorium is driven by two factors: (1) lower SA ratio (1.17 vs. 2.11) and (2) lower mass per seat (4.50 kg vs. 9.00 kg); the auditorium seat is approximately twice as heavy due to its larger frame, denser foam cushioning, solid hardwood armrests, and spring mechanism
- Low thermal capacitance (200,175 J/m³·K) — the lowest among religious building space types; the foam-dominated composite stores very little energy per unit volume; the zone responds quickly to changes in zone air temperature
- The steel chair frames (including legs, crossbraces, and ganging brackets) are the primary convective exchange surfaces during pre-conditioning; their thin-wall geometry and direct air exposure allow rapid heat transfer between chair surface and room air
- The foam cushioning body, despite being volumetrically dominant, has very low conductivity (0.038 W/m·K); its interior reaches thermal equilibrium slowly with room air even though the room air temperature itself may recover quickly

### Design Appropriateness

**Religious Building Multipurpose Audience Seating — Reconfigurable-Chair Profile:**
- **Padded stackable chairs are the overwhelmingly dominant component** (96.1% of SA, 91.1% of mass) — this is appropriate; the space is defined by rows of portable padded chairs, with all other furnishings serving support roles
- **The stackable chair is less thermally massive per seat than a fixed theater seat** (4.50 kg vs. 9.00 kg) — the theater seat carries solid hardwood armrests (1.30 kg), a spring-loaded folding mechanism with hinge brackets (included in 4.50 kg steel frame), and substantially more foam cushioning (1.50 kg vs. 0.61 kg); the stackable chair sacrifices mass for storability and reconfigurability
- **No aisle handrails** — unlike the performing arts auditorium with fixed sloped handrails (0.618 kg/m²) and row end aisle standards (1.246 kg/m²), the religious building multipurpose audience room uses portable chairs only; there are no permanent installed steel railing elements in the seating zone; this eliminates a significant steel mass component
- **Folding tables are thermally minor** (0.042 m²/m² SA, 0.347 kg/m² mass) but introduce MDF to the composite material mix; the MDF tabletop at 700 kg/m³ and 1,700 J/kg·K has favorable thermal properties but is simply too small in quantity to influence the composite meaningfully; it contributes 4.5% of mass and 1.66% of volume

### Comparison to Related Seating Space Types

| Parameter | Religious Bldg Audience Seating | Auditorium Audience Seating | Worship/Pulpit/Choir |
|-----------|--------------------------------|-----------------------------|--------------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 1.17 | 2.11 | 0.88 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 5.44 | 15.36 | 13.17 |
| Density (kg/m³) | 255 | 219 | 721 |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | 1.19 | 0.966 | 0.251 |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 785 | 859 | 1,568 |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 200,175 | 188,121 | 1,130,528 |
| Dominant volume material | PU foam (stackable chairs) | PU foam (fixed theater seats) | Solid hardwood (pews) |
| Seats/m² | 1.10 | 1.50 | ~0.55 (pew linear density) |

> All three space types have foam or wood as the volume-dominant material, but with very different thermal consequences. The religious building audience seating and auditorium are both foam-dominated (both ~90% of volume), so their densities and thermal capacitances are similar — but the auditorium achieves 2.8× the total mass per floor area through higher seating density (1.50 vs. 1.10 seats/m²), a seat that is twice as heavy (9.0 vs. 4.5 kg), and fixed steel handrails and row end standards not present in the reconfigurable chair arrangement. The worship/choir space, by contrast, uses solid hardwood pews that dominate by mass and raise both density (721 kg/m³) and specific heat (1,568 J/kg·K) dramatically; despite its very low SA ratio (0.88 m²/m²) from the compact pew slab geometry, it stores 2.4× the thermal energy per unit floor area as the religious building audience seating zone. Conductivity follows the metal fraction: the audience seating types (steel-framed chairs) have 4.7× and 3.8× higher conductivity than the pew-seated worship space.

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- The religious building audience seating room shares the intermittent occupancy pattern of the primary sanctuary but with added schedule variability — events may span multiple evenings per week (bible study, rehearsals, visiting speakers) with unpredictable timing
- At peak occupancy (330 persons in 300 m² = 1.10 p/m²), internal metabolic gains are significant: 330 × ~115 W/person (mixed activity, some standing) = 38 kW total in 300 m²; this dominates all other internal gains
- The low total thermal mass (5.44 kg/m²) means the seating zone has minimal flywheel effect; zone temperature responds quickly to both occupancy-driven heat gains and HVAC setback; pre-conditioning the audience room requires less lead time than a pew-seated sanctuary (which carries 2.4× the thermal mass)
- The room's lower ceiling height (5.0 m reference vs. 9.0 m for sanctuary) reduces thermal stratification; HVAC supply can be designed for full-room mixing more readily than in the high-vaulted nave

**Operational Patterns:**
- Highly variable weekly schedule — may be used for overflow Sunday services, Wednesday evening classes, special events, or community gatherings; HVAC scheduling logic must accommodate irregular events
- Night and weekday setback is practical given the low base occupancy; the low thermal mass of the padded chair arrangement means the space recovers from setback to comfort temperature relatively quickly (30–60 minutes vs. 2–4 hours for pew-seated sanctuary)
- Chair-storage configuration — when chairs are stacked on dollies and removed from the room for a different event layout, the internal thermal mass of the zone drops to near zero; modeling assumptions should reflect the expected configuration for the dominant use case

**Special Considerations:**
- **Reconfigurability**: unlike fixed theater seats or permanent pews, the padded stackable chairs can be stored, rearranged, or partially deployed; the InternalMass definition represents the room in full audience-seating configuration; if the room is frequently used in other configurations (banquet, reception, empty), a schedule-based internal mass fraction or separate thermal zone may be warranted
- **Chair stacking impact**: when chairs are stacked 8–10 high on dollies in a corner of the room or adjacent storage, their effective surface area is dramatically reduced; chairs in the stacking configuration exchange heat primarily through their bottom surfaces and partial side exposure rather than the full 1.022 m² per chair calculated for the deployed configuration
- **Contemporary megachurch teaching auditoriums** with fixed theater-style padded seats (not stackable chairs) would have a thermal mass profile closer to the Auditorium space type; the Religious Building Audience Seating definition applies to the multipurpose/fellowship-hall configuration; a fixed-seat contemporary worship auditorium should reference the Auditorium space type instead
- **Sound and acoustic treatment**: fellowship halls and multipurpose rooms in religious buildings often include portable acoustic panels or fabric-wrapped wall panels; if present in significant quantities, these panels would add surface area and fabric/foam mass; they are excluded here as non-standard furnishings

---

*End of Calculation Report*

# Internal Mass Calculations: CS Audience Seating Area - Sports Arena

**Report Date:** April 9, 2026
**Scope:** Audience Seating Area – Sports Arena Space Type
**Purpose:** Calculate OpenStudio InternalMass properties for thermal modeling

---

## CS Audience Seating Area - Sports Arena

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 500–20,000+ spectators (event-driven; near-zero between events)
**Floor Area:** 200–5,000+ m² (seating bowl sections, excluding playing area and concourse); reference area: **400 m²**
**Ceiling Height:** 10–30 m (large clear-span volume shared with the arena floor; the seating zone is embedded within the open arena air mass, with no independent ceiling at seat level)
**Function:** Fixed and fold-down spectator seating in a sports arena — professional or collegiate basketball, hockey, indoor soccer, arena football, wrestling, martial arts, and multi-event configurations. The seating zone encompasses the fixed-seat seating deck section: the fold-down plastic stadium seats, the concrete or steel riser structure (excluded as building structure), the in-section aisle handrails, and the guardrail barriers at the section perimeter and cross-aisles. The playing area floor, ice rink (if applicable), locker rooms, concourses, luxury suites, and press areas are separate zones. The reference configuration models a single lower-bowl section of a mid-size professional or Division I collegiate sports arena.

**Key Features:**
- Fold-down injection-molded polypropylene (PP) stadium seats (dominant element)
- Spring-loaded return mechanism (steel hinge and torsion spring per seat)
- Steel mounting bracket and channel (anchors each seat to the concrete riser)
- In-aisle steel pipe handrails running the full rake length of each aisle
- Steel section barrier guardrails at cross-aisles and section perimeter (top/front)
- Steel vertical posts supporting the barrier rails
- Concrete riser structure (excluded — building structure, not internal mass)
- Cup holders (integrated into PP seat body or armrest — negligible independent mass)
- Row and seat number placards (aluminum, negligible)
- Digital signage panels (perimeter — excluded; not thermally coupled to seating zone)

### Reference Configuration

**400 m² sports arena lower-bowl seating section:**
- 800 fold-down PP stadium seats
- Seating density: 2.0 seats/m² (including aisle area)
- Row pitch: 0.76 m (front-to-front)
- Seat width: 0.46 m (center-to-center); seat body: 0.42 m
- ~30 rows × ~27 seats per row average (variable — curved rows wider in center, narrower at ends)
- 5 longitudinal aisles; aisle width: 1.20 m
- 3 cross-aisle/barrier locations: bottom section guardrail, mid-section cross-aisle (at approximately row 15), and top section guardrail
- Barrier width: 12.4 m (spans full section width); post spacing: 2.0 m → 6 posts per barrier
- Aisle rake handrail length: 9.0 m per rail (accounts for sloped riser run length)

---

## Component Inventory

### 1. Fold-Down Polypropylene Stadium Seats (800 per 400 m²)

**Injection-Molded PP Stadium Seat (spring-loaded folding, hard plastic shell, no upholstery):**
- Seat body width: 0.42 m (within mounting brackets); center-to-center spacing: 0.46 m
- Row pitch: 0.76 m (front-to-front)
- Seat pan depth (deployed): 0.38 m
- Seat back height above pan pivot: 0.50 m
- Shell wall thickness: approximately 4 mm nominal; internal structural ribs add effective material volume
- Pivot and hinge height from riser surface: approximately 0.05 m (low-profile stanchion below seat pan)
- Construction: injection-molded high-impact polypropylene body (seat pan + back formed as two hinged shells with internal rib reinforcing); steel C-channel mounting bracket (anchored to riser nosing, 2 brackets per seat); steel torsion spring and pivot hinge (returns seat to upright when vacated)

**Surface Area per Seat:**

*Seat Pan (folding — both faces exposed to room air):*
- Top face (seating surface): 0.42 × 0.38 = 0.160 m²
- Bottom face (exposed when seat folded upright): 0.42 × 0.38 = 0.160 m²
- Perimeter edge (shell edge, ~25 mm thick): 2 × (0.42 + 0.38) × 0.025 = **0.040 m²**
- **Seat Pan SA: 0.360 m²**

*Seat Back (both faces exposed to room air):*
- Front face (sitting surface): 0.42 × 0.50 = 0.210 m²
- Rear face (back of shell): 0.42 × 0.50 = 0.210 m²
- Top edge: 0.42 × 0.025 = 0.011 m²
- Side edges (2): 2 × 0.50 × 0.025 = 0.025 m²
- **Seat Back SA: 0.456 m²**

*Steel Mounting Bracket (2 per seat, C-channel section):*
- Bracket footprint: 0.08 m × 0.04 m section, 0.10 m long; three exposed faces per bracket
- Approximate exposed SA: 2 × (0.08 × 0.10 + 0.04 × 0.10 + 0.08 × 0.04) / 2 = **0.030 m²** (both brackets combined; partially shielded by riser nosing)

**Total SA per Seat: 0.360 + 0.456 + 0.030 = 0.846 m²**

**Mass per Seat:**
- PP body (seat pan + back shells with rib reinforcing): 2.7 kg
- Steel mounting bracket (2 per seat, C-channel): 0.3 kg
- Steel spring/pivot hinge mechanism: 0.2 kg
- **Total Mass per Seat: 2.7 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 3.2 kg**

**Per Floor Area (800 seats in 400 m²):**
- Surface Area: (800 × 0.846) / 400 = 676.8 / 400 = **1.692 m²/m²**
- Mass: (800 × 3.2) / 400 = 2,560 / 400 = **6.400 kg/m²**

---

### 2. In-Aisle Handrails (10 rails per 400 m²)

**Sloped Aisle Handrails (round hollow steel pipe, runs full rake length of each aisle):**
- Configuration: 5 longitudinal aisles × 2 rails per aisle = 10 rails
- Effective rail length: 9.0 m (accounts for sloped riser run length)
- Outer diameter: 0.038 m (1½-inch nominal pipe); wall thickness: 3.7 mm (Schedule 40)
- Finish: galvanized or powder-coated steel

**Surface Area per Rail:**
- Lateral surface: π × 0.038 × 9.0 = 1.074 m²
- End caps (2): 2 × π × 0.019² = 0.002 m²
- **Total SA per Rail: 1.076 m²**

**Mass per Rail:**
- Schedule 40, 1½-inch pipe: 2.73 kg/m (standard; consistent with wall geometry at this nominal size)
- Mass: 2.73 × 9.0 = **24.6 kg**

**Per Floor Area (10 rails in 400 m²):**
- Surface Area: (10 × 1.076) / 400 = 10.76 / 400 = **0.027 m²/m²**
- Mass: (10 × 24.6) / 400 = 246.0 / 400 = **0.615 kg/m²**

---

### 3. Section Barrier Guardrails (3 barrier locations per 400 m²)

**Horizontal Barrier Rails and Vertical Posts (steel, at section bottom, mid-section cross-aisle, and section top):**
- Barrier locations: 3 (bottom guardrail at section front, cross-aisle at row ~15, top guardrail)
- Section width: 12.4 m per barrier
- Configuration: 2 horizontal round pipe rails per barrier (top rail and mid-height rail) + vertical square tube posts at 2.0 m spacing

**Horizontal Barrier Rails (6 rails total: 2 per barrier × 3 barriers, each 12.4 m long):**
- Pipe specification: 1½-inch nominal (OD 0.038 m), Schedule 40
- SA per rail: π × 0.038 × 12.4 + end caps ≈ 1.480 + 0.002 = 1.482 m²
- Mass per rail: 2.73 × 12.4 = 33.85 kg
- 6 rails total: SA = 6 × 1.482 = 8.892 m²; Mass = 6 × 33.85 = 203.1 kg

**Vertical Posts (18 total: 6 per barrier × 3 barriers):**
- Square hollow section: 0.040 m × 0.040 m outer, 3 mm wall
- Post height: 1.07 m (42-inch code minimum)
- Steel cross-section area: 0.040² − 0.034² = 1.600 × 10⁻³ − 1.156 × 10⁻³ = 4.44 × 10⁻⁴ m²
- SA per post: 4 × 0.040 × 1.07 = 0.171 m²
- Mass per post: 4.44 × 10⁻⁴ × 1.07 × 7,800 = 3.71 kg
- 18 posts total: SA = 18 × 0.171 = 3.078 m²; Mass = 18 × 3.71 = 66.78 kg

**Per Floor Area (3 barriers in 400 m²):**
- Surface Area: (8.892 + 3.078) / 400 = 11.970 / 400 = **0.030 m²/m²**
- Mass: (203.1 + 66.78) / 400 = 269.9 / 400 = **0.675 kg/m²**

---

## Component Summary Table

| Component | Qty / 400 m² | SA / Unit (m²) | Mass / Unit (kg) | SA / m² Floor | Mass / m² Floor | Primary Material |
|-----------|-------------|----------------|------------------|---------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Fold-down PP stadium seats | 800 | 0.846 | 3.20 | 1.692 | 6.400 | Polypropylene / Steel |
| Aisle handrails | 10 rails | 1.076 | 24.6 | 0.027 | 0.615 | Steel |
| Section barrier rails + posts | 3 barriers | 3.990 (avg) | 89.97 (avg) | 0.030 | 0.675 | Steel |
| **TOTALS** | — | — | — | **1.749** | **7.690** | — |

**Rounded Values:**
- **Surface Area per Floor Area: 1.75 m²/m²** (rounded from 1.749)
- **Total Thermal Mass: 7.69 kg/m²**

---

## Material Property Calculations

### Mass-Weighted Composite Properties

**Material Breakdown by Mass:**

*Polypropylene (seat pan bodies, seat back shells, internal rib reinforcing):*
- PP per seat: 2.7 kg × 800 / 400 = **5.400 kg/m²** (70.2%)

*Steel (seat mounting brackets, hinge/spring mechanisms, aisle handrails, barrier rails, barrier posts):*
- Seat brackets + springs: (0.3 + 0.2) × 800 / 400 = 1.000 kg/m²
- Aisle handrails: 0.615 kg/m²
- Barrier rails and posts: 0.675 kg/m²
- **Total steel: 2.290 kg/m²** (29.8%)

**Total: 5.400 + 2.290 = 7.690 kg/m²** ✓

### Volume Fractions (for Conductivity Weighting)

```
V_i = mass_i / density_i  [m³ per m² of floor area]

Polypropylene:  5.400 / 950   = 0.005684 m³/m²
Steel:          2.290 / 7,800 = 0.000294 m³/m²

V_total = 0.005684 + 0.000294 = 0.005978 m³/m²

Volume fractions:
  Polypropylene: 0.005684 / 0.005978 = 95.1%
  Steel:         0.000294 / 0.005978 =  4.9%
```

> Polypropylene occupies 95.1% of composite volume, despite contributing only 70.2% of composite mass. Steel contributes 29.8% of mass while occupying only 4.9% of volume. This is the defining characteristic of molded plastic stadium seating: the PP shell, at ~950 kg/m³, sets the volumetric character of the composite, while the steel mounting brackets and guardrail system contribute disproportionate mass through their dense but compact cross-sections.

### Weighted Average Density (True)

```
ρ_true = Total mass / Total volume
       = 7.690 / 0.005978
       = 1,286.7 kg/m³  →  1,287 kg/m³
```

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Σ(m_i × c_p,i) / Σ(m_i)

Material properties:
  Polypropylene:  1,800 J/kg·K
  Steel:            460 J/kg·K

Polypropylene:  5.400 × 1,800 = 9,720
Steel:          2.290 ×   460 = 1,053

c_p,composite = (9,720 + 1,053) / 7.690
              = 10,773 / 7.690
              = 1,401.0 J/kg·K  →  1,401 J/kg·K
```

### Weighted Average Conductivity (Volume-Weighted)

```
k_composite = Σ(V_frac_i × k_i)

Material conductivities:
  Polypropylene:  0.22 W/m·K
  Steel:         50.0 W/m·K

Polypropylene:  0.951 × 0.22 = 0.209
Steel:          0.049 × 50.0 = 2.450

k_composite = 0.209 + 2.450
            = 2.659 W/m·K  →  2.66 W/m·K
```

> Steel at 4.9% of total volume contributes 2.45 W/m·K — 92.1% of composite conductivity. Polypropylene at 95.1% of volume contributes only 0.21 W/m·K. The steel brackets, handrail pipes, and barrier posts function as concentrated thermal conductors embedded in the large PP seat shell volume, producing a composite conductivity (2.66 W/m·K) that is 12× the conductivity of PP alone but far below the conductivity of steel. This is not a EnergyPlus upper-bound issue — 2.66 W/m·K is well within normal material property ranges.

### True Effective Thickness

```
t_true = Total mass per m² / (SA_ratio × true density)
       = 7.690 / (1.75 × 1,287)
       = 7.690 / 2,252.25
       = 0.003414 m  ≈  3.4 mm
```

> The true effective thickness of 3.4 mm reflects the thin-shell geometry of the stadium seat: the PP and steel assembly is volumetrically compact — a hollow plastic shell and small-diameter pipe elements — with very little interior void volume. EnergyPlus applies a practical minimum slab thickness of 10 mm for numerical stability of surface convection calculations. Accordingly, density is adjusted to maintain mass equivalence at the 10 mm minimum thickness.

### EnergyPlus Thickness Adjustment

```
t_min    = 0.010 m (10 mm minimum, consistent with thin-shell seating types)

ρ_adj    = Total mass / (SA_ratio × t_min)
         = 7.690 / (1.75 × 0.010)
         = 7.690 / 0.01750
         = 439.4 kg/m³  →  440 kg/m³
```

> The adjusted density (440 kg/m³) is a modeling artifact required to preserve mass equivalence at the 10 mm minimum slab thickness — it does not represent a physical material property. The true composite density is 1,287 kg/m³. Specific heat and conductivity are unchanged.

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = ρ_adj × c_p
    = 440 × 1,401
    = 616,440 J/m³·K
```

---

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Plastic Shell-Dominated Space — Moderate Composite Density, Low Total Mass:**
- Moderate true composite density (1,287 kg/m³, adjusted to 440 kg/m³ for modeling) — PP shells at 950 kg/m³ are denser than organic building materials (wood ~700, foam ~35) but far below metals; the true composite density lies between a wood-framed space and a light concrete surface
- Moderate SA ratio (1.75 m²/m²) — the fold-down stadium seat produces a respectable SA ratio from its dual-face geometry (both seat pan faces and both seat back faces are exposed to room air when the seat is folded upright); however, the absence of armrests, side panels, and pedestal elements that appear in auditorium theater seats limits the per-seat SA to 0.846 m² vs. 1.347 m² for an upholstered theater seat; the higher seat density (2.0 vs. 1.5 seats/m²) partially compensates
- High specific heat (1,401 J/kg·K) — polypropylene has a substantially higher specific heat (1,800 J/kg·K) than steel (460 J/kg·K); with PP dominating at 70.2% of mass, the composite specific heat is pulled well above the steel value; this is the highest specific heat of any audience seating space type, reflecting the high c_p of thermoplastics
- Moderate conductivity (2.66 W/m·K) — steel's small volume fraction (4.9%) nonetheless contributes 2.45 W/m·K to the composite conductivity; the overall value is 12× higher than the auditorium's foam-dominated composite (0.966 W/m·K) but far below the aluminum bleacher types (188.6 W/m·K true); no EnergyPlus conductivity capping is needed

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Low total thermal mass (7.69 kg/m²) — the lowest of the fixed-seat audience seating types; the PP shell seat stores substantially less heat per seat than an upholstered theater seat (3.2 kg vs. 9.0 kg); even at the higher seat density of the sports arena, the total mass per floor area is only 50% of the auditorium
- Moderate thermal capacitance (616,440 J/m³·K, adjusted) — higher than the auditorium (188,121 J/m³·K) because the mass-weighted c_p (1,401 J/kg·K) substantially exceeds steel's 460 J/kg·K; the PP body raises the effective heat capacity of each seat despite the absence of foam
- The steel aisle handrails and barrier posts equilibrate with zone air rapidly due to their high conductivity and small thermal mass; they function as direct convective exchange surfaces during pre-event conditioning and setback recovery, similar to their role in other steel-rail seating types
- The PP seat shell responds more slowly to air temperature changes than a steel or aluminum bleacher element but faster than a foam-upholstered auditorium seat; the dominant time constant for seat temperature change is intermediate between the bleacher (seconds to minutes) and the upholstered theater seat (minutes to tens of minutes)

### Design Appropriateness

**Sports Arena Audience Seating — Distinguishing Thermal Profile:**
- **Fold-down PP stadium seats are the overwhelmingly dominant component** (88.2% of mass, 96.7% of SA) — the seating zone is essentially a monoculture of a single seat type; the seat selection (injection-molded PP vs. aluminum bleacher vs. upholstered theater seat) determines the composite thermal character more than any other design decision
- **The PP shell is the defining material** — sports arena seats are designed for durability under millions of cycles, UV exposure in daylight venues, easy cleaning, and low lifecycle cost; the polypropylene shell used in professional-grade arena seats has a nominal density of 950 kg/m³ and a specific heat of ~1,800 J/kg·K, giving it 3.9× the specific heat of steel per unit mass; this is the primary reason the sports arena specific heat (1,401 J/kg·K) exceeds all other audience seating types in this series
- **In-section barrier rails are significant despite their modest SA ratio** (0.030 m²/m²) — the three barrier locations at a 400 m² seating section total 269.9 kg of steel, contributing 0.675 kg/m² of thermal mass and 8.8% of total section mass; in contrast to the auditorium's aesthetic row end standards, the arena barriers are robust safety guardrails with structural posts, making them heavier per linear meter than auditorium aisle standards
- **Aisle handrails match auditorium performance** (0.615 kg/m² vs. 0.618 kg/m² in the auditorium) — the shorter rake length (9 m vs. 12 m per auditorium rail) is offset by the greater number of aisles (10 rails vs. 8 rails); the direct air-exposure of these smooth steel pipes makes them effective convective exchange surfaces in the aisle airflow during pre-event conditioning

### Comparison to Related Audience Seating Space Types

| Parameter | Sports Arena | Auditorium | Gymnasium | Exercise Center |
|-----------|-------------|------------|-----------|-----------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 1.75 | 2.11 | 0.71 | 1.03 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 7.69 | 15.36 | 2.71 | 3.42 |
| EnergyPlus Density (kg/m³) | 440 (adj.) | 219 | 382 (adj.) | 332 (adj.) |
| True Density (kg/m³) | 1,287 | 219 | ~2,700 | ~2,700 |
| Conductivity (W/m·K) | 2.66 | 0.966 | 50.0 (adj.) | 50.0 (adj.) |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 1,401 | 859 | 851 | 863 |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 616,440 | 188,121 | 325,082 | 286,516 |
| Dominant volume material | Polypropylene | PU foam | Aluminum | Aluminum |
| Seat type | Fold-down PP shell | Fixed upholstered | Aluminum plank | Aluminum plank |
| Seats/m² | 2.0 | 1.5 | 0.80 | ~1.25 |
| Thickness adjustment | Yes (10 mm) | No (33 mm true) | Yes (10 mm) | Yes (10 mm) |

> The sports arena occupies a distinctive middle position among audience seating types. Its SA ratio (1.75 m²/m²) and total mass (7.69 kg/m²) are intermediate — higher than the gymnasium and exercise center bleachers (aluminum plank systems with low seat density) but substantially lower than the auditorium (upholstered seats with foam dominance). The most striking differentiator is the specific heat: sports arena PP seats yield the highest composite c_p (1,401 J/kg·K) of any audience seating type — reflecting the thermoplastic seat material's high intrinsic specific heat — even though the total thermal mass per floor area is only 50% of the auditorium. The aluminum bleacher types (gymnasium, exercise center) have far higher true densities (~2,700 kg/m³) but require conductivity capping at 50 W/m·K for EnergyPlus stability; the sports arena's 2.66 W/m·K requires no adjustment and represents the physical composite behavior accurately.

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- Sports arenas operate on an extreme bimodal occupancy schedule: full capacity (800+ persons in a 400 m² section, ~2.0 p/m²) during events versus near-zero occupancy between events; the HVAC must recover from setback to event-comfort conditions within a 1–2 hour pre-event conditioning window
- High sensible and latent loads during events from dense occupancy: 800 persons × ~75 W sensible + ~55 W latent (sports event spectators, active engagement) = 60 kW sensible + 44 kW latent per 400 m² section; these transient gains dominate over internal mass thermal storage effects during the event
- The PP seat shell's moderate thermal response (intermediate between aluminum bleacher and upholstered theater seat) means seat surface temperatures track zone air temperature more closely than auditorium foam seats but less instantaneously than aluminum bleachers; the pre-event pre-conditioning period must condition both the zone air mass and the seat shells to provide comfort on arrival
- Under-seat or under-riser supply air is common in modern arena lower-bowl configurations; displacement ventilation at seat level pre-conditions the seating zone efficiently and conditions the PP seat surfaces from below, which is thermally significant given the two-face exposure of the folded seat pan

**Operational Patterns:**
- Event schedule: 40–80 events per season for professional venues; collegiate venues may add intramural and recreational use; the event frequency is higher than performing arts venues
- Pre-event conditioning: 1.5–2 hours before tip-off/puck-drop to recover from overnight setback and condition the seating zone; the lower total thermal mass of the PP seating (vs. upholstered auditorium seating) means the seating zone itself requires less pre-conditioning energy than the auditorium, but the large arena air volume creates the dominant pre-conditioning load
- Event duration: 2.5–3.5 hours (professional basketball, hockey) with halftime/intermission breaks; audience may briefly exit the seating zone at breaks but the zone remains conditioned
- Post-event: seating zone can transition to setback within 30–60 minutes of clearance, faster than the auditorium because the lower total thermal mass reduces the time required to dissipate the metabolic heat absorbed during the event

**Special Considerations:**
- **Ice hockey arenas** that include spectator seating in the same thermal model as the ice surface require special handling: the ice surface (extremely high thermal mass, below-freezing surface temperatures) creates radiant and convective interactions with the seating zone that are not captured by the standard InternalMass approach; in practice, the ice and seating zones should be modeled as separate thermal zones with defined surface boundary conditions
- **Premium seating levels** (club seats, suite-adjacent seating) in modern arenas may use padded or upholstered fold-down seats rather than hard PP shells; these would more closely resemble the auditorium seat profile (higher mass, lower density); the PP stadium seat definition is most appropriate for the standard lower-bowl and upper-bowl seating categories
- **Retractable and telescoping bleacher sections** within arena seating bowls (used to expand floor area for concerts or conventions) are best modeled using the Gymnasium or Exercise Center bleacher definitions rather than this sports arena definition, as the aluminum plank construction differs substantially from the fixed PP stadium seat
- **Occupied vs. unoccupied modes**: at full spectator capacity, patron clothing and bodies replace much of the seat surface as the effective zone thermal exchange boundary; EnergyPlus handles this through the People object; the unoccupied internal mass definition represents the seating zone in setback or pre-event conditioning mode, when the full 1.75 m²/m² seat surface area is exposed to the conditioned zone air

---

*End of Calculation Report*

# Internal Mass Calculations: CS Audience Seating Area - Transportation Facility

**Report Date:** April 9, 2026
**Scope:** Audience Seating Area – Transportation Facility Space Type
**Purpose:** Calculate OpenStudio InternalMass properties for thermal modeling

---

## CS Audience Seating Area - Transportation Facility

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 20–300 travelers (event-driven by departures/arrivals; continuous low occupancy between peaks)
**Floor Area:** 100–800 m² (gate seating areas, terminal waiting zones, and concourse seating pockets); reference area: **250 m²**
**Ceiling Height:** 4–12 m (varies widely — low in concourse stub gates, high in main terminal halls)
**Function:** Fixed and semi-fixed audience seating in airport terminals, rail stations, ferry terminals, and bus depots. The space is bounded by the seating area footprint: rows of ganged modular chairs on common support beams, organized in back-to-back or perimeter configurations around gate podiums and concourse nodes. Unlike performing arts or sports venues, the space is occupied continuously throughout operating hours at varying densities, with sharp occupancy peaks during boarding events and very low occupancy during off-peak hours. Charging stations, overhead monitors, and wayfinding kiosks are co-located in the zone but contribute negligible thermal mass relative to the seating structure. The reference configuration models a mid-size domestic gate seating area.

**Key Features:**
- Ganged modular seating units (groups of 3 seats on a shared structural beam — the overwhelmingly dominant thermal mass element)
- Mix of upholstered fabric/vinyl seats (foam-cushioned) and molded polypropylene seats (hard-shell)
- Steel cantilever arm brackets connecting each seat to the central support beam
- Steel central support beam (RHS section) spanning each multi-seat module
- Steel leg posts and floor-anchored base plates
- Polypropylene armrest caps (shared between adjacent seats; integral on plastic seats)
- Integrated USB/AC charging station housings mounted to seat frames (negligible thermal mass)
- Overhead departure display monitors (ceiling-mounted, not internal mass)

### Reference Configuration

**250 m² domestic gate seating area:**
- 150 ganged seats total in 50 three-seat modules
  - 105 upholstered fabric/vinyl seats (70%) in 35 modules
  - 45 molded polypropylene hard-shell seats (30%) in 15 modules
- Seat spacing: 0.52 m center-to-center
- Row pitch: 0.90 m (back-to-back pairs) or 0.80 m (single-sided perimeter rows)
- Seating density: 0.60 seats/m² (lower than performing arts venues; wide spacing to accommodate carry-on luggage beside seats)
- Module beam span: 1.60 m (3 seats × 0.52 m + end extensions)
- Aisle width: 1.20 m (ADA-compliant)

**Commercial Transportation Ganged Seat — Upholstered (fabric or vinyl over foam, cantilever-mounted):**

## Material Property Calculations

### Mass-Weighted Composite Properties

**Material Breakdown by Mass:**

*Steel (cantilever arm brackets, central support beams, leg posts, base plates, hardware):*
- Cantilever arms: 1.854 × 150 / 250 = **1.112 kg/m²**
- Beam/leg/base modules: 1.818 kg/m² (all steel by component)
- Upholstered seat hardware: 0.25 × 105 / 250 = 0.105 kg/m²
- Plastic seat hardware: 0.25 × 45 / 250 = 0.045 kg/m²
- **Total steel: 1.112 + 1.818 + 0.105 + 0.045 = 3.080 kg/m²** (73.5%)

*Polypropylene (hard-shell seat pans and backs; upholstered seat armrest caps):*
- Plastic seat shells: (1.576 + 1.748) × 45 / 250 = 0.598 kg/m²
- PP armrest caps (upholstered seats): 0.30 × 105 / 250 = 0.126 kg/m²
- **Total PP: 0.598 + 0.126 = 0.724 kg/m²** (17.3%)

*Fabric/vinyl upholstery (upholstered seats):*
- 0.50 × 105 / 250 = **0.210 kg/m²** (5.0%)

*Polyurethane foam (upholstered seat cushioning only):*
- (0.218 + 0.201) × 105 / 250 = **0.176 kg/m²** (4.2%)

**Total: 3.080 + 0.724 + 0.210 + 0.176 = 4.190 kg/m²** ✓

### Volume Fractions (for Conductivity Weighting)

```
V_i = mass_i / density_i  [m³ per m² of floor area]

Steel:          3.080 / 7,800  = 0.000395 m³/m²
Polypropylene:  0.724 /   950  = 0.000762 m³/m²
Fabric/vinyl:   0.210 /   550  = 0.000382 m³/m²
PU foam:        0.176 /    35  = 0.005029 m³/m²

V_total = 0.000395 + 0.000762 + 0.000382 + 0.005029 = 0.006568 m³/m²

Volume fractions:
  Steel:          0.000395 / 0.006568 = 6.01%
  Polypropylene:  0.000762 / 0.006568 = 11.60%
  Fabric/vinyl:   0.000382 / 0.006568 = 5.82%
  PU foam:        0.005029 / 0.006568 = 76.57%
```

> PU foam occupies 76.6% of composite volume despite contributing only 4.2% of composite mass. This is qualitatively consistent with auditorium and convention center seating but at a lower foam volume fraction than the auditorium (91.5%): transportation seating uses thinner cushioning (30 mm seat / 25 mm back versus 50 mm / 40 mm in auditorium), and 30% of seats are foam-free molded plastic, reducing the aggregate foam volume. The polypropylene plastic shell seats contribute 11.6% of volume at a moderate density (950 kg/m³) — a meaningful departure from the auditorium's all-foam-and-steel composite. Steel occupies 6.0% of volume (more than three times the auditorium's 1.85%), reflecting the heavier ganged-beam structural system compared to individual-seat slender pedestals.

### Weighted Average Density

```
ρ_composite = Total mass / Total volume
            = 4.190 / 0.006568
            = 637.9 kg/m³  →  638 kg/m³
```

> The moderate composite density (638 kg/m³) is much higher than the auditorium (219 kg/m³) because foam volume dominance is substantially reduced. The polypropylene shell seats and the heavy steel beam structure together raise the volume-averaged density well above what a purely foam-cushioned assembly would produce. The result is comparable to the convention center stacking chair (636 kg/m³), which is also a steel-frame/hard-seat assembly with minimal foam volume.

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Σ(m_i × c_p,i) / Σ(m_i)

Material properties:
  Steel:          460 J/kg·K   (carbon/mild steel)
  Polypropylene:  1,050 J/kg·K (injection-molded PP)
  Fabric/vinyl:   1,340 J/kg·K (commercial upholstery textile/vinyl)
  PU foam:        1,700 J/kg·K (polyurethane foam, semi-open cell)

Steel:          3.080 × 460   = 1,416.8
Polypropylene:  0.724 × 1,050 =   760.2
Fabric/vinyl:   0.210 × 1,340 =   281.4
PU foam:        0.176 × 1,700 =   299.2

c_p,composite = (1,416.8 + 760.2 + 281.4 + 299.2) / 4.190
              = 2,757.6 / 4.190
              = 658.1 J/kg·K  →  658 J/kg·K
```

### Weighted Average Conductivity (Volume-Weighted)

```
k_composite = Σ(V_frac_i × k_i)

Material conductivities:
  Steel:          50.0  W/m·K   (carbon/mild steel)
  Polypropylene:  0.20  W/m·K   (molded PP)
  Fabric/vinyl:   0.06  W/m·K   (upholstery textile/vinyl)
  PU foam:        0.038 W/m·K   (polyurethane foam)

Steel:          0.0601 × 50.0  = 3.005
Polypropylene:  0.1160 × 0.20  = 0.023
Fabric/vinyl:   0.0582 × 0.06  = 0.003
PU foam:        0.7657 × 0.038 = 0.029

k_composite = 3.005 + 0.023 + 0.003 + 0.029
            = 3.06 W/m·K
```

> Steel at 6.0% of total volume contributes 3.005 W/m·K — 98.2% of composite conductivity. The higher steel volume fraction in transportation seating (6.0%) compared to auditorium seating (1.85%) reflects the structural architecture: ganged beam assemblies use heavy structural members (RHS beams, SHS posts, base plates) that distribute load across many seats, resulting in more steel volume per seat than the slender individual pedestal columns in theater seating. The practical result is a composite conductivity (3.06 W/m·K) more than three times that of the auditorium (0.966 W/m·K), similar to the convention center stacking chair assembly (3.73 W/m·K).

### Effective Thickness

```
t_eff = Total mass per m² / (SA_ratio × composite density)
      = 4.190 / (0.66 × 638)
      = 4.190 / 421.1
      = 0.00995 m  ≈  0.0100 m  (10 mm)
```

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = ρ × c_p
    = 638 × 658
    = 419,804 J/m³·K
```

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Steel-Frame-Dominated Space — Moderate Composite Density, Low SA Ratio:**
- Lowest SA ratio of any audience seating category (0.66 m²/m²) — driven by the combination of low seating density (0.60 seats/m²) and non-folding seat geometry; without the folding seat mechanism that exposes both pan faces to room air, and without the extended decorative side panels of performing arts seating, the per-seat surface area (0.974 m²/seat) is lower than theater seats (1.347 m²/seat) despite similar overall dimensions; the sparse layout compounds this
- Lowest total thermal mass of any audience seating category (4.19 kg/m²) — a direct consequence of the low seating density; 0.60 seats/m² at ~7 kg/seat yields approximately 4.2 kg/m² from seating alone; unlike performing arts or sports venues, no secondary components (aisle handrails, row end standards, bleacher framing) add meaningful mass
- Moderate composite density (638 kg/m³) — substantially higher than the auditorium (219 kg/m³) because foam volume is reduced on two fronts: thinner cushioning (30/25 mm vs. 50/40 mm) and 30% of seats are foam-free plastic shells; the heavy steel beam framing raises the steel volume fraction to 6.0%, well above the auditorium's 1.85%
- Moderate-high conductivity (3.06 W/m·K) — the steel-volume-fraction effect on conductivity is disproportionate; at 6.0% volume, steel contributes 3.005 W/m·K of the 3.06 total; this is consistent with the convention center stacking chair assembly (3.73 W/m·K at similar steel fraction) and physically reflects the heavy ganged-beam structural members present in all transit seating systems

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Moderate volumetric heat storage (419,804 J/m³·K) — higher than the auditorium (188,121) because the reduced foam volume and addition of polypropylene raise both density and composite cp relative to a pure foam-and-steel assembly; moderate compared to pew or planter-heavy seating spaces
- Low total thermal mass per floor area (4.19 kg/m²) means the zone responds quickly to occupancy and HVAC changes — the seating contributes less thermal flywheel effect than any other audience seating type; the zone air temperature is more strongly governed by ventilation and occupant loads than by stored heat in the seat mass
- The molded polypropylene hard-shell seats (30% of seats by count, 17% of mass) provide direct convective exchange surfaces with the zone air at their exposed polymer surfaces — smooth PP has lower surface emissivity variation than fabric, making the radiative component of heat exchange slightly more predictable than fabric-covered assemblies
- The steel beam/leg/base system (43.4% of total mass at 1.818 kg/m²) represents a relatively high base-level steel mass contribution from structure alone; in auditorium seating, the structural elements (pedestals + handrails) contribute approximately 10.4 kg/m² — proportionally far more — but the transportation beam system is a larger fraction of a much smaller total mass

### Design Appropriateness

**Transportation Facility Seating — Sparse, Structurally Efficient:**
- **Low seating density is the defining characteristic** (0.60 seats/m² versus 1.50 in performing arts and 1.0+ in convention center): airport and transit seating allocates generous space per traveler to accommodate carry-on luggage stored beside or below seats, wheelchair adjacency, and frequent, non-synchronized occupant movement; the wide pitch directly suppresses both the SA ratio and the total mass per floor area
- **The ganged beam module is the dominant structural component**: unlike performing arts seating where the individual seat pedestal carries its own load, transportation ganged seating transfers all seat loads to a single structural beam serving 3–6 seats; this beam-leg-base assembly (9.09 kg per 3-seat module, 1.82 kg/m²) is heavier per seat than theater pedestals but serves multiple seats simultaneously, and its structural members are exposed steel surfaces that exchange heat directly with zone air
- **The seat type mix (70% upholstered / 30% plastic) is characteristic of US domestic terminals circa 2021**: premium gates and international terminals trend toward fully upholstered seats with padded armrests; budget and regional gates retain molded plastic; the 70/30 split represents a mid-tier configuration; a 100% upholstered configuration would slightly lower the SA ratio (foams and fabrics replace some exposed PP shell area) and reduce composite density toward ~500–550 kg/m³
- **No aisle handrails or row end standards** are included in this space type — unlike a raked auditorium, transportation seating is installed on flat floors without continuous longitudinal handrails; any queuing barriers or retractable stanchions are mobile and not modeled as internal mass

### Comparison to Related Seating Space Types

| Parameter | Transportation Facility | Convention Center | Auditorium | Gymnasium (Bleachers) |
|-----------|------------------------|-------------------|------------|----------------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 0.66 | 1.05 | 2.11 | 0.71 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 4.19 | 5.58 | 15.36 | 2.71 |
| Density (kg/m³) | 638 | 636 | 219 | 382* |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | 3.06 | 3.73 | 0.966 | 50.0* |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 658 | 562 | 859 | 851 |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 419,804 | 357,432 | 188,121 | 324,882* |
| Dominant volume material | PU foam (76.6%) | PU foam (similar) | PU foam (91.5%) | Aluminum |
| Seats/m² | 0.60 | ~1.0 (stacked) | 1.50 (fixed) | 0.80 (bleacher) |

*Gymnasium bleacher values are density- and conductivity-adjusted due to minimum thickness constraint in EnergyPlus.

> The transportation facility occupies the lowest positions for both SA ratio (0.66 m²/m²) and total thermal mass (4.19 kg/m²) among audience seating types, reflecting its uniquely low seating density. Its composite density (638 kg/m³) and conductivity (3.06 W/m·K) closely match the convention center (636 kg/m³; 3.73 W/m·K) because both are ganged steel-frame assemblies with limited foam volume — the architectural similarity of "heavy beam carrying multiple seats" creates nearly identical composite material signatures despite very different use patterns. The auditorium's extreme foam-volume dominance (91.5%) produces an anomalously low density (219 kg/m³) and conductivity (0.966 W/m·K) that transportation and convention center seating cannot approach. The gymnasium bleacher is a pure-aluminum structure with fundamentally different thermal behavior.

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- With a total thermal mass of only 4.19 kg/m² and SA ratio of 0.66, the internal mass contributes minimal thermal buffering — less than any other audience seating type; the zone's thermal response is driven primarily by ventilation, occupant sensible loads, and envelope gains rather than by stored heat in the seating
- Transportation seating zones operate under continuous occupancy throughout terminal operating hours (typically 05:00–24:00), with sharp occupancy peaks aligned to departure banks; the peak-to-trough ratio is lower than performing arts venues but the zone never reaches true setback; the internal mass thermal flywheel effect is consequently less important than in intermittent-use auditoriums or gyms
- The higher conductivity (3.06 W/m·K) relative to auditorium seating means the equivalent internal mass slab exchanges heat with zone air more readily per unit surface area; combined with the low SA ratio (0.66 m²/m²), the net convective conductance of the internal mass assembly is modest but not negligible during temperature recovery after overnight shutdown or weekend setback

**Operational Patterns:**
- Operating schedule: continuous during terminal hours; overnight setback at hub airports is uncommon (24-hour operations), but regional airports may setback between last arrival and first departure (~3–6 hours)
- Occupancy peaks: aligned to departure banks at gates — typically 80–90% of seats filled 30–60 minutes before scheduled departure, then near-zero after boarding; this creates brief, high-intensity heat and moisture loads followed by rapid vacating
- Unoccupied periods: in multi-gate concourses, sections of seating may remain at very low occupancy for extended periods between banks; the seating mass re-equilibrates with zone air during these intervals

**Special Considerations:**
- **Seat mix variability**: the 70% upholstered / 30% plastic split should be adjusted for specific terminal types; airports undergoing modernization or premium repositioning may be 100% upholstered; budget or regional terminals may approach 60–80% plastic; adjusting the split would modestly change density (range approximately 550–700 kg/m³) and conductivity (range approximately 2.5–3.5 W/m·K)
- **Charging station thermal mass**: USB and AC power charging stations integrated into seat armrests or mounted to seat frames consist of small plastic housings (typically <1 kg per station); at a density of ~0.3 stations per seat, their contribution is under 0.05 kg/m² and is appropriately excluded from the internal mass object
- **Queuing barrier systems**: retractable stanchion systems used to organize boarding queues are mobile and should not be modeled as internal mass; fixed gate podiums (desks, counters, equipment housings) are present in the seating zone but should be accounted for under separate internal mass or equipment objects if materially significant
- **Single-zone vs. multi-gate modeling**: in OpenStudio models where multiple gate seating areas are aggregated into a single zone (common in concourse-level models), the internal mass definition `AudienceSeating_Transportation_IntMass` can be applied with a total surface area proportional to the combined floor area of all aggregated gate seating sections

# Internal Mass Calculations: CS Audience Seating Area - Other

**Report Date:** April 9, 2026
**Scope:** Audience Seating Area – Other Space Type
**Purpose:** Calculate OpenStudio InternalMass properties for thermal modeling

---

## CS Audience Seating Area - Other

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 50–500 attendees (event-driven; near-zero between events)
**Floor Area:** 100–1,000 m² (flat or nominally raked floor; general assembly configuration); reference area: **300 m²**
**Ceiling Height:** 3.5–7.0 m (flat or coffered ceiling; moderate volume relative to floor area)
**Function:** Audience seating in multipurpose or general-assembly spaces not captured by the specific building-type classifications (Auditorium, Convention Center, Exercise Center, Gymnasium, Motion Picture Theater, Penitentiary, Performing Arts Theater, Religious Building, Sports Arena, or Transportation Facility). Representative occupancy types include community center assembly rooms, civic hall meeting spaces, hotel ballrooms or banquet halls configured in theater-style seating for presentations or award programs, corporate or institutional auditoriums, university lecture halls outside the classroom category, club or association meeting rooms, and exhibition spaces used intermittently for seated presentations. These spaces share a defining characteristic: seating is portable and temporarily arranged rather than fixed; the furniture inventory between events may differ from the event-day configuration. The reference configuration models a mid-size multipurpose assembly room in a community or civic facility, arranged in theater-style rows for an audience of 300.

**Key Features:**
- Portable padded folding chairs deployed in theater-style rows (the dominant element)
- Tubular steel frame (folding-leg mechanism) with padded seat and back cushions
- Gang/row connecting clips (steel brackets linking adjacent chairs within each row)
- Portable rolling lectern or podium at front of seating zone
- Flat floor (no rake, no fixed seating deck structure)
- No fixed aisle handrails (flat-floor assembly does not require continuous railing at seat level)
- Temporary floor-mounted power strips and AV cabling (negligible thermal mass)
- Stacked surplus chairs stored at room perimeter or in adjacent storage room (not modeled — stored chairs are outside the conditioned zone or enclosed in a storage mass object)

### Reference Configuration

**300 m² multipurpose assembly room in theater-style seating:**
- 300 portable padded folding chairs
- Seating density: 1.0 chairs/m² (accounting for aisle widths and perimeter clearance)
- Row pitch: 0.95 m (front-to-front); seat center-to-center: 0.48 m
- ~30 rows; ~10 chairs per row average
- 2 longitudinal aisles (1.00 m wide) + perimeter aisle (1.00 m wide)
- Gang clips: 1 clip per chair (300 clips total) linking chairs within each row
- Portable rolling lectern: 1 per 300 m² at front of seating zone

## Component Inventory

### 1. Portable Padded Folding Chairs (300 per 300 m²)

**Commercial Padded Folding Chair (steel frame, padded seat and back, vinyl upholstery):**
- Seat pad width: 0.44 m; seat pad depth: 0.41 m
- Back pad width: 0.44 m; back pad height: 0.42 m
- Seat height (floor to top of seat pad): 0.44 m
- Back top height from floor: 0.44 + 0.42 = 0.86 m
- Frame: round steel tube, 19 mm OD, 1.2 mm wall — folding-leg configuration with 2 front legs and 2 folding rear legs
- Seat foam: 25 mm polyurethane foam pad, 30 kg/m³
- Back foam: 20 mm polyurethane foam pad, 30 kg/m³
- Upholstery: vinyl-coated polyester fabric (both faces of seat and back pads)
- Glides or rubber foot caps on all four leg ends

**Surface Area per Chair:**

*Seat Pad (both faces exposed to room air when unoccupied):*
- Top face (upholstered): 0.44 × 0.41 = 0.180 m²
- Bottom face (exposed): 0.44 × 0.41 = 0.180 m²
- Perimeter edge (foam thickness 30 mm): 2 × (0.44 + 0.41) × 0.030 = 2 × 0.85 × 0.030 = 0.051 m²
- **Seat Pad SA: 0.411 m²**

*Back Pad (both faces exposed to room air when unoccupied):*
- Front face (upholstered): 0.44 × 0.42 = 0.185 m²
- Rear face (upholstered): 0.44 × 0.42 = 0.185 m²
- Perimeter edge (foam thickness 25 mm): 2 × (0.44 + 0.42) × 0.025 = 2 × 0.86 × 0.025 = 0.043 m²
- **Back Pad SA: 0.413 m²**

*Steel Frame (legs, cross-braces, back bar, hardware):*
- Front legs (2 legs, 19 mm OD, 0.72 m exposed above floor): 2 × π × 0.019 × 0.72 = **0.086 m²**
- Rear legs (2 legs, 19 mm OD, 0.82 m deployed): 2 × π × 0.019 × 0.82 = **0.098 m²**
- Seat cross-braces (2 horizontal tubes, 0.44 m span): 2 × π × 0.019 × 0.44 = **0.053 m²**
- Back vertical support bar (1 tube, 0.42 m): π × 0.019 × 0.42 = **0.025 m²**
- Pivot/hinge mechanism and seat mounting hardware (simplified): **0.015 m²**
- **Frame SA: 0.277 m²**

**Total SA per Chair: 0.411 + 0.413 + 0.277 = 1.101 m²**

**Mass per Chair:**

*Steel frame:*
- Tube cross-section area: π × (0.0095² − 0.0083²) = π × (9.025 − 6.889) × 10⁻⁵ = 6.71 × 10⁻⁵ m²
- Front legs (2 × 0.72 m): 2 × 0.72 × 6.71×10⁻⁵ × 7,850 = **0.760 kg**
- Rear legs (2 × 0.82 m): 2 × 0.82 × 6.71×10⁻⁵ × 7,850 = **0.866 kg**
- Cross-braces (2 × 0.44 m): 2 × 0.44 × 6.71×10⁻⁵ × 7,850 = **0.465 kg**
- Back bar (1 × 0.42 m): 0.42 × 6.71×10⁻⁵ × 7,850 = **0.222 kg**
- Pivot hardware, glides, seat brackets: **0.190 kg**
- **Steel total per chair: 2.503 kg → use 2.5 kg**

*Polyurethane foam:*
- Seat pad: 0.44 × 0.41 × 0.025 × 30 = **0.135 kg**
- Back pad: 0.44 × 0.42 × 0.020 × 30 = **0.111 kg**
- **Foam total per chair: 0.246 kg**

*Vinyl-coated polyester fabric upholstery (areal density ~0.50 kg/m²):*
- Seat faces (top + bottom): 2 × 0.180 = 0.360 m² → 0.360 × 0.50 = **0.180 kg**
- Back faces (front + rear): 2 × 0.185 = 0.370 m² → 0.370 × 0.50 = **0.185 kg**
- Edge wrapping (50% coverage of perimeter area): 0.50 × (0.051 + 0.043) × 0.50 = **0.024 kg**
- **Vinyl total per chair: 0.389 kg → use 0.39 kg**

**Total Mass per Chair: 2.50 + 0.246 + 0.39 = 3.136 kg → use 3.14 kg**

**Per Floor Area (300 chairs in 300 m²):**
- Surface Area: (300 × 1.101) / 300 = 330.3 / 300 = **1.101 m²/m²**
- Mass: (300 × 3.14) / 300 = 942.0 / 300 = **3.140 kg/m²**

**Steel Chair Gang Clips (1 clip per chair, deployed with each row):**
- Function: small stamped steel bracket hooks onto adjacent chair frames to keep rows straight and prevent individual chairs from drifting during occupancy
- Dimensions: 0.10 m long × 0.04 m wide × 0.025 m tall (approximate bounding box)
- Construction: 3 mm stamped steel with powder-coat finish; approximately 50% solid fraction within bounding box

**Surface Area per Clip:**
- Long faces (2): 2 × (0.10 × 0.025) = 0.005 m²
- Wide faces (2): 2 × (0.10 × 0.04) = 0.008 m²
- End faces (2): 2 × (0.04 × 0.025) = 0.002 m²
- **Total SA per Clip: 0.015 m²** (effective exposed, accounting for hook geometry)

**Mass per Clip:**
- Approximate volume (50% solid fraction): 0.10 × 0.04 × 0.025 × 0.50 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ m³
- Mass: 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 7,850 = **0.039 kg → use 0.04 kg**

**Per Floor Area (300 clips in 300 m²):**
- Surface Area: (300 × 0.015) / 300 = **0.015 m²/m²**
- Mass: (300 × 0.04) / 300 = **0.040 kg/m²**

## Material Property Calculations

### Mass-Weighted Composite Properties

**Material Breakdown by Mass:**

*Steel (chair frames, folding hardware, gang clips):*
- Chair frames: 2.50 × 300 / 300 = 2.500 kg/m²
- Gang clips: 0.040 kg/m²
- **Total steel: 2.540 kg/m²** (77.8%)

*Polyurethane foam (seat and back pads):*
- 0.246 × 300 / 300 = **0.246 kg/m²** (7.5%)

*Vinyl-coated polyester fabric (upholstery):*
- 0.390 × 300 / 300 = **0.390 kg/m²** (11.9%)

*MDF/plywood (lectern panels):*
- **0.083 kg/m²** (2.5%)

**Verification: 2.540 + 0.246 + 0.390 + 0.083 = 3.259 kg/m² ≈ 3.26 kg/m² ✓**

---

### Volume Fractions (for Conductivity Weighting)

```
V_i = mass_i / density_i  [m³ per m² of floor area]

Steel (carbon):     2.540 / 7,800  = 3.256 × 10⁻⁴ m³/m²
Foam (PU, 30 kg/m³):  0.246 /    30  = 8.200 × 10⁻³ m³/m²
Vinyl fabric:       0.390 / 1,300  = 3.000 × 10⁻⁴ m³/m²
MDF/plywood:        0.083 /   700  = 1.186 × 10⁻⁴ m³/m²

V_total = 3.256×10⁻⁴ + 8.200×10⁻³ + 3.000×10⁻⁴ + 1.186×10⁻⁴
        = 0.0003256 + 0.008200 + 0.0003000 + 0.0001186
        = 8.944 × 10⁻³ m³/m²

Volume fractions:
  Steel:        3.256×10⁻⁴ / 8.944×10⁻³ = 3.64%
  Foam:         8.200×10⁻³ / 8.944×10⁻³ = 91.68%
  Vinyl fabric: 3.000×10⁻⁴ / 8.944×10⁻³ = 3.35%
  MDF/plywood:  1.186×10⁻⁴ / 8.944×10⁻³ = 1.33%
```

> Polyurethane foam at 30 kg/m³ occupies 91.7% of composite volume — nearly identical to the auditorium's foam volume dominance (91.5%) — despite containing only 7.5% of composite mass. The folding chair's 25 mm seat and 20 mm back pads, though substantially thinner than a fixed theater seat's 50 mm and 40 mm pads, still govern composite volume because of foam's extreme low density. Steel at 3.64% of volume represents nearly double the auditorium's 1.85% steel volume fraction, reflecting the folding chair's relatively longer, unshielded steel frame legs compared to the short hollow pedestals of a fixed theater seat.

---

### Weighted Average Density

```
ρ_composite = Total mass / Total volume
            = 3.259 / 8.944×10⁻³
            = 364.4 kg/m³  →  364 kg/m³
```

> The composite density (364 kg/m³) is intermediate between the foam-dominated fixed auditorium seat (219 kg/m³) and the sled-frame stacking convention center chair (636 kg/m³). The folding chair's foam pads are thinner than a fixed theater seat's — reducing the absolute foam volume per chair — but the shorter frame height reduces steel volume as well. The net result is a foam volume fraction nearly equal to the auditorium, but with a higher steel mass fraction (77.8% vs 65.8%) that pushes density upward from the auditorium value.

---

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Σ(m_i × c_p,i) / Σ(m_i)

Material properties:
  Steel:         460 J/kg·K  (carbon steel)
  Foam:        1,700 J/kg·K  (polyurethane foam, open/semi-open cell)
  Vinyl fabric: 1,340 J/kg·K (vinyl-coated polyester, commercial grade)
  MDF/plywood:  1,700 J/kg·K (wood-based panel product)

Steel:        2.540 × 460   = 1,168.4
Foam:         0.246 × 1,700 =   418.2
Vinyl fabric: 0.390 × 1,340 =   522.6
MDF/plywood:  0.083 × 1,700 =   141.1

c_p,composite = (1,168.4 + 418.2 + 522.6 + 141.1) / 3.259
              = 2,250.3 / 3.259
              = 690.5 J/kg·K  →  691 J/kg·K
```

---

### Weighted Average Conductivity (Volume-Weighted)

```
k_composite = Σ(V_frac_i × k_i)

Material conductivities:
  Steel:        50.0 W/m·K  (carbon steel)
  Foam:          0.035 W/m·K (polyurethane foam)
  Vinyl fabric:  0.17 W/m·K  (vinyl-coated textile)
  MDF/plywood:   0.15 W/m·K  (medium-density fiberboard)

Steel:        0.0364 × 50.0  = 1.820
Foam:         0.9168 × 0.035 = 0.032
Vinyl fabric: 0.0335 × 0.17  = 0.006
MDF/plywood:  0.0133 × 0.15  = 0.002

k_composite ≈ 1.820 + 0.032 + 0.006 + 0.002
            ≈ 1.860 W/m·K  →  1.86 W/m·K
```

> Steel at 3.64% of volume contributes 1.820 W/m·K — 97.8% of composite conductivity. Although the steel volume fraction (3.64%) falls between the auditorium's 1.85% and the convention center's 7.39%, it produces a composite conductivity (1.86 W/m·K) nearly double the auditorium's (0.966 W/m·K) and about half the convention center's (3.73 W/m·K), consistent with the proportional steel volume ordering. The foam at 91.7% of volume contributes only 0.032 W/m·K, confirming that foam sets the thermal mass envelope while steel provides the conductive thermal bridge path through each chair's leg geometry.

---

### Effective Thickness

```
t_eff = Total mass per m² / (SA_ratio × composite density)
      = 3.259 / (1.13 × 364)
      = 3.259 / 411.3
      = 0.00792 m  ≈  0.0079 m  (7.9 mm)
```

---

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = ρ × c_p
    = 364 × 691
    = 251,524 J/m³·K
```

---
