## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Foam-Volume-Dominated Space — Low Total Mass, Intermediate Density:**
- Very low total thermal mass (3.26 kg/m²) — the second-lowest among all audience seating space types; driven by the combination of lightweight portable folding chairs (3.14 kg/chair) at moderate density (1.0 chair/m²) with minimal secondary components; this is less than 60% of the convention center seating zone (5.58 kg/m²) and 21% of the auditorium (15.36 kg/m²)
- Moderate SA ratio (1.13 m²/m²) — slightly above the convention center (1.05 m²/m²) and gymnasium (0.71 m²/m²) audience seating types; the folding chair's four independent exposed legs and two pad faces generate approximately 1.10 m² per chair, and at 1.0 chair/m² this produces a ratio comparable to lightweight seating spaces; the chair's folding geometry does not add enclosed cavity volume the way a fixed theater seat's hollow pedestal does
- Intermediate composite density (364 kg/m³) — falls between the foam-dominant auditorium (219 kg/m³) and the sled-frame convention center chair (636 kg/m³); the folding chair's thinner foam pads reduce absolute foam volume per floor area compared to the auditorium, allowing steel's higher density to pull the composite toward 364 kg/m³
- Moderate-low specific heat (691 J/kg·K) — steel's 77.8% mass dominance pulls the composite toward its 460 J/kg·K value; vinyl (11.9% of mass, 1,340 J/kg·K) and foam (7.5% of mass, 1,700 J/kg·K) provide upward moderation; the result is intermediate between the auditorium (859 J/kg·K, more foam and hardwood by mass fraction) and the convention center (562 J/kg·K, even greater steel mass dominance at 90.6%)
- Intermediate conductivity (1.86 W/m·K) — steel at 3.64% of volume (nearly double the auditorium's 1.85%) contributes 1.820 W/m·K, producing a composite conductivity approximately double the auditorium's (0.966 W/m·K) and half the convention center's (3.73 W/m·K); the folding chair's exposed straight-tube legs provide somewhat longer uninterrupted steel thermal bridge paths than the short hollow pedestal stubs of fixed theater seats

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Moderate-low thermal capacitance per unit volume (251,524 J/m³·K) — between the auditorium (188,121 J/m³·K) and the convention center (357,432 J/m³·K); the higher density relative to the auditorium partially offsets the lower specific heat, yielding a volumetric heat storage capacity modestly above the foam-dominated auditorium
- Very low absolute thermal storage per floor area (3.26 kg/m² × 691 J/kg·K = 2,253 J/m²·K) — the lowest thermal energy storage contribution of any audience seating type; a 5°C excursion in zone temperature is absorbed or released by approximately 11,265 J/m² of floor area, compared to approximately 52,000 J/m² for the auditorium
- The zone responds rapidly to changes in HVAC supply conditions; low total mass combined with direct-exposure steel frame legs means the folding chair assembly equilibrates to zone air temperature faster than fixed upholstered theater seats, which have thick foam cushioning acting as a radial insulating buffer around each steel pedestal
- Gang clips, while contributing negligible SA and mass at the zone level (0.015 m²/m²; 0.040 kg/m²), are fully exposed steel with no foam buffering; they equilibrate to zone air temperature rapidly and are the most thermally active individual elements in the inventory

---

### Design Appropriateness

**Multipurpose "Other" Audience Seating — Lightest Furnished Thermal Profile:**
- **Portable padded folding chairs are the appropriate archetype** for this catch-all category — they represent the common denominator across the broadest range of non-specialized audience seating contexts; fixed theater seats, pew-style benches, bleacher systems, and molded plastic stadium seats are all captured by their respective specific building-type categories; what remains is the general multipurpose space served by the most ubiquitous portable chair type in North American commercial and civic facilities
- **The "Other" category thermal mass is notably light** — 3.26 kg/m² is low even among audience seating types; this reflects the stripped-down, utilitarian character of general-purpose assembly seating: thin foam pads, minimal armrest mass, no fixed pedestals, no continuous aisle handrails; the space thermal mass budget is almost entirely determined by the steel tube frame, which despite being structurally necessary contributes thermal mass only through its thin-wall cross-sections
- **No continuous aisle handrails** — unlike the auditorium (8 sloped handrails totaling 247 kg per 400 m²; 0.618 kg/m²) and performing arts theater, the flat-floor "Other" space has no regulatory requirement for continuous aisle handrails at seat level; the absence of this component, which contributes meaningful SA and steel mass in raked venues, further depresses the "Other" composite relative to fixed-seat auditorium types
- **The portable lectern is a minor contributor** (0.009 m²/m², 0.083 kg/m²; 2.5% of zone mass) but is included as a realistic inventory element present in virtually all "Other" audience seating configurations for presentations, lectures, and general assemblies; its MDF/plywood construction provides a small wood-like component in an otherwise steel/foam/vinyl dominated inventory

---

### Comparison to Related Audience Seating Space Types

| Parameter | Other (This Report) | Convention Center | Auditorium |
|-----------|-------------------|-------------------|------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 1.13 | 1.05 | 2.11 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 3.26 | 5.58 | 15.36 |
| Density (kg/m³) | 364 | 636 | 219 |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | 1.86 | 3.73 | 0.966 |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 691 | 562 | 859 |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 251,524 | 357,432 | 188,121 |
| Dominant volume material | PU foam | PU foam | PU foam |
| Dominant mass material | Steel (77.8%) | Steel (90.6%) | Steel (65.8%) |
| Chair/seat density (/m²) | 1.0 (folding) | 1.0 (stacking) | 1.5 (fixed) |
| Chair mass (kg/chair) | 3.14 | 5.50 | 9.00 |

> All three foam-dominant audience seating types have similar foam volume fractions (~90%), yet differ substantially in total thermal mass — entirely because the per-chair steel frame weight and seating density diverge. The auditorium's fixed theater seat (9.0 kg, 1.5/m²) is nearly three times the mass of the folding chair (3.14 kg, 1.0/m²) and more than five times the total mass per floor area. The convention center's stacking chair (5.50 kg, 1.0/m²) is intermediate; its sled-base frame runs continuous steel uprights to full back height (0.87 m), adding frame mass relative to the folding chair's shorter leg runs. The "Other" folding chair is the lightest design of the three: no continuously welded back-upright-to-seat-rail sled geometry, no armrests, no fixed pedestals, and no spring hardware. The consequence for HVAC modeling is that the "Other" seating zone has negligible thermal flywheel effect — it neither absorbs nor delays zone temperature response meaningfully. Pre-conditioning loads for the "Other" space type are driven almost entirely by envelope and ventilation, not by internal mass heat storage.

---

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- Multipurpose "Other" audience seating spaces typically operate at lower density than dedicated performing arts venues; a community center assembly room may achieve 60–80% of chair count as actual occupants, compared to sold-out auditorium events at near-100% occupancy; HVAC design should use actual occupancy schedules rather than peak chair-count density
- The very low thermal mass (3.26 kg/m²) means the zone air temperature tracks supply air conditions closely; pre-conditioning times are short (15–30 minutes is typically sufficient for a small multipurpose room); setback recovery is rapid compared to auditorium or performing arts theater types
- High conductivity relative to mass (1.86 W/m·K at only 3.26 kg/m²) means the thin equivalent slab exchanges heat with zone air relatively efficiently; in EnergyPlus simulation, the internal mass object will equilibrate to zone temperature quickly due to both low heat capacity and adequate surface conductance
- Flat-floor assembly spaces often use mixed HVAC strategies (ceiling supply diffusers, perimeter baseboard in older civic buildings, or fan coil units); supply air delivery directly to the occupied zone at ceiling level means the folding chair thermal mass is not in the direct supply air stream in the way that under-seat displacement ventilation at auditoriums is; convective exchange coefficients at the internal mass surfaces follow standard EnergyPlus assumptions for still-air conditions

**Operational Patterns:**
- Event schedule: variable but often daytime — community meetings, lectures, presentation events, awards programs; setback periods during nights and weekends
- Setup and teardown time: folding chairs are typically deployed 30–60 minutes before events and struck immediately after; during chair storage, the room thermal mass is reduced to envelope and structural elements only; this variability may justify separate thermal zone definitions for event-configuration vs. cleared-configuration scenarios in high-fidelity models
- Occupancy duration: 1–3 hours typical for community/civic assembly events; shorter than performing arts events, with less latent load accumulation per event
- Between-event clearing: folding chairs are often stacked at room perimeter or rolled to adjacent storage; the "event day" internal mass definition should be used for peak-load design; non-event periods with chairs stored should reference a reduced-mass definition if scheduling accuracy is required

**Special Considerations:**
- **Chair storage configuration**: folding chairs stored in stacks at the room perimeter are not in free-air contact the same way deployed chairs are; stacked chairs have contact between adjacent surfaces and reduced convective exchange; if a significant fraction of the chair inventory is stored within the conditioned space rather than adjacent storage rooms, a small adjustment to the SA ratio may be warranted for the non-event operating mode; the 1.13 m²/m² applies to the event-day deployed configuration only
- **Hybrid configurations**: some "Other" spaces are configured with a mix of folding chairs (main floor) and fixed tablet-arm or ganged chairs at the rear or sides; in such cases the SA ratio and composite material properties should be recalculated as a weighted blend of the folding-chair and ganged-chair inventories; the `AudienceSeating_Other_IntMass` definition represents the pure folding-chair scenario most representative of the general category
- **Hotel ballroom applications**: hotel ballrooms used for audience-seating events typically use the same padded folding chair type modeled here, at similar density (0.9–1.1/m²); however, ballrooms also contain permanent interior architectural elements — decorative wall panels, built-in millwork, heavy window treatments — that are not captured in the seating-zone internal mass definition and should be modeled as separate internal mass objects or surface constructions
- **Category applicability**: the `AudienceSeating_Other_IntMass` definition is appropriate for any audience seating context not better served by one of the ten specific venue-type definitions; if the actual seating type is known to be significantly different from portable padded folding chairs (e.g., fixed molded plastic shell seats without upholstery, or ganged tablet-arm lecture chairs), the energy modeler should consider whether a more specific assembly more accurately represents the actual installation

---

*End of Calculation Report*

# Internal Mass Calculations: CS Atrium - Less than or equal to 40 ft

**Report Date:** April 7, 2026
**Scope:** Atrium - Less than or equal to 40 ft (≤12.2 m) Space Type
**Purpose:** Calculate OpenStudio InternalMass properties for thermal modeling

---

## CS Atrium - Less than or Equal to 40 ft

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** Non-occupiable atrium volume (occupied floors below are separate zones)
**Floor Area:** Reference area: footprint of the atrium volume
**Ceiling Height:** Up to 40 ft (≤12.2 m)
**Function:** Multi-story open interior volume — small hotel lobbies, two-story open office atriums, modest retail gathering spaces. The energy code classifies atriums by height because structural member size and quantity scale with span and height, directly affecting the internal thermal mass of the exposed structural elements.

**Key Features:**
- Light wood trusses or small steel beams (primary structural element exposed to the atrium volume)
- Minimal artificial lighting (atrium relies primarily on roof daylighting through horizontal fenestration)
- No interior furnishings or equipment — the atrium is an open, non-occupiable volume
- Exposed structural members are the sole thermal mass contributor

### Design Basis

**Structural assumption:** Light Douglas Fir trusses with limited supplemental steel beam support, typical of smaller atrium spans (≤12.2 m clear height). Exposed structural member surface area estimated at **0.31 m²/m²** of atrium floor area — substantially less than any occupied space type, reflecting the intentionally open, unencumbered character of an atrium.

This calculation is derived from the comprehensive atrium analysis documented in **Atrium_InternalMass_Complete_Report.md** (January 20, 2026). That report provides full component-level derivation; this document reformats the results to match the standard project calculation report format.

---

## Component Inventory

### 1. Light Wood Trusses (Douglas Fir)

**Structural Configuration:**
- Member type: Douglas Fir light wood trusses (bottom chord, web members partially visible from below)
- Exposed surface area: **0.25 m²/m²** floor area
- Effective member thickness: 100 mm (representative exposed dimension)

**Material Properties:**
- Density: 550 kg/m³
- Specific Heat: 1,600 J/kg·K
- Thermal Conductivity: 0.12 W/m·K

**Per Floor Area:**
```
Volume = 0.25 × 0.100 = 0.02500 m³/m²
Mass   = 0.02500 × 550 = 13.750 kg/m²
Thermal Capacitance = 13.750 × 1,600 = 22,000 J/K·m²
```

- **SA/Floor: 0.250 m²/m²**
- **Mass/Floor: 13.750 kg/m²**

---

### 2. Steel Beams (Supplemental Support)

**Structural Configuration:**
- Member type: Structural steel at connection points and supplemental support locations
- Exposed surface area: **0.05 m²/m²** floor area
- Effective member thickness: 25 mm (equivalent exposed dimension of wide-flange beam)

**Material Properties:**
- Density: 7,850 kg/m³
- Specific Heat: 460 J/kg·K
- Thermal Conductivity: 45.0 W/m·K

**Per Floor Area:**
```
Volume = 0.05 × 0.025 = 0.00125 m³/m²
Mass   = 0.00125 × 7,850 = 9.813 kg/m²
Thermal Capacitance = 9.813 × 460 = 4,514 J/K·m²
```

- **SA/Floor: 0.050 m²/m²**
- **Mass/Floor: 9.813 kg/m²**

---

### 3. Minimal Lighting Fixtures

**Configuration:**
- Suspended fixtures: very sparse (atrium relies on daylight)
- Exposed surface area: **0.01 m²/m²** floor area
- Effective thickness: 10 mm

**Material Properties (metal/glass composite):**
- Density: 2,500 kg/m³
- Specific Heat: 840 J/kg·K
- Thermal Conductivity: 1.0 W/m·K

**Per Floor Area:**
```
Volume = 0.01 × 0.010 = 0.00010 m³/m²
Mass   = 0.00010 × 2,500 = 0.250 kg/m²
Thermal Capacitance = 0.250 × 840 = 210 J/K·m²
```

- **SA/Floor: 0.010 m²/m²**
- **Mass/Floor: 0.250 kg/m²**

---

## Summary Table

| Component | SA/Floor (m²/m²) | Mass/Floor (kg/m²) | Thermal Cap. (J/K·m²) | % of Total |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------|----------------------|------------|
| Light wood trusses (Douglas Fir) | 0.250 | 13.750 | 22,000 | 82.3% |
| Steel beams (supplemental) | 0.050 | 9.813 | 4,514 | 16.9% |
| Minimal lighting fixtures | 0.010 | 0.250 | 210 | 0.8% |
| **TOTAL** | **0.310** | **23.813** | **26,724** | **100%** |

---

## Composite Property Calculations

### Effective Thickness

```
Total volume = (0.250 × 0.100) + (0.050 × 0.025) + (0.010 × 0.010)
             = 0.025000 + 0.001250 + 0.000100
             = 0.026350 m³/m²

t_eff = Total volume / SA ratio
      = 0.026350 / 0.310
      = 0.08500 m = 85.0 mm
```

### Composite Density

```
ρ_composite = Total mass / Total volume
            = 23.813 / 0.026350
            = 904 kg/m³
```

### Composite Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Total thermal capacitance / Total mass
              = 26,724 / 23.813
              = 1,122 J/kg·K
```

### Composite Thermal Conductivity

```
Mass-weighted average:

Wood:   (13.750 / 23.813) × 0.12 = 0.5774 × 0.12  = 0.069
Steel:  ( 9.813 / 23.813) × 45.0 = 0.4120 × 45.0  = 18.540
Glass: (  0.250 / 23.813) × 1.0  = 0.0105 × 1.0   = 0.011

k_mass-weighted = 0.069 + 18.540 + 0.011 = 18.620 W/m·K
```

> The mass-weighted conductivity is dominated by steel. For an InternalMass object representing primarily wood structural members, the volume-weighted approach is more physically appropriate for estimating heat exchange with room air:

```
k_volume-weighted:

Wood:   (0.025000 / 0.026350) × 0.12 = 0.9488 × 0.12 = 0.114
Steel:  (0.001250 / 0.026350) × 45.0 = 0.0474 × 45.0 = 2.134
Glass:  (0.000100 / 0.026350) × 1.0  = 0.0038 × 1.0  = 0.004

k_volume-weighted ≈ 0.114 + 2.134 + 0.004 = 2.252 W/m·K
```

> The prior comprehensive report used **2.56 W/m·K** (intermediate between mass- and volume-weighted approaches). This value is retained for consistency with the project's established atrium baseline.

### Thermal Capacitance Verification

```
C_v = ρ × c_p
    = 904 × 1,122
    = 1,014,288 J/m³·K

Total capacitance per m² floor = C_v × thickness × SA ratio
= 1,014,288 × 0.085 × 0.310 = 26,727 J/K·m²  ✓ (matches 26,724; <0.1% variance)
```

---

## OpenStudio InternalMass Properties

**OS:InternalMass:Definition**
- **Name:** `Atrium_LTE40ft_IntMass`
- **Surface Area per Space Floor Area:** `0.31` {dimensionless}
- **Surface Area per Person:** — {blank}

**OS:Material**
- **Name:** `Mixed_Atrium_LTE40ft_85mm`
- **Roughness:** `MediumRough`
- **Thickness:** `0.0850` {m}
- **Conductivity:** `2.56` {W/m-K}
- **Density:** `904` {kg/m³}
- **Specific Heat:** `1122` {J/kg-K}
- **Thermal Absorptance:** `0.90` {dimensionless}
- **Solar Absorptance:** `0.70` {dimensionless}
- **Visible Absorptance:** `0.70` {dimensionless}

**Verification:**
```
Thermal Mass = SA ratio × Thickness × Density
             = 0.31 × 0.0850 × 904
             = 23.81 kg/m²  ✓ (matches component total of 23.81 kg/m²)

Thermal Capacitance per m² floor = SA × t × ρ × cp
= 0.31 × 0.0850 × 904 × 1,122
= 26,714 J/K·m²  ✓ (matches 26,724; <0.1% variance)
```

**IDF Format:**
```idf
OS:Material,
  Mixed_Atrium_LTE40ft_85mm,             !- Name
  MediumRough,                           !- Roughness
  0.0850,                                !- Thickness {m}
  2.56,                                  !- Conductivity {W/m-K}
  904,                                   !- Density {kg/m3}
  1122,                                  !- Specific Heat {J/kg-K}
  0.90,                                  !- Thermal Absorptance
  0.70,                                  !- Solar Absorptance
  0.70;                                  !- Visible Absorptance

OS:Construction,
  Construction_AtriumLTE40ft,            !- Name
  ,                                      !- Surface Rendering Name
  Mixed_Atrium_LTE40ft_85mm;             !- Layer 1

OS:InternalMass:Definition,
  Atrium_LTE40ft_IntMass,                !- Name
  Construction_AtriumLTE40ft,            !- Construction Name
  0.31,                                  !- Surface Area per Space Floor Area {dimensionless}
  ;                                      !- Surface Area per Person {m2/person}
```

---

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Wood-Dominated Open Structural Volume:**
- Moderate composite density (904 kg/m³) — between Douglas Fir (550) and steel (7,850); steel beams are heavy but represent limited volume
- Very low SA ratio (0.31 m²/m²) — the lowest of any space type with exposed structural elements; atriums are by definition open volumes with minimal interior surfaces
- High specific heat (1,122 J/kg·K) — Douglas Fir at 1,600 J/kg·K dominates; the composite is elevated above steel's 460 J/kg·K baseline by the wood trusses
- Low conductivity (2.56 W/m·K) — wood trusses at 94.9% of total volume set a low conductivity baseline; steel beams add moderate uplift

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Total capacitance per m² floor: 26,724 J/K·m² — by far the lowest of any space type, reflecting the intentionally minimal internal mass of an open atrium
- The 85 mm effective thickness is among the largest in the dataset — a consequence of the low SA ratio (only 0.31 m²/m² to spread the mass across) combined with moderate density

### Comparison to CS Atrium - More than 40 ft

| Parameter | ≤40 ft | >40 ft |
|-----------|--------|--------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 0.31 | 0.36 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 23.81 | 41.27 |
| Density (kg/m³) | 904 | 886 |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | 2.56 | 3.01 |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 1,122 | 1,270 |
| Thermal Capacitance / floor (J/K·m²) | 26,724 | 52,426 |
| Primary structural member | Douglas Fir | Glulam |

The taller atrium requires nearly twice the thermal capacitance per floor area despite only 16% more exposed surface area — reflecting the much heavier structural members needed for larger spans.

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- Atrium volumes are notoriously difficult to model with single-zone assumptions — strong thermal stratification means floor-level temperatures may be 5–15°C lower than upper-level temperatures in tall atriums
- The internal mass of the structural members is modest; the dominant thermal behavior of the atrium zone is driven by the glazed roof/skylight solar gains and the envelope conduction, not by internal mass
- Night setback: atrium temperatures tend to equalize with outdoor temperatures overnight if nighttime ventilation is used; structural mass stores some daytime solar gain and releases it slowly overnight

**Operational Patterns:**
- Atrium zones are typically conditioned continuously during building operating hours
- Solar gain through roof glazing is the primary driver of atrium zone thermal behavior
- Occupied floors opening onto the atrium create complex inter-zone heat exchange

---

*End of Calculation Report*

# Internal Mass Calculations: CS Atrium - More than 40 ft

**Report Date:** April 7, 2026
**Scope:** Atrium - More than 40 ft (>12.2 m) Space Type
**Purpose:** Calculate OpenStudio InternalMass properties for thermal modeling

---

## CS Atrium - More than 40 ft

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** Non-occupiable atrium volume (occupied floors below are separate zones)
**Floor Area:** Reference area: footprint of the atrium volume
**Ceiling Height:** Greater than 40 ft (>12.2 m); typically 50–80 ft (15.2–24.4 m)
**Function:** Large multi-story open interior volume — major hotel lobbies, convention center atriums, large retail galleria, airport terminal interior volumes. Greater height requires heavier structural members for increased span and load, producing more thermal mass than the shorter atrium variant.

**Key Features:**
- Heavy glulam beams or substantial steel members (primary structural element)
- Larger, more numerous structural members required for greater spans
- Minimal artificial lighting (relies on daylighting through roof fenestration)
- No interior furnishings — open non-occupiable volume
- Greater visual exposure of structural elements due to taller clear height

### Design Basis

**Structural assumption:** Heavy glulam or equivalent heavy timber beams with supplemental structural steel, typical of large-span atrium construction (>12.2 m clear height). Exposed structural member surface area estimated at **0.36 m²/m²** of atrium floor area — slightly higher than the ≤40 ft case due to larger, more numerous beams required for greater spans.

This calculation is derived from the comprehensive atrium analysis documented in **Atrium_InternalMass_Complete_Report.md** (January 20, 2026). That report provides full component-level derivation; this document reformats the results to match the standard project calculation report format.

---

## Component Inventory

### 1. Heavy Glulam Beams (Primary Structure)

**Structural Configuration:**
- Member type: Glulam (glued laminated timber) or equivalent heavy timber; larger beams required for greater spans and greater visual exposure in tall atrium
- Exposed surface area: **0.30 m²/m²** floor area
- Effective member thickness: 150 mm (heavier members than ≤40 ft case)

**Material Properties:**
- Density: 650 kg/m³ (glulam — denser than standard dimensional lumber)
- Specific Heat: 1,600 J/kg·K
- Thermal Conductivity: 0.15 W/m·K

**Per Floor Area:**
```
Volume = 0.30 × 0.150 = 0.04500 m³/m²
Mass   = 0.04500 × 650 = 29.250 kg/m²
Thermal Capacitance = 29.250 × 1,600 = 46,800 J/K·m²
```

- **SA/Floor: 0.300 m²/m²**
- **Mass/Floor: 29.250 kg/m²**

---

### 2. Steel Support Elements

**Structural Configuration:**
- Member type: Structural steel connections, tension members, supplemental supports; larger than ≤40 ft case due to greater loads
- Exposed surface area: **0.05 m²/m²** floor area
- Effective member thickness: 30 mm (larger than the ≤40 ft steel elements)

**Material Properties:**
- Density: 7,850 kg/m³
- Specific Heat: 460 J/kg·K
- Thermal Conductivity: 45.0 W/m·K

**Per Floor Area:**
```
Volume = 0.05 × 0.030 = 0.00150 m³/m²
Mass   = 0.00150 × 7,850 = 11.775 kg/m²
Thermal Capacitance = 11.775 × 460 = 5,416 J/K·m²
```

- **SA/Floor: 0.050 m²/m²**
- **Mass/Floor: 11.775 kg/m²**

---

### 3. Minimal Lighting Fixtures

**Configuration:**
- Same as ≤40 ft atrium — sparse suspended fixtures; atrium relies on daylighting
- Exposed surface area: **0.01 m²/m²** floor area
- Effective thickness: 10 mm

**Material Properties (metal/glass composite):**
- Density: 2,500 kg/m³
- Specific Heat: 840 J/kg·K
- Thermal Conductivity: 1.0 W/m·K

**Per Floor Area:**
```
Volume = 0.01 × 0.010 = 0.00010 m³/m²
Mass   = 0.00010 × 2,500 = 0.250 kg/m²
Thermal Capacitance = 0.250 × 840 = 210 J/K·m²
```

- **SA/Floor: 0.010 m²/m²**
- **Mass/Floor: 0.250 kg/m²**

---

## Summary Table

| Component | SA/Floor (m²/m²) | Mass/Floor (kg/m²) | Thermal Cap. (J/K·m²) | % of Total |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------|----------------------|------------|
| Heavy glulam beams | 0.300 | 29.250 | 46,800 | 89.3% |
| Steel support elements | 0.050 | 11.775 | 5,416 | 10.3% |
| Minimal lighting fixtures | 0.010 | 0.250 | 210 | 0.4% |
| **TOTAL** | **0.360** | **41.275** | **52,426** | **100%** |

---

## Composite Property Calculations

### Effective Thickness

```
Total volume = (0.300 × 0.150) + (0.050 × 0.030) + (0.010 × 0.010)
             = 0.045000 + 0.001500 + 0.000100
             = 0.046600 m³/m²

t_eff = Total volume / SA ratio
      = 0.046600 / 0.360
      = 0.12944 m ≈ 129.4 mm
```

### Composite Density

```
ρ_composite = Total mass / Total volume
            = 41.275 / 0.046600
            = 886 kg/m³
```

### Composite Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Total thermal capacitance / Total mass
              = 52,426 / 41.275
              = 1,270 J/kg·K
```

### Composite Thermal Conductivity

```
Volume-weighted:

Glulam: (0.045000 / 0.046600) × 0.15 = 0.96567 × 0.15 = 0.145
Steel:  (0.001500 / 0.046600) × 45.0 = 0.03219 × 45.0 = 1.449
Glass:  (0.000100 / 0.046600) × 1.0  = 0.00215 × 1.0  = 0.002

k_volume-weighted ≈ 0.145 + 1.449 + 0.002 = 1.596 W/m·K
```

> As with the ≤40 ft case, the prior comprehensive report used a value intermediate between mass- and volume-weighted approaches. The established project value of **3.01 W/m·K** is retained for consistency — it reflects the mass-weighted contribution of steel more substantially, which is appropriate given that steel, while volumetrically minor, dominates the structural conductivity path.

### Thermal Capacitance Verification

```
C_v = ρ × c_p
    = 886 × 1,270
    = 1,125,220 J/m³·K

Total capacitance per m² floor = C_v × thickness × SA ratio
= 1,125,220 × 0.12944 × 0.360 = 52,436 J/K·m²  ✓ (matches 52,426; <0.1% variance)
```

             = 0.36 × 0.1294 × 886

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Glulam-Dominated Tall Structural Volume:**
- Moderate composite density (886 kg/m³) — glulam (650 kg/m³) dominates at 96.6% of total volume; steel provides mass uplift at limited volume; composite falls between wood and steel
- Low SA ratio (0.36 m²/m²) — slightly higher than the ≤40 ft case (0.31) due to larger, more numerous beams but still among the lowest in the dataset
- High specific heat (1,270 J/kg·K) — glulam at 1,600 J/kg·K dominates; higher than the ≤40 ft case because glulam is more prevalent and denser than Douglas Fir lumber
- Low conductivity (3.01 W/m·K) — glulam at 96.6% of volume sets a low baseline; steel (3.22% of volume) provides moderate uplift at 1.449 W/m-K contribution

**Why the Larger Atrium Has Higher Specific Heat:**
The ≤40 ft atrium uses Douglas Fir (cp = 1,600 J/kg·K, ρ = 550 kg/m³) while the >40 ft atrium uses glulam (cp = 1,600 J/kg·K, ρ = 650 kg/m³). Both have the same specific heat, but glulam is 18% denser and uses thicker members — so total mass per floor area is substantially higher (41.3 vs. 23.8 kg/m²). The composite specific heat is also higher for the larger atrium (1,270 vs. 1,122 J/kg·K) because steel, which has low cp (460 J/kg·K), represents a smaller fraction of the total mass in the >40 ft case (steel is 11.78/41.28 = 28.5% of mass) vs. the ≤40 ft case (steel is 9.81/23.81 = 41.2% of mass). In other words, the heavier glulam members dilute the low-cp steel's influence on the composite specific heat.

### Comparison — Both Atrium Types

| Parameter | ≤40 ft | >40 ft | Ratio |
|-----------|--------|--------|-------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 0.31 | 0.36 | 1.16× |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 23.81 | 41.28 | 1.73× |
| Effective Thickness (mm) | 85.0 | 129.4 | 1.52× |
| Density (kg/m³) | 904 | 886 | 0.98× |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 1,122 | 1,270 | 1.13× |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | 2.56 | 3.01 | 1.18× |
| Thermal Cap./floor (J/K·m²) | 26,724 | 52,426 | 1.96× |
| Primary structural member | Douglas Fir (100 mm) | Glulam (150 mm) | — |

The >40 ft atrium has **nearly double the thermal capacitance per floor area** despite only 16% more exposed surface. The driver is the heavier structural members — glulam beams at 150 mm effective thickness vs. 100 mm Douglas Fir produce 80% more mass per unit area from the primary structural element, and this mass has nearly the same high specific heat.

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations for Tall Atriums:**
- Thermal stratification is more severe in taller atriums — floor-to-ceiling temperature differentials of 10–20°C are common in atriums >15 m tall; single-zone EnergyPlus models significantly underestimate this effect
- The internal mass of exposed glulam beams at upper levels exchanges heat primarily with upper-zone air (warmer in summer, cooler in winter) — floor-level conditioning is largely decoupled from the structural thermal mass
- Solar gain through roof glazing drives the dominant thermal loads; the structural mass moderates temperature swings at roof level but has limited influence on occupied-floor conditions
- Night ventilation strategies that flush the atrium volume can be effective in mild climates — the glulam mass absorbs overnight cool air and releases it during the following day

**Code Implications — Height Threshold:**
The 40 ft threshold in the space type reflects a structural engineering inflection point: below 40 ft, light wood framing is viable; above 40 ft, heavier structural systems (glulam, steel, or heavy timber) become necessary for structural performance. This structural necessity directly drives the difference in internal thermal mass between the two space type categories, validating the code's use of height as a proxy for thermal mass in atrium spaces.

# Internal Mass Calculations: CS Banking Activity Area

**Report Date:** April 7, 2026
**Scope:** Banking Activity Area Space Type
**Purpose:** Calculate OpenStudio InternalMass properties for thermal modeling

---

## CS Banking Activity Area

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 5–25 staff + 10–50 customers (variable throughout day)
**Floor Area:** 100–400 m² (retail bank branch floor); reference area: **200 m²**
**Ceiling Height:** 3.0–4.5 m
**Function:** Retail banking services — teller transactions, personal banking, loan consultations, safe deposit box access, and ATM services. Includes the public banking floor (teller line, customer waiting, service desks) and the behind-the-counter teller operations area. Branch banks in commercial buildings are the primary reference; main banking halls in dedicated bank buildings may be larger and more elaborately furnished.

**Key Features:**
- Teller transaction counter and workstations (the dominant element)
- Teller drawers and cash handling equipment (steel security equipment)
- Customer queue management system (stanchions)
- Customer service desks for consultations
- Waiting area seating
- ATM machine(s) — if interior
- Vault door and safe area (if present; typically partial room)
- Security transaction windows (bullet-resistant glazing)

- Night deposit unit (wall-mounted, steel)
- Moderate to high security hardware throughout

## Composite Property Calculations

### Revised Material Breakdown for Calculations

| Material | Mass (kg/m²) | % |
|----------|-------------|---|
| Steel | 8.710 | 54.2% |
| MDF / particleboard | 5.365 | 33.4% |
| Granite | 1.021 | 6.4% |
| Cast iron | 0.814 | 5.1% |
| Polycarbonate | 0.681 | 4.2% |
| Wood / foam / fabric / other | 0.555 | 3.5% |
| **Adjusted total** | **17.146** | |

> For composite calculations, using component-derived masses reconciled at 16.074 kg/m² with material fractions proportionally scaled:

| Material | Adjusted kg/m² |
|----------|---------------|
| Steel | 8.148 |
| MDF | 5.016 |
| Granite | 0.955 |
| Cast iron | 0.761 |
| Polycarbonate | 0.637 |
| Other | 0.557 |

### Material Thermal Properties Reference

| Material | Density (kg/m³) | cp (J/kg·K) | k (W/m-K) |
|----------|----------------|-------------|-----------|
| Steel (incl. hardened) | 7,850 | 460 | 45.0 |
| MDF / particleboard | 720 | 1,300 | 0.14 |
| Granite | 2,700 | 790 | 3.00 |
| Cast iron | 7,200 | 460 | 52.0 |
| Polycarbonate | 1,200 | 1,300 | 0.20 |
| Other (avg wood/foam/fabric) | 400 | 1,500 | 0.08 |

### Weighted Average Density

```
Volume per m² of floor:

Steel:         8.148 / 7850  = 0.001038 m³/m²
MDF:           5.016 / 720   = 0.006967 m³/m²
Granite:       0.955 / 2700  = 0.000354 m³/m²
Cast iron:     0.761 / 7200  = 0.000106 m³/m²
Polycarbonate: 0.637 / 1200  = 0.000531 m³/m²
Other:         0.557 / 400   = 0.001393 m³/m²

Total volume = 0.001038 + 0.006967 + 0.000354 + 0.000106 + 0.000531 + 0.001393
             = 0.010389 m³/m²

Composite density = 16.074 / 0.010389
                  = 1,547 kg/m³
```

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Σ(m_i × c_p,i) / Σ(m_i)

Steel:         8.148 × 460  = 3,748
MDF:           5.016 × 1300 = 6,521
Granite:       0.955 × 790  =   754
Cast iron:     0.761 × 460  =   350
Polycarbonate: 0.637 × 1300 =   828
Other:         0.557 × 1500 =   836

c_p,composite = (3,748 + 6,521 + 754 + 350 + 828 + 836) / 16.074
              = 13,037 / 16.074
              = 811 J/kg·K
```

### Weighted Average Conductivity

```
k_composite ≈ Σ(V_i / V_total × k_i)

Steel:        (0.001038 / 0.010389) × 45.0  = 0.09991 × 45.0  = 4.496
MDF:          (0.006967 / 0.010389) × 0.14  = 0.67061 × 0.14  = 0.094
Granite:      (0.000354 / 0.010389) × 3.00  = 0.03408 × 3.00  = 0.102
Cast iron:    (0.000106 / 0.010389) × 52.0  = 0.01020 × 52.0  = 0.530
Polycarbonate:(0.000531 / 0.010389) × 0.20  = 0.05112 × 0.20  = 0.010
Other:        (0.001393 / 0.010389) × 0.08  = 0.13408 × 0.08  = 0.011

k_composite ≈ 4.496 + 0.094 + 0.102 + 0.530 + 0.010 + 0.011
            ≈ 5.243 W/m·K
```

> Steel at 9.99% of total volume contributes 4.50 W/m-K — 86% of composite conductivity. MDF at 67% of volume contributes only 0.094 W/m-K; cast iron (vault door components at 1.02% volume) provides 0.530 W/m-K through its high conductivity.

### Effective Thickness

```
t_eff = Total mass per m² / (SA_ratio × composite density)
      = 16.074 / (0.690 × 1,547)
      = 16.074 / 1,067.4
      = 0.01506 m ≈ 0.015 m  (15 mm)
```

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = ρ × c_p
    = 1,547 × 811
    = 1,254,617 J/m³·K
```

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Security-Equipment-and-MDF Space — Vault and Safe Deposit Box Drive Mass:**
- Moderate composite density (1,547 kg/m³) — steel and cast iron vault/security equipment (54%) pull density high; MDF counter carcass (67% of volume) pulls toward 720 kg/m³; the composite sits in between
- Moderate SA ratio (0.690 m²/m²) — the teller counter dominates at 0.296 (43% of total SA); no single large-surface component reaches the SA of library shelving or sort case cubbies; security items (vault door, safe deposit cabinet) are compact and dense with low SA per unit mass
- Moderate specific heat (811 J/kg·K) — MDF (1,300) and polycarbonate (1,300) partially offset steel's low 460 J/kg·K; the balance produces a moderate composite
- Moderate conductivity (5.243 W/m-K) — steel at 86% of composite conductivity from 10% of volume; the MDF counter carcass at 67% of volume contributes a mere 0.094 W/m-K

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Moderate thermal capacitance (1,254,617 J/m³·K)
- Moderate thermal response — MDF dominates volume (67%) and slows heat transfer at the counter; vault door and safe deposit cabinet exchange heat slowly (thick steel with limited SA) but store significant energy
- The vault door (450 kg, SA = 4.69 m²) and safe deposit cabinet (600 kg, SA = 9.32 m²) are uniquely high-mass, low-SA components — they store substantial thermal energy with limited heat exchange rate; this makes them effective long-duration thermal buffers during setback periods

### Design Appropriateness

**Banking Floor Thermal Mass Features:**
- **Safe deposit box cabinet and vault door together contribute 5.25 kg/m²** — the single largest mass pair after the teller counter; these security components have no parallel in other commercial space types; their all-steel construction and exceptional mass density (600 kg per cabinet) place them in the same mass class as a CNC machining center per unit footprint
- **Teller counter** is the dominant SA element (0.296 m²/m²) — the combination of large customer-facing panels, interior cabinet shelving, and the security glazing frame all contribute; the granite ledge adds 1.02 kg/m² of dense, moderate-cp stone
- **Bullet-resistant glazing** (polycarbonate composite) is a distinctive material unique to banking spaces — at 0.637 kg/m² and 1,300 J/kg·K, it contributes meaningfully to the specific heat, and its low conductivity (0.20 W/m-K) acts as a thermal separator between the customer and teller zones
- **Queue stanchions** (40 units) contribute 2.55 kg/m² — the bank has more stanchions per floor area than most other space types given the narrow, winding queue lanes typical of bank branches; the cast iron ballast bases are again the heaviest stanchion component per unit
- **ATM machine** — at 200 kg for a single unit, the ATM is the third-heaviest individual item (after vault door and safe deposit cabinet); its steel vault enclosure is the primary mass driver

**The Banking Space as a Security-Driven Thermal Profile:**
The banking activity area is the only space type in the dataset where **security requirements** are the primary determinant of thermal mass, rather than functional workflow or furniture standards. The vault door, safe deposit cabinet, and ATM are all substantially heavier than their visual footprint suggests precisely because their design prioritizes physical resistance to forced entry — a property that incidentally also produces high thermal mass.

### Comparison to Similar Counter-Heavy Space Types

| Parameter | Banking | Ticket Counter | Museum Restoration |
|-----------|---------|---------------|-------------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 0.690 | 1.070 | 1.260 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 16.07 | 15.40 | 16.11 |
| Density (kg/m³) | 1,547 | 1,374 | 2,490 |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | 5.243 | 5.172 | 13.36 |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 811 | 952 | 668 |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 1,254,617 | 1,307,448 | 1,663,320 |
| Unique element | Vault door + SDB cabinet | Granite countertops | Fume hood + flat files |

> The banking and ticket counter spaces have remarkably similar total mass (~16 kg/m²) but different SA ratios — the bank's security equipment is compact and dense while the airport counter has long runs of public-facing panel surface. Both spaces have conductivity near 5.2 W/m-K, driven by steel in the bank and aluminum+steel in the ticket counter.

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- Retail banking branches are typically open to the public 8–9 hours per day, 5–6 days per week; significant setback opportunity on evenings and weekends
- Customer occupancy is transient (average 10–15 minutes per transaction); peak occupancy at lunch hour and late afternoon
- Electronic equipment (ATM, teller workstations, digital signage, security cameras and monitors) generates approximately 500–1,500 W of continuous heat gain during operating hours
- Drive-through banking (if adjacent) creates infiltration and thermal bridge concerns through the transaction window opening — not modeled as internal mass but relevant to zone design
- Vault room (where the vault door connects) is a separate, typically unconditioned or separately conditioned zone — the vault door itself straddles two zones thermally

**Operational Patterns:**
- Banking hours: Monday–Friday 9 AM–5 PM; Saturday limited hours; closed Sunday
- Night setback: applicable; 6–8°C setback feasible during closed hours
- ATM operates 24/7 — provides continuous minor heat gain (~300–500 W) even when branch is closed; vault door and SDB cabinet continue to store and release heat during unoccupied periods
- Pre-open conditioning: 1–2 hours to recover from overnight setback

**Special Considerations:**
- Large main banking halls (historic bank buildings, financial district flagship branches) have dramatically different thermal mass profiles — marble floors, stone walls, and monumental teller counters create very high internal and structural mass; the reference configuration models a standard suburban retail branch
- In-store bank branches (in grocery stores or retail centers) may have simplified furnishings — fewer or no vault doors and safe deposit facilities; SA ratio and mass would be lower
- Currency counting rooms (back-of-house) contain high-value counting machines and currency processing equipment (steel) — separate zone with different thermal mass profile

## CS Classroom/Lecture/Training - Penitentiary

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 20–30 students plus 1 instructor (program-scheduled; near-zero between sessions)
**Floor Area:** 60–110 m² (standard single-classroom module); reference area: **90 m²**
**Ceiling Height:** 2.7–3.0 m (standard institutional construction; no skylights; security-rated fixtures at ceiling)
**Function:** Academic instruction and vocational training within a correctional facility — GED completion, adult basic education, workforce readiness, and certificate programs. The space is designed for controlled access: a single secure entry, no exterior windows (or narrow security-glazed windows), security-rated light fixtures flush-mounted at ceiling level, and institutional furniture selected for durability and security rather than comfort. The room accommodates a student group of 20–30 within standard row or clustered desk arrangements. The instructor station is positioned to provide clear sightlines to all students and to the entry.

**Key Features:**
- Individual student desks (melamine-laminate top over particleboard core on steel tube legs with wire book basket)
- Institutional armless chairs (steel tube frame, formed polypropylene seat and back; no cushioning)
- Instructor's steel double-pedestal desk (heavy-gauge institutional specification)
- Wall-mounted porcelain-on-steel whiteboards (security-fastened)
- Steel lockable storage cabinet (instructor materials)
- No upholstered seating, soft furnishings, or decorative items
- No plants, drapes, or carpet (hard floor — sealed concrete or vinyl composition tile)
- Security-rated ceiling light fixtures (recessed, no exposed trim mass of significance)

### Reference Configuration

**90 m² penitentiary classroom/training room:**
- 30 institutional student desks (5 rows × 6 columns)
- 30 institutional armless chairs (one per desk)
- Desk spacing: 0.90 m center-to-center across rows; 1.20 m center-to-center along rows
- 1 instructor's steel double-pedestal desk (front of room)
- 2 wall-mounted porcelain-on-steel whiteboards (front wall)
- 1 steel lockable storage cabinet (side or rear wall)
- Aisle width: 0.90 m minimum (security circulation requirement)
- Occupant density: 30 students in 90 m² = 3.0 m²/student (dense but standard for correctional programs)

## Material Property Calculations

### Mass-Weighted Composite Properties

**Material Breakdown by Mass:**

*Steel (chair frames, desk frames, wire baskets, instructor's desk, whiteboard substrates, whiteboard hardware, storage cabinet):*
- Chair steel frames: 2.8 × 30 / 90 = 0.933 kg/m²
- Student desk steel frames (legs + cross-members): (2.682 + 1.009) × 30 / 90 = 1.230 kg/m²
- Student desk wire baskets: 0.500 × 30 / 90 = 0.167 kg/m²
- Student desk hardware/glides: 0.800 × 30 / 90 = 0.267 kg/m²
- Instructor's desk (all steel): 60.0 / 90 = 0.667 kg/m²
- Whiteboard steel substrates: 17.09 × 2 / 90 = 0.380 kg/m²
- Whiteboard mounting hardware: 1.00 × 2 / 90 = 0.022 kg/m²
- Storage cabinet (all steel): 79.0 / 90 = 0.878 kg/m²
- **Total steel: 4.544 kg/m²** (64.2%)

*Polypropylene (chair seat and back):*
- 1.8 × 30 / 90 = **0.600 kg/m²** (8.5%)

*Particleboard core (student desk tops):*
- 4.914 × 30 / 90 = **1.638 kg/m²** (23.1%)

*Melamine laminate (student desk top faces):*
- 0.631 × 30 / 90 = **0.210 kg/m²** (3.0%)

*Aluminum (whiteboard frames):*
- 3.89 × 2 / 90 = **0.087 kg/m²** (1.2%)

*Porcelain enamel (whiteboard coating):*
- 0.72 × 2 / 90 = **0.016 kg/m²** (0.2%; negligible but included for completeness)

**Total: 4.544 + 0.600 + 1.638 + 0.210 + 0.087 + 0.016 = 7.095 kg/m²**

> Minor rounding variance (7.095 vs 7.082 from component table) reflects rounding of per-desk component masses across 30 desks. Use **7.08 kg/m²** for the final composite, consistent with the component summary table.

### Volume Fractions (for Conductivity Weighting)

```
V_i = mass_i / density_i  [m³ per m² of floor area]

Effective material groupings:
  Steel:          4.544 / 7,800    = 5.826 × 10⁻⁴ m³/m²
  Polypropylene:  0.600 / 1,050    = 5.714 × 10⁻⁴ m³/m²
  Particleboard:  1.638 /   700    = 2.340 × 10⁻³ m³/m²
  Laminate:       0.210 / 1,400    = 1.500 × 10⁻⁴ m³/m²
  Aluminum:       0.087 / 2,700    = 3.222 × 10⁻⁵ m³/m²
  Porcelain:      0.016 / 2,500    = 6.400 × 10⁻⁶ m³/m²

V_total = 5.826×10⁻⁴ + 5.714×10⁻⁴ + 2.340×10⁻³ + 1.500×10⁻⁴ + 3.222×10⁻⁵ + 6.400×10⁻⁶
        = 0.000583 + 0.000571 + 0.002340 + 0.000150 + 0.000032 + 0.000006
        = 0.003682 m³/m²

Volume fractions:
  Steel:          5.826×10⁻⁴ / 3.682×10⁻³ = 15.82%
  Polypropylene:  5.714×10⁻⁴ / 3.682×10⁻³ = 15.52%
  Particleboard:  2.340×10⁻³ / 3.682×10⁻³ = 63.55%
  Laminate:       1.500×10⁻⁴ / 3.682×10⁻³ =  4.07%
  Aluminum:       3.222×10⁻⁵ / 3.682×10⁻³ =  0.875%
  Porcelain:      6.400×10⁻⁶ / 3.682×10⁻³ =  0.174% (negligible)
```

> Particleboard occupies 63.6% of composite volume despite contributing only 23.1% of composite mass. This is the defining characteristic of the penitentiary classroom thermal mass: the laminate-top student desk is the volumetrically dominant element, driven by the low density of the particleboard core (~700 kg/m³) relative to steel (7,800 kg/m³). Steel contributes 64.2% of total mass but only 15.8% of total volume. This mass–volume inversion results in a composite density substantially lower than any other penitentiary space type, all of which are all-steel compositions.

### Weighted Average Density

```
ρ_composite = Total mass / Total volume
            = 7.082 / 0.003682
            = 1,923 kg/m³

Verification via volume-weighted sum:
  0.1582 × 7,800  = 1,234
  0.1552 × 1,050  =   163
  0.6355 ×   700  =   445
  0.0407 × 1,400  =    57
  0.00875 × 2,700 =    24
                  = 1,923 kg/m³  ✓
```

> The composite density of 1,923 kg/m³ is the lowest of all penitentiary space types modeled, reflecting the particleboard-dominant volume composition. All other penitentiary space types (audience seating, dining, confinement cells) are all-steel or near-all-steel constructions, with densities of 7,746–7,800 kg/m³. The classroom's wood-based desk tops introduce a fundamentally different thermal character into the composite.

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Σ(m_i × c_p,i) / Σ(m_i)

Material properties:
  Steel:          460 J/kg·K   (carbon steel)
  Polypropylene: 1,800 J/kg·K  (injection-molded, unfilled)
  Particleboard: 1,700 J/kg·K  (wood-fiber composite, similar to solid wood)
  Laminate:      1,400 J/kg·K  (melamine-phenolic composite)
  Aluminum:        900 J/kg·K  (structural aluminum)
  Porcelain:       900 J/kg·K  (vitreous ceramic enamel)

Steel:         4.544 × 460   = 2,090
Polypropylene: 0.600 × 1,800 = 1,080
Particleboard: 1.638 × 1,700 = 2,785
Laminate:      0.210 × 1,400 =   294
Aluminum:      0.087 ×   900 =    78
Porcelain:     0.016 ×   900 =    14

c_p,composite = (2,090 + 1,080 + 2,785 + 294 + 78 + 14) / 7.082
              = 6,341 / 7.082
              = 895.4 J/kg·K  →  895 J/kg·K
```

> The composite specific heat of 895 J/kg·K is substantially higher than the 460 J/kg·K of pure steel (all other penitentiary space types range 460–492 J/kg·K). The wood-based particleboard and polypropylene components drive the specific heat upward: particleboard at 1,700 J/kg·K and polypropylene at 1,800 J/kg·K both have specific heats nearly 4× that of steel, and together they contribute 43.5% of the total mass-weighted sum despite accounting for only 31.6% of the total mass.

### Weighted Average Conductivity (Volume-Weighted)

```
k_composite = Σ(V_frac_i × k_i)

Material conductivities:
  Steel:          50.0 W/m·K   (carbon steel)
  Polypropylene:   0.20 W/m·K  (unfilled PP)
  Particleboard:   0.15 W/m·K  (wood composite, across grain)
  Laminate:        0.20 W/m·K  (melamine-phenolic, similar to dense polymer)
  Aluminum:       160.0 W/m·K  (structural alloy)

Steel:         0.1582 × 50.0  = 7.910
Polypropylene: 0.1552 ×  0.20 = 0.031
Particleboard: 0.6355 ×  0.15 = 0.095
Laminate:      0.0407 ×  0.20 = 0.008
Aluminum:      0.00875 × 160.0 = 1.400

k_composite ≈ 7.910 + 0.031 + 0.095 + 0.008 + 1.400
            ≈ 9.444 W/m·K  →  9.44 W/m·K
```

> Steel at 15.8% of volume contributes 7.910 W/m·K — 83.8% of composite conductivity. Aluminum at 0.875% of volume contributes another 1.400 W/m·K (14.8%). The particleboard, polypropylene, and laminate — which collectively occupy 83.1% of total volume — contribute only 0.134 W/m·K combined. The steel tube legs and frames of every component act as thermal bridges through the insulating wood and polymer volumes, setting the composite conductivity far above what any individual non-metallic material would suggest.

### Effective Thickness

```
t_eff = Total mass per m² / (SA_ratio × composite density)
      = 7.082 / (0.85 × 1,923)
      = 7.082 / 1,634.6
      = 0.004333 m  ≈  0.0043 m  (4.3 mm)
```

> The very thin effective slab thickness (4.3 mm) reflects the high composite density combined with a modest SA ratio. Unlike space types with large volumes of low-density material (foam, wood pews), the penitentiary classroom composite is dense — driven by steel and particleboard — producing a thin equivalent slab for the given surface area and mass budget. This is physically correct: the actual furniture items have thin steel walls, thin laminate panels, and modest depths, yielding limited volumetric mass per unit of exposed surface area.

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = ρ × c_p
    = 1,923 × 895
    = 1,721,085 J/m³·K
```

- **Visible Absorptance:** `0.50` {dimensionless}

> Roughness is set to MediumSmooth because the dominant exposed surfaces — injection-molded polypropylene (seat and back), melamine laminate (desk top), and powder-coated steel (frames and panels) — are all smooth-to-semi-smooth finishes. The porcelain whiteboard surface is the smoothest element but contributes minimally to surface area.

> Solar and visible absorptance are set to 0.55 and 0.50 respectively to reflect the characteristically pale institutional palette: cream or light grey melamine laminate desk surfaces, light grey or tan polypropylene chair shells, and white-to-light-grey powder-coated steel frames. These tones are lighter than typical commercial office furniture and meaningfully lower the blended absorptance below the 0.65 used for darker fabric-upholstered seating.

**Verification:**
```
Thermal Mass = SA ratio × Thickness × Density
             = 0.85 × 0.0043 × 1,923
             = 0.85 × 8.269
             = 7.03 kg/m²  ✓  (matches component total of 7.08 kg/m²; <0.7% variance)

Thermal Capacitance = ρ × c_p
                    = 1,923 × 895
                    = 1,721,085 J/m³·K  ✓
```

**IDF Format:**
```idf
OS:Material,
  Mixed_Classroom_Penitentiary_4mm,      !- Name
  MediumSmooth,                          !- Roughness
  0.0043,                                !- Thickness {m}
  9.44,                                  !- Conductivity {W/m-K}
  1923,                                  !- Density {kg/m3}
  895,                                   !- Specific Heat {J/kg-K}
  0.90,                                  !- Thermal Absorptance
  0.55,                                  !- Solar Absorptance
  0.50;                                  !- Visible Absorptance

OS:Construction,
  Construction_ClassroomPenitentiary,    !- Name
  ,                                      !- Surface Rendering Name
  Mixed_Classroom_Penitentiary_4mm;      !- Layer 1

OS:InternalMass:Definition,
  Classroom_Penitentiary_IntMass,        !- Name
  Construction_ClassroomPenitentiary,    !- Construction Name
  0.85,                                  !- Surface Area per Space Floor Area {dimensionless}
  ;                                      !- Surface Area per Person {m2/person}
```

---

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Particleboard-Volume-Dominated Composite — Low Density by Penitentiary Standards:**
- Low composite density (1,923 kg/m³) relative to all other penitentiary space types (7,746–7,800 kg/m³); the laminate-top student desk introduces particleboard at 700 kg/m³ as the volumetrically dominant material (63.6% of total volume), pulling the composite density down by a factor of 4× compared to the all-steel spaces
- Low SA ratio (0.85 m²/m²) — the institutional austerity of the penitentiary classroom minimizes surface-area-generating elements; no bookshelves, no curtains, no plants, no upholstered lounge seating, and no teacher's workstation beyond the standard desk; the 30 desks and chairs generate most of the exposed area but are individually compact
- Elevated specific heat (895 J/kg·K) — the highest of all penitentiary space types modeled; driven by particleboard and polypropylene, which have specific heats of 1,700–1,800 J/kg·K, nearly 4× that of steel; despite steel dominating by mass fraction (64.2%), the wood-fiber and polymer components shift the mass-weighted composite substantially upward from the 460 J/kg·K of all-steel spaces
- Moderate conductivity (9.44 W/m·K) — still high in absolute terms, but substantially lower than the all-steel penitentiary spaces (33.8–50.0 W/m·K); the particleboard volume fraction (63.6% at 0.15 W/m·K) suppresses the steel's contribution, though the steel tube legs and frames remain the dominant thermal bridges

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Moderate thermal capacitance per unit volume (1,721,085 J/m³·K) — substantially higher than any other penitentiary space type (which range 3,588,000–3,811,000 J/m³·K by ρ × c_p, but at much lower volume because their near-zero composite thickness means the stored energy per m² of floor area is modest); this space type stores thermal energy at a moderate rate relative to the small exposed area
- Low total thermal mass (7.08 kg/m²) — the sparse, security-hardened room furnishing inventory limits the mass budget; all-steel spaces like the dining room (15.35 kg/m²) or confinement cells (24.41 kg/m²) carry far more mass per floor area because they are dominated by heavy structural steel elements (fixed tables, bunk beds, door frames)
- The student desk particleboard top, despite its modest thermal properties, provides the majority of the room's exposed low-conductivity surface area; this means pre-conditioning of the room air takes longer to fully temper the desk surfaces than the steel elements, because the particleboard's low conductivity (0.15 W/m·K) limits heat penetration depth
- Steel frame elements (chair legs, desk legs, cabinet shell) exchange heat rapidly with circulating air but store very little energy per unit of exposed surface; the wood-based desk tops store more energy per unit volume but exchange it more slowly

### Design Appropriateness

**Penitentiary Classroom — Institutionally Austere, Thermally Distinctive:**
- **Student desks are the dominant component by volume and SA contribution** (40.3% of SA ratio from desks alone, 49.4% of mass) — unlike most institutional classrooms where multiple furniture systems share the thermal mass budget more evenly, the 30-desk inventory at 30 desks / 90 m² = 0.33 desks/m² creates a strong single-component signature; their laminate tops introduce the space type's only substantial low-density volume material
- **No cushioning or soft furnishings anywhere in the space** — this is the defining physical departure from all civilian classroom types and most other commercial space types; the complete absence of upholstered chairs, acoustic panels, carpet, and fabric elements means there is no polyurethane foam, mineral fiber, or textile to moderate the composite; every surface is hard, smooth, and either metal or laminate
- **The instructor's desk carries disproportionate mass** (0.667 kg/m², versus 0.087 from whiteboards and 0.085 from the cabinet) — the all-steel double-pedestal desk at 60 kg dominates the fixed equipment mass per unit area; in a 90 m² room with 30 students, one heavy steel desk represents 8.5% of total room thermal mass
- **The storage cabinet contributes more SA than it appears** (0.085 m²/m², 9.97% of total SA) — the interior surface area of the 4 shelves, at 50% open-time factor, adds meaningful thermal exchange area for a single item; the heavy shell (79 kg) also adds 0.878 kg/m² of mass, making the cabinet the second-largest mass contributor per unit after the student desk array

### Comparison to Other Penitentiary Space Types

| Parameter | Classroom / Training | Audience Seating | Dining Area | Confinement Cells |
|-----------|---------------------|------------------|-------------|-------------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 0.85 | 1.17 | 0.74 | 0.73 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 7.08 | 11.86 | 15.35 | 24.41 |
| Density (kg/m³) | 1,923 | 7,800 | 7,746 | 7,746 |
| Conductivity (W/m·K) | 9.44 | 50.0 | 42.6 | 33.8 |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 895 | 460 | 478 | 492 |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 1,721,085 | 3,588,000 | 3,702,588 | 3,811,032 |
| Dominant volume material | Particleboard/PP | Steel | Steel | Steel |

> The classroom/training space type is the clear outlier among penitentiary space types: it is the only one whose composite is not steel-dominated by volume. The introduction of 30 laminate-top student desks — each with a particleboard core — shifts the volumetric composition from monolithic steel to a layered mix. This produces a density 4× lower (1,923 vs 7,746–7,800 kg/m³), a specific heat nearly 2× higher (895 vs 460–492 J/kg·K), and a conductivity 4–5× lower (9.44 vs 33.8–50.0 W/m·K) than any other space type in the penitentiary category. The SA ratio (0.85) and total mass (7.08 kg/m²) are both the lowest of the group, consistent with the educational use function: a classroom has comparatively few fixed heavy elements compared to sleeping quarters, dining infrastructure, or a spectator seating arrangement.

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- The penitentiary classroom operates on a strict program schedule; occupancy is either full (30 students + 1 instructor = 31 people in 90 m² = 0.344 people/m²) or effectively zero between sessions; pre-conditioning the thermal mass ahead of each session must account for the relatively low mass budget (7.08 kg/m²) and modest SA ratio (0.85 m²/m²)
- Sensible loads during occupied periods: 31 people × ~75 W sensible (sedentary/light educational activity) = 2,325 W sensible in 90 m²; these transient occupant loads are large relative to the thermal mass storage capacity; the room will respond quickly to occupancy changes
- The all-hard-surface construction (no carpet, no acoustic panels) means the room will have high acoustic reverberation — HVAC supply diffusers must be selected and positioned to avoid creating audible turbulence noise, which constrains airflow velocity and delivery method; perforated supply at low velocity is preferred
- The sealed or security-glazed windows (minimal daylight) mean solar gains are negligible; the envelope-dominated load is primarily conductive through the concrete/CMU walls; the internal thermal mass is modest relative to the wall mass, so envelope pre-conditioning dominates the recovery energy budget

**Operational Patterns:**
- Session schedule: typically 2–4 sessions per day (morning, afternoon, possibly evening for different inmate cohorts); each session: 1–3 hours; inter-session break: 30–90 minutes
- The short inter-session interval may not allow full thermal setback recovery; partial setback (1–2°C) between sessions is more practical than full setback
- Weekend and holiday scheduling varies by facility; some programs run 5 days/week, reducing setback opportunities on weekdays
- The hard-surface construction means no residual off-gassing or moisture buffering from soft furnishings; humidity control follows occupancy load only, not material adsorption/desorption cycles

**Special Considerations:**
- **Furniture variability by security level**: minimum-security correctional programs may use the same laminate-top desks modeled here; maximum-security or administrative segregation settings may use all-steel furniture bolted to the floor — in those cases, the composite density would approach 7,800 kg/m³ (near the all-steel spaces), and the conductivity would increase substantially; the modeler should confirm furniture specification when applying this space type to high-security zones
- **Whiteboard location and wall coverage**: in facilities that use a full front-wall whiteboard system (two or three boards, total front wall coverage), the whiteboard mass and SA would increase proportionally; the current model uses 2 boards totaling 2 × 3.25 m² = 6.50 m² of whiteboard surface, consistent with a single primary teaching wall; additional boards at the side or rear should be added as additional components
- **Projector or display screens**: many correctional education programs now use wall-mounted flat-panel displays or ceiling-mounted projectors; these electronic items have negligible thermal mass and are excluded; a projector screen, if present (retractable, fabric/vinyl), would contribute minimal thermal mass and can be ignored
- **The IDF material thickness of 4.3 mm** is unrealistically thin for physical interpretation as a slab but is mathematically correct for the InternalMass object's surface-area-based formulation; EnergyPlus uses the material properties (density, specific heat, conductivity) and thickness to compute the effective thermal storage and surface heat flux — the result is a correctly calibrated thermal response regardless of the physical interpretability of the slab thickness; this is a known modeling artifact when composite density is high

---

*End of Calculation Report*

# Internal Mass Calculations: CS Classroom/Lecture/Training - K-12 - Laboratory and Shops

**Report Date:** July 10, 2026
**Scope:** Classroom/Lecture/Training - K-12 - Laboratory and Shops Space Type
**Purpose:** Calculate OpenStudio InternalMass properties for thermal modeling

---

## CS Classroom/Lecture/Training - K-12 - Laboratory and Shops

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 20-24 students + 1 instructor (K-12 labs and shops are commonly capped near 24 for safety and supervision)
**Floor Area:** 90-150 m2 (larger than a standard classroom to accommodate benches, service casework, and machine floor space); reference area: **100 m2**
**Ceiling Height:** 3.0-3.7 m (elevated to clear fume/exhaust hoods, tall storage, and dust-collection ducting)
**Function:** Combined hands-on instruction space covering both K-12 science laboratories (chemistry, biology, physics) and technical-education shops (wood shop, metal shop, general fabrication). This category groups the two together because they share the same defining internal-mass signature: fixed heavy-duty benching, extensive metal casework, service utilities at each station, and a modest complement of floor/benchtop equipment. The reference configuration models a single representative K-12 combined lab/shop room serving a middle-school or high-school program. The space is bounded by the instructional room proper; chemical storage rooms, tool cribs, and mechanical/dust-collection rooms are modeled as separate zones.

**Key Features:**
- Fixed student lab/work benches with steel frames and chemical-resistant or hardwood tops (the dominant element)
- Continuous perimeter casework with base cabinets, service sinks, and gas/electrical utilities
- Tall steel tool and chemical storage cabinets (lockable, ventilated)
- Demonstration fume hood or exhaust/dust-collection hood at the front or perimeter
- Shop machine tools (drill press, band saw, sander, bench grinder) - cast iron and steel
- Lab/shop stools (steel frame, wood or poly seat)
- Instructor demonstration bench with utilities
- Porcelain-on-steel markerboard
- Safety equipment (eyewash, safety shower, fire extinguisher cabinets, machine guards)
- LED lighting and HVAC diffusers (minor contributors)

### Reference Configuration

**100 m2 K-12 combined laboratory/shop room:**
- 6 student lab/work benches (2.4 m x 0.75 m x 0.90 m), seating ~4 students each = 24 students
- 14 m of continuous perimeter service casework (0.60 m deep x 0.90 m high)
- 6 tall storage cabinets (1.0 m x 0.55 m x 1.9 m)
- 1 demonstration fume/exhaust hood (1.5 m x 0.75 m x 2.2 m)
- 4 shop machine tools (benchtop/floor, cast-iron and steel construction)
- 24 lab/shop stools
- 1 instructor demonstration bench (3.0 m x 0.90 m x 0.90 m)
- 1 markerboard (4.0 m x 1.2 m)
- Safety equipment cluster (eyewash, shower, extinguisher cabinets, guards)
- 12 LED fixtures, 8 HVAC diffusers

## Material Property Calculations

### Mass-Weighted Composite Properties

**Material Breakdown by Mass:**

*Steel (bench and casework frames, storage cabinets, hood cabinet, machine guards/stands, stools, markerboard, safety fixtures, and stainless sinks):*
- Bench frames + sinks: (52.0 + 10.0) x 6 / 100 = 3.720 kg/m2
- Casework bodies + sinks: (200.0 + 30.0) / 100 = 2.300 kg/m2
- Storage cabinets: 84.0 x 6 / 100 = 5.040 kg/m2
- Hood cabinet: 229.0 / 100 = 2.290 kg/m2
- Machine guards/stands: 29.0 x 4 / 100 = 1.160 kg/m2
- Stool frames: 5.0 x 24 / 100 = 1.200 kg/m2
- Demonstration bench + sink: (70.0 + 25.0) / 100 = 0.950 kg/m2
- Markerboard: 0.350 kg/m2
- Safety fixtures: 0.700 kg/m2
- **Total steel: 17.710 kg/m2** (68.4%)

*Laminate/particleboard (bench tops, casework tops and carcasses, demonstration bench top):*
- (20.0 x 6 + 151.0 + 58.0) / 100 = **3.290 kg/m2** (12.7%)

*Cast iron (shop machine castings):*
- 50.0 x 4 / 100 = **2.000 kg/m2** (7.7%)

*Wood/hardwood (bench tops, stool seats):*
- (18.0 x 6 + 2.0 x 24) / 100 = **1.560 kg/m2** (6.0%)

*Other (hood ductwork, cabinet hardware, machine motors/belts):*
- (15.0 + 6.0 x 6 + 3.5 x 4) / 100 = **0.686 kg/m2** (2.6%)

*Aluminum (light fixtures, diffusers):*
- (2.0 x 12 + 0.9 x 8) / 100 = **0.312 kg/m2** (1.2%)

*Glass (hood sash):*
- 27.0 / 100 = **0.270 kg/m2** (1.0%)

*Plastic (safety fixtures):*
- 6.0 / 100 = **0.060 kg/m2** (0.2%)

**Total: 17.710 + 3.290 + 2.000 + 1.560 + 0.686 + 0.312 + 0.270 + 0.060 = 25.888 kg/m2** [VERIFIED]

### Volume Fractions (for Conductivity Weighting)

```
V_i = mass_i / density_i  [m3 per m2 of floor area]

Steel:      17.710 / 7,850 = 0.002256 m3/m2
Laminate:    3.290 /   720 = 0.004569 m3/m2
Cast iron:   2.000 / 7,200 = 0.000278 m3/m2
Wood:        1.560 /   650 = 0.002400 m3/m2
Other:       0.686 / 2,500 = 0.000274 m3/m2
Aluminum:    0.312 / 2,700 = 0.000116 m3/m2
Glass:       0.270 / 2,500 = 0.000108 m3/m2
Plastic:     0.060 /   950 = 0.000063 m3/m2

V_total = 0.010064 m3/m2

Volume fractions:
  Steel:     0.002256 / 0.010064 = 22.42%
  Laminate:  0.004569 / 0.010064 = 45.40%
  Cast iron: 0.000278 / 0.010064 =  2.76%
  Wood:      0.002400 / 0.010064 = 23.85%
  Other:     0.000274 / 0.010064 =  2.73%
  Aluminum:  0.000116 / 0.010064 =  1.15%
  Glass:     0.000108 / 0.010064 =  1.07%
  Plastic:   0.000063 / 0.010064 =  0.63%
```

> The laminate tops/carcasses and hardwood surfaces together occupy 69.3% of composite volume while contributing only 18.7% of composite mass. Steel, though 68.4% of the mass, occupies only 22.4% of the volume - its high density concentrates a large mass into thin sheet and tube sections. This volume/mass inversion is the defining feature of the lab/shop composite and drives both the moderate composite density and the volume-weighted conductivity below.

### Weighted Average Density

```
rho_composite = Total mass / Total volume
              = 25.888 / 0.010064
              = 2,572 kg/m3
```

> The composite density (2,572 kg/m3) is computed volumetrically (total mass divided by total volume), consistent with the effective-thickness relationship used below. It sits well above the auditorium seating composite (219 kg/m3, foam-dominated) but below the pure metal-equipment reports because the wood and laminate work surfaces contribute large volume with little mass.

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Sum(m_i x c_p,i) / Sum(m_i)

Material properties:
  Steel:      460 J/kg-K
  Laminate: 1,300 J/kg-K
  Cast iron:  460 J/kg-K
  Wood:     1,600 J/kg-K
  Other:      900 J/kg-K
  Aluminum:   900 J/kg-K
  Glass:      840 J/kg-K
  Plastic:  1,400 J/kg-K

Steel:     17.710 x 460   = 8,146.6
Laminate:   3.290 x 1,300 = 4,277.0
Cast iron:  2.000 x 460   =   920.0
Wood:       1.560 x 1,600 = 2,496.0
Other:      0.686 x 900   =   617.4
Aluminum:   0.312 x 900   =   280.8
Glass:      0.270 x 840   =   226.8
Plastic:    0.060 x 1,400 =    84.0

c_p,composite = 17,048.6 / 25.888
              = 659 J/kg-K
```

### Weighted Average Conductivity (Volume-Weighted)

```
k_composite = Sum(V_frac_i x k_i)

Material conductivities:
  Steel:     45.0 W/m-K
  Laminate:   0.15 W/m-K
  Cast iron: 50.0 W/m-K   (capped at 50 per project convention)
  Wood:       0.14 W/m-K
  Other:      5.0 W/m-K
  Aluminum: 200.0 W/m-K
  Glass:      1.0 W/m-K
  Plastic:    0.25 W/m-K

Steel:     0.2242 x 45.0  = 10.089
Cast iron: 0.0276 x 50.0  =  1.380
Aluminum:  0.0115 x 200.0 =  2.300
Other:     0.0273 x 5.0   =  0.137
Laminate:  0.4540 x 0.15  =  0.068
Wood:      0.2385 x 0.14  =  0.033
Glass:     0.0107 x 1.0   =  0.011
Plastic:   0.0063 x 0.25  =  0.002

k_composite = 10.089 + 1.380 + 2.300 + 0.137 + 0.068 + 0.033 + 0.011 + 0.002
            = 14.0 W/m-K
```

> Steel supplies 10.09 W/m-K (72% of the composite conductivity) from a 22.4% volume fraction. Aluminum is a notable secondary contributor: at just 1.15% of volume it adds 2.30 W/m-K because of its very high conductivity (200 W/m-K) - the light fixtures and diffusers act as small but effective thermal bridges. The wood and laminate surfaces, despite dominating the volume, contribute almost nothing to conductivity.

### Effective Thickness

```
t_eff = Total mass per m2 / (SA_ratio x composite density)
      = 25.888 / (2.35 x 2,572)
      = 25.888 / 6,044.2
      = 0.00428 m  (4.28 mm)
```

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = rho x c_p
    = 2,572 x 659
    = 1,694,948 J/m3-K
```
