## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Solid Hardwood — The Most Compositionally Pure Space Type:**
- Low composite density (721 kg/m³) — essentially the density of solid hardwood itself; the most material-pure result in the dataset
- Moderate SA ratio (0.88 m²/m²) — fixed pews dominate at 0.601; organ casework and choir seating add moderate area; the chancel and altar area is less densely furnished than the nave
- **Highest composite specific heat calculated (1,568 J/kg·K)** — solid oak and maple at 91% of total mass drive the composite to within 2% of pure hardwood's cp of 1,600 J/kg·K
- Second-lowest conductivity calculated (0.251 W/m-K) — only the library reading area (0.180) is lower; both are wood-dominated with negligible metal by volume
- Moderate thermal capacitance (1,130,528 J/m³·K) — high specific heat partially compensates for low density

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Slow thermal response — hardwood's low conductivity means heat moves slowly into and out of pew mass
- Significant thermal storage relative to mass — the high cp of oak means 13.2 kg/m² of hardwood stores more thermal energy per degree of temperature change than equivalent mass of steel (460 J/kg·K) or concrete (~840 J/kg·K)
- Pews act as long-duration thermal buffers — during a 2-hour service with 300 occupants generating significant metabolic heat, the pew mass absorbs a portion of this gain and releases it slowly afterward
- The organ casework (1.764 kg/m²) is a notable thermal element — solid hardwood panels several centimeters thick represent concentrated thermal mass that responds slowly to temperature changes

### Design Appropriateness

**Worship Space Thermal Mass Features:**
- **Fixed pews dominate absolutely** (68% of SA ratio, 69% of mass) — this is appropriate; pews are the defining furniture of a traditional worship space, and their solid hardwood construction makes them among the heaviest per-unit furnishings in any space type
- **Organ casework** contributes more mass than any single furnishing except the pews — at 882 kg for console + casework, the pipe organ is the second-largest mass item; its solid hardwood panels are thermally equivalent to a significant quantity of structural timber
- **Kneelers** — both the rail-mounted pew kneelers (foam) and the communion rail pad — add meaningful SA with negligible mass; their foam/fabric composition is purely insulating
- **Liturgical metal** (brass appointments) contribute trivially to thermal mass but, through conductivity leverage, account for 21% of composite conductivity from 0.05% of volume
- **Hymnals** in pew racks parallel the library stacks calculation — only spine and top edge are exposed; 168 books contribute minimal SA but meaningful paper mass

**The Pew as a Thermal Element:**
Each solid hardwood pew at 161 kg is heavier than: a hospital bed frame (80 kg), a dumbbell rack with weights (134 kg), a museum display case (310 kg base — actually heavier), or a CNC workbench (55 kg). A full nave of 28 pews represents 4,519 kg of solid hardwood — comparable in mass to a small CNC machining center.

### Comparison Within the Religious Building Space Type Family

| Parameter | Worship/Choir | Fellowship Hall |
|-----------|--------------|----------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 0.88 | 1.15 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 13.17 | 7.53 |
| Density (kg/m³) | 721 | 902 |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | 0.251 | 2.614 |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | **1,568** | 1,157 |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 1,130,528 | 1,043,614 |
| Dominant material | Solid hardwood (91%) | Steel frames + MDF |

> The worship space has lower SA ratio than the fellowship hall (fixed pews are more mass-efficient than folding chairs at equal seating capacity) but nearly twice the mass per floor area. Its conductivity is 10× lower — the steel chair frames in the fellowship hall dominate conductivity, while the worship space's brass appointments and hardware contribute only trace conductivity in a predominantly wood thermal environment.

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- Extreme occupancy variability — 300 worshippers at peak service vs. near-zero on weekdays
- At peak occupancy, 300 persons × ~120 W/person = 36 kW internal gain in 500 m² (72 W/m²) — dominates all other internal gains
- High ceilings (9 m reference) create strong thermal stratification — worshippers at floor level may experience different temperatures than the organ loft or high windows
- The pew mass absorbs metabolic heat from worshippers during services, releasing it slowly afterward — this extends the effective cooling load beyond the service itself
- High-quality pipe organs are highly sensitive to temperature and humidity — 18–21°C, 45–55% RH is typically required for tuning stability; this often governs HVAC design in worship spaces
- Stained glass creates significant radiant heat gain and cold radiation (in winter) — building envelope effect, not internal mass

**Operational Patterns:**
- Peak use: Sunday morning (1–3 hours); occasional midweek services, weddings, funerals
- Weekly frequency of peak events differentiates this from spaces with daily peak occupancy
- HVAC must pre-condition the space before services — the hardwood pew mass requires 2–4 hours to reach equilibrium after a setback of 5–8°C
- Night and weekday setback is strongly advantageous given the high ceiling volume and low base occupancy

**Special Considerations:**
- Pipe organ thermal sensitivity may require HVAC to maintain conditioning during unoccupied periods — reducing the setback opportunity
- Bell towers and steeples (often connected to worship space) create complex air movement through openings
- Stone or masonry worship spaces (common in older churches) have substantial building-envelope thermal mass not captured by interior furnishings — the InternalMass object here captures only the furniture component
- Contemporary worship spaces with theater-style seating would have very different thermal mass profiles — padded fixed seating with upholstered armrests rather than solid wood pews would reduce both mass and specific heat substantially

## SS Retail - Dressing/Fitting Room

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 1–2 customers per stall (brief, transient)
**Floor Area:** 30–120 m² (cluster of individual stalls); reference area: **60 m²**
**Ceiling Height:** 2.7–3.0 m
**Function:** Private changing area for customers trying on clothing in retail apparel stores — individual stalls with privacy curtain or door, mirror, hook, and bench or seat. May include attendant area and garment return rack. Highly intermittent occupancy; each visit is typically 3–10 minutes.

**Key Features:**
- Individual stall partitions (floor-to-ceiling or partial-height panels)
- Full-length mirrors (wall-mounted in each stall)
- Clothing hooks and hangers
- Small bench or seat in each stall
- Privacy curtain or door per stall
- Attendant counter or garment sorting area at entry
- Return rack for tried-on garments
- High turnover, transient occupancy pattern

### Reference Configuration

**60 m² dressing room cluster:**
- 8 individual stalls, each approximately 1.50 m × 1.80 m = 2.70 m² (internal floor area)
- Common circulation space: 60 − (8 × 2.70) = 38.4 m²
- Stall height: 2.40 m (full-height partition)

## Composite Property Calculations

### Material Thermal Properties Reference

| Material | Density (kg/m³) | cp (J/kg·K) | k (W/m-K) |
|----------|----------------|-------------|-----------|
| MDF / particleboard | 720 | 1,300 | 0.14 |
| Glass | 2,500 | 840 | 1.00 |
| Steel | 7,850 | 460 | 45.0 |
| Fabric / polyester | 200 | 1,340 | 0.05 |
| Foam / vinyl | 400 | 1,300 | 0.05 |
| Aluminum | 2,700 | 900 | 160.0 |
| Zinc alloy | 6,600 | 390 | 113.0 |
| Other (hardware avg) | 4,000 | 500 | 30.0 |

### Weighted Average Density

```
Volume per m² of floor:

MDF:        24.15 / 720  = 0.033542 m³/m²
Glass:       1.133 / 2500 = 0.000453 m³/m²
Steel:       0.701 / 7850 = 0.000089 m³/m²
Fabric:      0.179 / 200  = 0.000895 m³/m²
Foam/vinyl:  0.253 / 400  = 0.000633 m³/m²
Aluminum:    0.077 / 2700 = 0.000029 m³/m²
Zinc alloy:  0.043 / 6600 = 0.000007 m³/m²
Other:       1.240 / 4000 = 0.000310 m³/m²

Total volume = 0.033542 + 0.000453 + 0.000089 + 0.000895
             + 0.000633 + 0.000029 + 0.000007 + 0.000310
             = 0.035958 m³/m²

Composite density = 27.776 / 0.035958
                  = 773 kg/m³
```

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Σ(m_i × c_p,i) / Σ(m_i)

MDF:        24.15 × 1300 = 31,395
Glass:       1.133 × 840  =    952
Steel:       0.701 × 460  =    323
Fabric:      0.179 × 1340 =    240
Foam/vinyl:  0.253 × 1300 =    329
Aluminum:    0.077 × 900  =     69
Zinc alloy:  0.043 × 390  =     17
Other:       1.240 × 500  =    620

c_p,composite = (31,395 + 952 + 323 + 240 + 329 + 69 + 17 + 620) / 27.776
              = 33,945 / 27.776
              = 1,222 J/kg·K
```

### Weighted Average Conductivity

```
k_composite ≈ Σ(V_i / V_total × k_i)

MDF:       (0.033542 / 0.035958) × 0.14  = 0.93282 × 0.14  = 0.131
Glass:     (0.000453 / 0.035958) × 1.00  = 0.01260 × 1.00  = 0.013
Steel:     (0.000089 / 0.035958) × 45.0  = 0.00248 × 45.0  = 0.112
Fabric:    (0.000895 / 0.035958) × 0.05  = 0.02489 × 0.05  = 0.001
Foam/vinyl:(0.000633 / 0.035958) × 0.05  = 0.01760 × 0.05  = 0.001
Aluminum:  (0.000029 / 0.035958) × 160.0 = 0.00081 × 160.0 = 0.129
Zinc alloy:(0.000007 / 0.035958) × 113.0 = 0.00019 × 113.0 = 0.022
Other:     (0.000310 / 0.035958) × 30.0  = 0.00862 × 30.0  = 0.259

k_composite ≈ 0.131 + 0.013 + 0.112 + 0.001 + 0.001 + 0.129 + 0.022 + 0.259
            ≈ 0.668 W/m·K
```

> MDF dominates the volume at 93.3% and naturally sets the conductivity baseline at 0.131 W/m-K. Steel, aluminum, zinc alloy, and hardware together add only 0.522 W/m-K despite their high individual conductivities — their combined volume fraction is under 0.6%. The "other" hardware category is the largest non-MDF conductivity contributor (0.259 W/m-K) due to mounting tracks and curtain hardware.

### Effective Thickness

```
t_eff = Total mass per m² / (SA_ratio × composite density)
      = 27.776 / (3.905 × 773)
      = 27.776 / 3,018.6
      = 0.009201 m ≈ 0.009 m  (9.2 mm)
```

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = ρ × c_p
    = 773 × 1,222
    = 944,606 J/m³·K
```

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**MDF-Dominated with High SA from Partitions and Curtains:**
- Low-moderate composite density (773 kg/m³) — MDF at 93% of volume defines the composite; glass and fabric are minor by volume
- Very high surface area ratio (3.91 m²/m²) — the highest wood-product-dominated SA ratio in the dataset; driven by the double-faced partition panels (2.465) and privacy curtain fabric (0.909)
- High specific heat (1,222 J/kg·K) — MDF (1,300) dominates; minor contributions from fabric and foam maintain a high composite; metals are volumetrically negligible
- Low conductivity (0.668 W/m-K) — MDF at 93% volume sets the conductivity firmly in the wood-product range; hardware and metals provide modest uplift from the 0.14 W/m-K pure MDF baseline

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Moderate thermal capacitance (944,606 J/m³·K) — comparable to the museum general exhibition (961,056)
- Very slow thermal response — MDF at 93% volume means heat conducts through the material slowly; thin partition panels have low thermal inertia per panel but collectively provide significant surface area
- Privacy curtains (0.909 m²/m² SA) are a distinctive feature — fabric presents large surface area with very low mass and near-zero conductivity; they interact with room air primarily through convection

### Design Appropriateness

**Dressing Room Thermal Mass Features:**
- **Partition panels are the overwhelming dominant element** — 8 stalls with 3 panels each (2 sides + 1 back) at 25 mm MDF generate 2.465 m²/m² of the 3.905 total (63%) and 81% of total mass; this is the most partition-dominated space type in the dataset
- **Privacy curtains** contribute the second-largest SA term (0.909 m²/m²) — fabric curtains are acoustically and visually functional but thermally negligible by mass; their surface area is real but their thermal exchange capacity is minimal (both faces of 6.7 m² of fabric per stall)
- **Mirrors** are a notable material element — glass at 4.1% of total mass and 1.0 W/m-K conductivity contributes modest uplift to both mass and conductivity; 8 mirrors at 10.9 kg each add 87 kg of glass to the 60 m² space
- **MDF partition panels represent the largest absolute mass per floor area** in any non-manufacturing, non-library space type dominated by a single material category — 22.69 kg/m² from partition panels alone approaches the total mass of most standard office or classroom space types

**Why the SA Ratio is High:**
The 3.91 m²/m² SA ratio is unintuitive at first glance for what appears to be a lightly furnished space. The driver is geometry: each stall has two full-height side panels and one back panel, each with two exposed faces. Eight stalls produce 24 panels with 48 faces — and the stall floor area (2.70 m² each) is small relative to the partition surface area (18.49 m² per stall). The ratio of partition surface area to stall floor area is approximately 6.8:1, which is high even by library stack standards for individual-unit comparison.

### Comparison to Other High-SA-Ratio, Non-Metal Space Types

| Parameter | Dressing Room | Library Stacks | Post Office Sorting |
|-----------|--------------|---------------|---------------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 3.91 | 8.85 | 3.09 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 27.78 | 146.0 | 31.79 |
| Density (kg/m³) | 773 | 1,346 | 6,314 |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | 0.668 | 1.707 | 42.18 |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 1,222 | 1,140 | 491 |
| Dominant SA driver | MDF partition panels | Steel shelf decks | Steel sort case cubbies |

> All three space types achieve high SA ratios through internal subdivision geometry — partitions in dressing rooms, shelves in stacks, cubby dividers in sort cases — but the material compositions are dramatically different. The dressing room achieves its high SA from a low-conductivity, high-cp material (MDF), while the sort case achieves even higher SA from the opposite extreme (near-pure steel).

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- Transient, brief occupancy — each customer visit is 3–10 minutes; at any moment 1–2 customers may occupy the space
- Low average occupancy density but sporadic peak loading during busy retail periods
- High SA ratio of partition panels creates significant surface area for convective exchange with room air — despite the low conductivity, the large exposed surface means the MDF panels interact meaningfully with air temperature changes
- Curtains act as air movement barriers — they reduce convective mixing between stalls and the common area when closed
- No significant equipment gains — hooks, mirrors, and benches are entirely passive

**Operational Patterns:**
- Retail store hours (typically 10 AM–9 PM); closed at night
- Occupancy varies dramatically — may be empty for extended periods during slow business; heavily used on weekends and during sales events
- Night setback applicable — fast recovery due to the moderate thermal mass
- No special conditioning requirements — typical retail HVAC (21–23°C) is appropriate

**Special Considerations:**
- Individual stall HVAC supply and return — some dressing room clusters have individual diffusers in each stall; others rely on common-area air distribution with curtain gaps providing mixing
- Larger flagship store dressing rooms may have upholstered seating (full chair vs. simple bench), lighting fixtures per stall, and phone-charging stations — each of these would add minor mass not captured in the reference configuration
- In high-end retail, partition panels may be floor-to-ceiling solid wood (higher mass and lower SA per panel) rather than MDF — this would reduce SA ratio while increasing mass and specific heat
- The reference configuration models a mid-market apparel retailer; luxury and discount formats would bracket these values

## SS Retail - Mall Concourse

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 20–200 persons (highly variable; foot traffic driven)
**Floor Area:** 500–3,000 m² (enclosed mall common area); reference area: **1,000 m²**
**Ceiling Height:** 5.0–15.0 m (often skylighted atrium or vaulted); reference height: **8.0 m**
**Function:** Interior pedestrian circulation spine of an enclosed shopping mall — the common area between tenant storefronts. Includes seating areas, decorative planters, kiosk retail, food court adjacencies, wayfinding and signage, and seasonal display. Distinct from individual retail stores and from the food court dining area.

**Key Features:**
- Freestanding kiosk retail structures (cart vendors, pushcart-style kiosks)
- Mall seating — benches and occasional chairs
- Decorative planters (masonry or concrete base, planted)
- Wayfinding directory structures (steel/aluminum)
- Temporary seasonal display structures (lightweight)
- Decorative lighting elements (suspended fixtures, sconces)
- Flooring is typically polished stone, tile, or terrazzo (part of structure — excluded per internal mass convention)
- Open, high-volume circulation space with minimal fixed furnishings
- High foot traffic but low dwell time per person

### Reference Configuration

**1,000 m² concourse segment:**
- 6 permanent kiosk structures
- 15 mall benches
- 4 decorative planters
- 2 directory / wayfinding structures
- Seasonal display: 1 representative feature (average across year)

### 3. Decorative Planters (4 per 1,000 m²)

- Live plants (estimated, negligible thermal mass): 10.0 kg
- **Total Mass per Planter: 836.6 + 824.0 + 10.0 = 1,670.6 kg**

**Per Floor Area (4 planters in 1,000 m²):**
- Surface Area: (4 × 5.982) / 1,000 = **0.024 m²/m²**
- Mass: (4 × 1,670.6) / 1,000 = **6.682 kg/m²**

## Composite Property Calculations

### Material Thermal Properties Reference

| Material | Density (kg/m³) | cp (J/kg·K) | k (W/m-K) |
|----------|----------------|-------------|-----------|
| Concrete (normal weight) | 2,300 | 880 | 1.73 |
| Moist soil | 1,200 | 1,480 | 0.52 |
| MDF / plywood | 720 | 1,300 | 0.14 |
| Aluminum | 2,700 | 900 | 160.0 |
| Steel | 7,850 | 460 | 45.0 |
| Hardwood | 750 | 1,600 | 0.16 |
| Cast iron | 7,200 | 460 | 52.0 |
| Glass | 2,500 | 840 | 1.00 |
| Other | 1,500 | 1,000 | 1.00 |

### Weighted Average Density

```
Volume per m² of floor:

Concrete:    3.346 / 2300  = 0.001455 m³/m²
Soil:        3.296 / 1200  = 0.002747 m³/m²
MDF/plywood: 1.855 / 720   = 0.002576 m³/m²
Aluminum:    0.570 / 2700  = 0.000211 m³/m²
Steel:       0.410 / 7850  = 0.000052 m³/m²
Hardwood:    0.291 / 750   = 0.000388 m³/m²
Cast iron:   0.216 / 7200  = 0.000030 m³/m²
Glass:       0.138 / 2500  = 0.000055 m³/m²
Other:       0.220 / 1500  = 0.000147 m³/m²
Plants:      0.040 / 400   = 0.000100 m³/m²

Total volume = 0.001455 + 0.002747 + 0.002576 + 0.000211 + 0.000052
             + 0.000388 + 0.000030 + 0.000055 + 0.000147 + 0.000100
             = 0.007761 m³/m²

Composite density = 10.382 / 0.007761
                  = 1,338 kg/m³
```

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Σ(m_i × c_p,i) / Σ(m_i)

Concrete:    3.346 × 880  = 2,944
Soil:        3.296 × 1480 = 4,878
MDF/plywood: 1.855 × 1300 = 2,412
Aluminum:    0.570 × 900  =   513
Steel:       0.410 × 460  =   189
Hardwood:    0.291 × 1600 =   466
Cast iron:   0.216 × 460  =    99
Glass:       0.138 × 840  =   116
Other:       0.220 × 1000 =   220
Plants:      0.040 × 3500 =   140

c_p,composite = (2,944 + 4,878 + 2,412 + 513 + 189 + 466 + 99 + 116 + 220 + 140)
              / 10.382
              = 11,977 / 10.382
              = 1,154 J/kg·K
```

> Soil contributes 4,878 of 11,977 total mass-weighted cp (40.7%) despite being only 31.7% of mass — its specific heat of 1,480 J/kg·K and high mass fraction make it the dominant cp driver. This is the first space type in the dataset where soil is a significant material component; the moist soil fill in the decorative planters fundamentally shapes the composite thermal properties.

### Weighted Average Conductivity

```
k_composite ≈ Σ(V_i / V_total × k_i)

Concrete:    (0.001455 / 0.007761) × 1.73  = 0.18748 × 1.73  = 0.324
Soil:        (0.002747 / 0.007761) × 0.52  = 0.35399 × 0.52  = 0.184
MDF/plywood: (0.002576 / 0.007761) × 0.14  = 0.33193 × 0.14  = 0.046
Aluminum:    (0.000211 / 0.007761) × 160.0 = 0.02719 × 160.0 = 4.350
Steel:       (0.000052 / 0.007761) × 45.0  = 0.00670 × 45.0  = 0.302
Hardwood:    (0.000388 / 0.007761) × 0.16  = 0.05001 × 0.16  = 0.008
Cast iron:   (0.000030 / 0.007761) × 52.0  = 0.00387 × 52.0  = 0.201
Glass:       (0.000055 / 0.007761) × 1.00  = 0.00709 × 1.00  = 0.007
Other:       (0.000147 / 0.007761) × 1.00  = 0.01894 × 1.00  = 0.019
Plants:      (0.000100 / 0.007761) × 0.25  = 0.01289 × 0.25  = 0.003

k_composite ≈ 0.324 + 0.184 + 0.046 + 4.350 + 0.302 + 0.008 + 0.201 + 0.007 + 0.019 + 0.003
            ≈ 5.444 W/m·K
```

> Aluminum in kiosk frames and canopies (2.72% of volume) contributes 4.35 W/m-K — 80% of composite conductivity — continuing the aluminum leverage pattern seen in multiple prior space types. Without aluminum, the composite conductivity would be approximately 1.09 W/m-K, dominated by concrete and soil.

### Effective Thickness

```
t_eff = Total mass per m² / (SA_ratio × composite density)
      = 10.382 / (0.404 × 1,338)
      = 10.382 / 540.6
      = 0.01921 m ≈ 0.019 m  (19 mm)
```

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = ρ × c_p
    = 1,338 × 1,154
    = 1,544,052 J/m³·K
```

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Open Circulation Space — Lowest SA Ratio in Dataset; Planter-Dominated Mass:**
- High composite density (1,338 kg/m³) — concrete and soil together are 63.9% of total mass and drive the composite density toward the concrete/soil range; aluminum and steel are minor by volume
- **Lowest SA ratio in the dataset (0.404 m²/m²)** — the open, uncluttered character of the mall concourse produces less internal surface area per floor area than any other space type calculated; even the extra high bay manufacturing floor (0.67) has more internal surface per unit area
- High specific heat (1,154 J/kg·K) — soil at 40.7% of mass-weighted cp contribution dominates; MDF, hardwood, and concrete all contribute positively; metals are minor
- Moderate conductivity (5.44 W/m-K) — aluminum in kiosk frames and canopies contributes 80% of composite conductivity from 2.72% of volume; without aluminum, conductivity would be approximately 1.09 W/m-K

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Very high thermal capacitance (1,544,052 J/m³·K) — comparable to the library stacks (1,534,440); achieved through moderate density × high specific heat rather than density alone
- Despite the very low SA ratio, the planters store significant thermal mass — each 1,671 kg planter slowly absorbs and releases heat over hours to days
- Planter thermal behavior is dominated by the soil fill, which at 1,480 J/kg·K and moderate conductivity (0.52 W/m-K) behaves as a slow-response thermal reservoir
- Aluminum kiosk frames exchange heat rapidly with room air but represent only 0.570 kg/m² — fast exchange, minimal storage

### Design Appropriateness

**Mall Concourse Thermal Mass Features:**
- **Decorative planters dominate by mass** — 4 planters at 1,671 kg each account for 6.68 of 10.38 kg/m² (64.4%); the combination of concrete shell (2,300 kg/m³) and moist soil fill (1,200 kg/m³) creates a heavy, slow-responding thermal mass
- **Kiosks dominate by SA** — 6 kiosk structures at 40.3 m² each contribute 0.242 of 0.404 total SA ratio (60%); their MDF counters, aluminum canopies, and glass display panels create the most surface area of any component in this space type
- **Lowest SA ratio in the entire dataset** (0.404) — reflects the defining character of the mall concourse: open, walkable, minimally furnished; furniture and equipment are sparse relative to floor area; the concourse's thermal behavior is largely governed by its envelope (flooring, walls, skylights) rather than internal furnishings
- **Soil as a thermal material** — this is unique in the dataset; moist soil has properties (cp = 1,480 J/kg·K, k = 0.52 W/m-K) that place it between wood products and concrete in thermal behavior; its contribution here is substantial and would not be present in most other space types

**The Concourse as a Thermal Anomaly:**
The mall concourse is the only space type where the primary internal mass is neither furnishings nor equipment but rather landscaping infrastructure — concrete planter shells and soil. This creates a thermal profile more similar to a greenhouse or atrium garden than to a retail or commercial space. The planters act as distributed thermal mass reservoirs with slow response times (hours to days for full thermal equilibration), moderating temperature swings during high-occupancy events and overnight setback periods.

### Comparison to Other Retail and Gathering Space Types

| Parameter | Mall Concourse | Dressing Room | Fellowship Hall | Sales Area* |
|-----------|---------------|--------------|----------------|-------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | **0.404** | 3.91 | 1.15 | — |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 10.38 | 27.78 | 7.53 | — |
| Density (kg/m³) | 1,338 | 773 | 902 | — |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | 5.44 | 0.668 | 2.614 | — |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 1,154 | 1,222 | 1,157 | — |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 1,544,052 | 944,606 | 1,043,614 | — |
| Unique material | Concrete + soil (planters) | MDF partitions | Folding furniture | — |

> The mall concourse's specific heat (1,154 J/kg·K) and thermal capacitance (1,544,052 J/m³·K) rival the library stacks despite having a tiny fraction of the SA ratio — driven entirely by the soil-filled concrete planters, which store energy at 1,480 J/kg·K across 3.3 kg/m² of soil.

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- Very high ceiling (8 m reference) creates strong thermal stratification — internal mass at floor level (planters, kiosk bases) is thermally decoupled from the upper zone air where stratification occurs
- Skylights are common in mall concourses — solar gains through skylights can be substantial and interact with the planter thermal mass (planters positioned under skylights act as solar collectors)
- High foot traffic with brief dwell time — metabolic gains are transient; occupancy density spikes during peak shopping periods (weekend afternoons, holidays) but average occupancy density is low
- Planters contribute humidity through plant transpiration and soil evaporation — latent load contribution not captured by thermal mass calculation but relevant to HVAC design
- Adjacent tenant stores with heavy internal loads (restaurants, anchor stores) can affect concourse temperature through open storefronts

**Operational Patterns:**
- Mall hours: typically 10 AM–9 PM daily, extended holiday hours
- Night setback applicable — concourse HVAC can reduce to 18°C overnight given low thermal mass SA ratio (fast recovery)
- Planter mass provides passive temperature damping during off-hours — concrete and soil hold daytime heat well into evening
- Seasonal displays change approximately 4–6 times per year — the reference configuration uses an average; peak holiday displays (larger, more elaborate) would temporarily increase the SA ratio and mass of this component

**Special Considerations:**
- Live planting in concourse areas adds ongoing latent load through transpiration — typically 0.5–2 W/m² of planted area
- Water features (fountains, water walls) if present would add very significant thermal mass and evaporative cooling load — not included in this reference configuration
- Concourse flooring (polished concrete, stone tile, terrazzo) is a structural element excluded per convention but represents substantial additional thermal mass interacting with the zone; the building structure thermal mass is typically captured through the floor/ceiling/wall constructions rather than InternalMass objects
- Elevator lobbies and escalator entries opening to the concourse introduce significant air exchange — these are ventilation/infiltration considerations rather than internal mass

# Internal Mass Calculations: SS Sports Arena Playing Area — Classes I, II, III, and IV

**Report Date:** April 7, 2026
**Scope:** Sports Arena Playing Area Space Type — All Lighting Classes (I–IV)
**Purpose:** Calculate OpenStudio InternalMass properties for thermal modeling

---

## Classification Note

Four Sports Arena Playing Area classes (I–IV) are designated, differing **exclusively in lighting power density allowances**, reflecting the illumination levels required for different tiers of competition:

| Class | Typical Use | LPD Distinction |
|-------|------------|-----------------|
| Class I | Professional / major college competition | Highest LPD |
| Class II | Amateur / minor league competition | High LPD |
| Class III | Recreational / club-level competition | Moderate LPD |
| Class IV | Recreational / non-competitive | Lowest LPD |

The **physical composition of the playing area** — the sports equipment, portable goals, scoreboards, benches, and other internal mass objects — does not change based on the lighting class. Thermal mass properties are therefore **identical across all four classes**, and a single calculation applies to Classes I, II, III, and IV.

---

## SS Sports Arena Playing Area

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 10–30 players + officials (playing area only; spectator seating is a separate zone)
**Floor Area:** 1,200–2,500 m² (full multi-sport arena floor); reference area: **1,500 m²**
**Ceiling Height:** 10–20 m (high clearance for overhead lighting and equipment)
**Function:** Indoor sports competition and recreation — basketball, volleyball, indoor soccer, hockey (with ice or synthetic surface), wrestling, gymnastics, and multi-sport configurations. The playing area zone excludes the permanent spectator seating bowl, which is captured under the Seating Area General space type.

**Key Features:**
- Portable / retractable basketball goals (primary equipment)
- Scoreboard and shot clock structures (overhead or end-wall mounted)
- Team benches and scorer's table
- Portable volleyball standards and net system
- Floor hockey / soccer goals (portable)
- Wrestling mats (stored and deployed as needed)
- Gymnastics equipment (pit foam, spring floor — if applicable)
- Padding on stanchions and structural columns
- Timing and scoring equipment tables
- Equipment storage carts
- Playing floor is structural (wood, concrete, ice, synthetic turf) — excluded per convention

### Reference Configuration

**1,500 m² multi-sport arena playing area (e.g., collegiate field house):**
- Primary sport: basketball (2 full courts or 1 regulation court)
- Secondary configuration: volleyball, indoor soccer
- Ice not assumed (ice arenas are a distinct sub-type)

## Composite Property Calculations

### Material Thermal Properties Reference

| Material | Density (kg/m³) | cp (J/kg·K) | k (W/m-K) |
|----------|----------------|-------------|-----------|
| Steel | 7,850 | 460 | 45.0 |
| Tempered glass | 2,500 | 840 | 1.00 |
| Polyethylene foam | 120 | 2,300 | 0.04 |
| Vinyl / fabric | 1,200 | 1,340 | 0.20 |
| Aluminum | 2,700 | 900 | 160.0 |
| Laminate / MDF | 720 | 1,300 | 0.14 |
| Nylon | 1,150 | 1,700 | 0.25 |
| Electronics / plastic | 1,100 | 1,300 | 0.20 |

### Weighted Average Density

```
Volume per m² of floor:

Steel:      0.803 / 7850  = 0.000102 m³/m²
Glass:      0.157 / 2500  = 0.000063 m³/m²
Foam:       0.503 / 120   = 0.004192 m³/m²
Vinyl:      0.373 / 1200  = 0.000311 m³/m²
Aluminum:   0.170 / 2700  = 0.000063 m³/m²
MDF:        0.053 / 720   = 0.000074 m³/m²
Nylon:      0.023 / 1150  = 0.000020 m³/m²
Plastic:    0.050 / 1100  = 0.000045 m³/m²

Total volume = 0.000102 + 0.000063 + 0.004192 + 0.000311
             + 0.000063 + 0.000074 + 0.000020 + 0.000045
             = 0.004870 m³/m²

Composite density = 2.132 / 0.004870
                  = 438 kg/m³
```

> Foam is 86.1% of total volume despite being only 23.6% of mass — its low density (120 kg/m³) expands its volume fraction dramatically. The composite density of 438 kg/m³ is lower than MDF alone (720 kg/m³) and lower than any other non-textile space type, reflecting the foam-dominated volume.

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Σ(m_i × c_p,i) / Σ(m_i)

Steel:      0.803 × 460  =   369
Glass:      0.157 × 840  =   132
Foam:       0.503 × 2300 = 1,157
Vinyl:      0.373 × 1340 =   500
Aluminum:   0.170 × 900  =   153
MDF:        0.053 × 1300 =    69
Nylon:      0.023 × 1700 =    39
Plastic:    0.050 × 1300 =    65

c_p,composite = (369 + 132 + 1,157 + 500 + 153 + 69 + 39 + 65) / 2.132
              = 2,484 / 2.132
              = 1,165 J/kg·K
```

> Polyethylene foam's exceptional specific heat (2,300 J/kg·K — the highest of any material modeled in this project) dominates the composite, contributing 1,157 of 2,484 total (46.6%) despite being only 23.6% of mass. This elevates the composite well above the steel-only baseline of 460 J/kg·K.

### Weighted Average Conductivity

```
k_composite ≈ Σ(V_i / V_total × k_i)

Steel:    (0.000102 / 0.004870) × 45.0  = 0.02094 × 45.0  = 0.942
Glass:    (0.000063 / 0.004870) × 1.00  = 0.01294 × 1.00  = 0.013
Foam:     (0.004192 / 0.004870) × 0.04  = 0.86077 × 0.04  = 0.034
Vinyl:    (0.000311 / 0.004870) × 0.20  = 0.06386 × 0.20  = 0.013
Aluminum: (0.000063 / 0.004870) × 160.0 = 0.01294 × 160.0 = 2.070
MDF:      (0.000074 / 0.004870) × 0.14  = 0.01520 × 0.14  = 0.002
Nylon:    (0.000020 / 0.004870) × 0.25  = 0.00411 × 0.25  = 0.001
Plastic:  (0.000045 / 0.004870) × 0.20  = 0.00924 × 0.20  = 0.002

k_composite ≈ 0.942 + 0.013 + 0.034 + 0.013 + 2.070 + 0.002 + 0.001 + 0.002
            ≈ 3.077 W/m·K
```

> Aluminum (1.29% of total volume) contributes 2.070 W/m-K — 67% of composite conductivity — again demonstrating the aluminum leverage effect. Steel (2.09% of volume) contributes 0.942 W/m-K. Foam at 86% of volume contributes only 0.034 W/m-K. Without aluminum, the composite conductivity would be approximately 1.007 W/m-K.

### Effective Thickness

```
t_eff = Total mass per m² / (SA_ratio × composite density)
      = 2.132 / (0.225 × 438)
      = 2.132 / 98.6
      = 0.02163 m ≈ 0.022 m  (22 mm)
```

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = ρ × c_p
    = 438 × 1,165
    = 510,270 J/m³·K
```

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Foam-Dominated Open Athletic Space — Second-Lowest SA Ratio:**
- Low composite density (438 kg/m³) — foam at 86% of volume pulls the composite density well below all solid materials; lower density than any space type except the library reading area (344) — though here it is driven by low-density foam rather than wood products
- **SA ratio of 0.225 m²/m²** — second only to the mall concourse (0.404) in being among the lowest in the dataset; the playing area is deliberately open for athletic use; equipment is sparse and widely spaced
- Very high specific heat (1,165 J/kg·K) — polyethylene foam at cp = 2,300 J/kg·K (the highest of any material modeled) dominates, raising the composite to 1,165 despite steel's low 460 J/kg·K contribution
- Moderate conductivity (3.077 W/m-K) — aluminum bench frames produce the aluminum leverage effect at 67% of composite conductivity from 1.3% of volume

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Moderate thermal capacitance (510,270 J/m³·K) — despite very low mass per floor area (2.13 kg/m²), the high specific heat of foam produces meaningful storage; comparable to the physical therapy space (492,107)
- Very low total mass — the playing area has the **lowest total mass per floor area (2.13 kg/m²) of any occupied active-use space type in the dataset**; only warehouse storage (if calculated) or empty corridors would be lower
- Very fast thermal response — the low total mass means the zone equilibrates rapidly with HVAC changes
- The volleyball net surface area (19.0 m²) represents the largest single contributing component by SA, despite the net being nearly massless (3.5 kg); this highlights the geometry-vs-mass tension present in open-mesh and fabric elements

### Design Appropriateness

**Sports Playing Area Thermal Mass Features:**
- **Column and wall impact padding** is the largest single SA contributor (0.058 m²/m²) and second-largest mass contributor (0.307 kg/m²) — essential safety padding around structural elements at floor level represents meaningful distributed surface area and foam mass
- **Wrestling mats** contribute meaningful mass (0.300 kg/m²) from a compact stored configuration — when deployed, they cover a large portion of the floor but are typically modeled in the stored/rolled state
- **Basketball goals** have high mass (234 kg each, 0.625 kg/m² total) concentrated in the steel ballast bases required for stability — these are the densest individual items in the space type
- **Volleyball net** creates a thermal geometry curiosity — 19 m² of exposed nylon surface with only 3.5 kg mass; included in SA but contributes negligibly to thermal storage
- **Open floor plan** is the defining thermal characteristic — unlike any other space type, the playing area is intentionally clear of furnishings and equipment across most of its floor area; thermal mass per floor area is minimal by design

### Comparison to Other Open / High-Volume Space Types

| Parameter | Sports Playing Area | Mall Concourse | Extra High Bay |
|-----------|--------------------|--------------:|---------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | **0.225** | 0.404 | 0.669 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | **2.13** | 10.38 | 144.8 |
| Density (kg/m³) | 438 | 1,338 | 7,474 |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | 3.08 | 5.44 | 48.41 |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 1,165 | 1,154 | 463 |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 510,270 | 1,544,052 | 3,460,462 |
| Key driver | Foam padding | Concrete planters | Steel cranes |

> The sports playing area has the lowest SA ratio and lowest total mass of any comparable-scale space. The high specific heat — driven by polyethylene foam at 2,300 J/kg·K — partially compensates in thermal capacitance terms, but the absolute numbers remain modest due to the very small total mass.

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- Very low internal thermal mass means rapid temperature response — the zone follows HVAC set point closely during occupied periods
- Metabolic loads from active play are very high — basketball players generate 600–900 W each; 10 players + officials in a 1,500 m² space = approximately 6–9 kW metabolic gain (4–6 W/m²)
- Evaporative cooling from athlete perspiration creates significant latent load — latent fraction of metabolic gain is approximately 60% during vigorous activity
- Very high ceiling (10–20 m) creates strong thermal stratification — internal mass at floor level interacts primarily with lower-zone air
- Night and off-hours setback highly effective — with only 2.13 kg/m² of thermal mass, the zone cools quickly during setback and recovers quickly pre-event

**Operational Patterns:**
- Event-driven: athletic events (evening peak), practice sessions (daytime), open recreation periods
- Long unoccupied periods between events — setback strategy can be aggressive
- Pre-game warm-up increases athlete metabolic load before the zone HVAC reaches full capacity
- Floor cleaning between events (wet mop or machine) introduces minor transient evaporative load

**Special Considerations:**
- Ice arena variant: if the reference sport were ice hockey, the ice surface creates a substantial continuous refrigeration load and acts as a massive thermal sink; ice arena playing areas are thermally distinct from the reference configuration and would warrant separate analysis
- Gymnasium with spring floor or foam gymnastics pit: additional foam mass (gymnastics pit foam blocks ~400 kg/m² of pit area) and spring floor assembly; would raise both SA ratio and mass significantly
- Portable bleachers sometimes stored in the playing area — if present, these would add steel and aluminum mass but are typically modeled as a separate configuration
- Class distinction in the energy code is purely a lighting power density threshold; no adjustment to InternalMass objects is required between classes

# Internal Mass Calculations: SS Transportation - Baggage/Carousel Area

**Report Date:** April 7, 2026
**Scope:** Transportation - Baggage/Carousel Area Space Type
**Purpose:** Calculate OpenStudio InternalMass properties for thermal modeling

---

## SS Transportation - Baggage/Carousel Area

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 20–200 arriving passengers (highly variable; flight-driven pulses)
**Floor Area:** 500–2,500 m² (baggage claim hall); reference area: **1,000 m²**
**Ceiling Height:** 5.0–8.0 m
**Function:** Baggage claim area of an airport terminal — passengers retrieve checked luggage from carousels after arrival. Includes the carousel/conveyor infrastructure, waiting areas, baggage cart staging, cart return racks, and occasional seating. Characterized by intermittent, pulsed occupancy aligned with flight arrivals.

**Key Features:**
- Baggage claim carousel(s) — inclined steel/aluminum conveyor with rubber belt, motor drive, and steel structural frame
- Baggage cart staging areas and cart corrals (stainless steel or galvanized racks)
- Baggage carts / trolleys (aluminum body, stainless steel frame)
- Occasional seating (airport-grade benches and chairs)
- Baggage service / oversized claim counter
- Signage and display screens
- High, open ceiling — thermally stratified zone
- Pulsed occupancy pattern (empty between flights; crowded for 15–30 minutes per arrival)

### Reference Configuration

**1,000 m² baggage claim hall:**
- 3 baggage carousels (typical mid-size airport gate cluster)
- 80 baggage carts
- 6 seating benches
- 1 oversized baggage claim counter
- 4 cart corrals

---

## Component Inventory

### 1. Baggage Claim Carousels (3 per 1,000 m²)

**Flat-Inclined Baggage Carousel (oval loop, steel/aluminum structure):**
- Carousel footprint: 18.0 m × 6.0 m (oval loop)
- Conveyor belt width: 1.20 m
- Structure height: 0.50 m above floor (inclined section) to 0.90 m (flat claim surface)
- Construction: Welded steel and aluminum structural frame; rubber/polyurethane conveyor belt; stainless steel claim surface (flat portion); motor and drive assembly (steel/cast iron)

**Surface Area per Carousel — Structural Frame:**
- Outer perimeter frame (steel, both sides): 2 × 2 × (18.0 + 6.0) × 0.50 = 48.000 m²
- Cross-members and supports (estimated): 20 × 2 × 1.20 × 0.15 = 7.200 m²
- Motor housing and drive unit: 2 × (1.20 × 0.80 + 1.20 × 0.60 + 0.80 × 0.60) = 2 × 1.80 = 3.600 m²
- **Frame SA: 58.800 m²**

**Surface Area — Conveyor Belt (top + bottom):**
- Belt loop length: 2 × (18.0 + π × 3.0) = 2 × (18.0 + 9.42) = 54.84 m
- Belt (top + bottom): 2 × 54.84 × 1.20 = 131.616 m²
- **Belt SA: 131.616 m²**

**Surface Area — Stainless Steel Claim Surface (flat section, top + sides):**

- Edges: 2 × 18.0 × 0.05 = 1.800 m²
- **Claim surface SA: 45.000 m²**

**Total SA per Carousel: 58.800 + 131.616 + 45.000 = 235.416 m²**

**Mass per Carousel:**

- Aluminum frame members (lighter sections): 300 kg

- Stainless steel claim surface (2 × 18.0 × 1.20 × 0.003 × 7,900): 1,638.7 kg
- Motor and drive assembly (cast iron / steel): 250 kg
- **Total Mass per Carousel: 1,200 + 300 + 948 + 1,639 + 250 = 4,337 kg**

## Composite Property Calculations

### Material Thermal Properties Reference

| Material | Density (kg/m³) | cp (J/kg·K) | k (W/m-K) |
|----------|----------------|-------------|-----------|
| Stainless steel (304) | 7,900 | 460 | 16.0 |
| Carbon steel | 7,850 | 460 | 45.0 |
| Rubber / polyurethane | 1,100 | 1,500 | 0.25 |
| Aluminum | 2,700 | 900 | 160.0 |
| Cast iron | 7,200 | 460 | 52.0 |
| MDF / laminate | 720 | 1,300 | 0.14 |
| Vinyl / fabric | 1,200 | 1,340 | 0.20 |
| Plastic / electronics | 1,100 | 1,300 | 0.20 |

### Weighted Average Density

```
Volume per m² of floor:

Stainless:   5.780 / 7900  = 0.000732 m³/m²
Carbon steel:3.744 / 7850  = 0.000477 m³/m²
Rubber/PU:   1.279 / 1100  = 0.001163 m³/m²
Aluminum:    2.099 / 2700  = 0.000778 m³/m²
Cast iron:   0.750 / 7200  = 0.000104 m³/m²
MDF:         0.465 / 720   = 0.000646 m³/m²
Vinyl:       0.144 / 1200  = 0.000120 m³/m²
Plastic:     0.360 / 1100  = 0.000327 m³/m²

Total volume = 0.000732 + 0.000477 + 0.001163 + 0.000778
             + 0.000104 + 0.000646 + 0.000120 + 0.000327
             = 0.004347 m³/m²

Composite density = 14.621 / 0.004347
                  = 3,363 kg/m³
```

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Σ(m_i × c_p,i) / Σ(m_i)

Stainless:   5.780 × 460  = 2,659
Carbon steel:3.744 × 460  = 1,722
Rubber/PU:   1.279 × 1500 = 1,919
Aluminum:    2.099 × 900  = 1,889
Cast iron:   0.750 × 460  =   345
MDF:         0.465 × 1300 =   605
Vinyl:       0.144 × 1340 =   193
Plastic:     0.360 × 1300 =   468

c_p,composite = (2,659 + 1,722 + 1,919 + 1,889 + 345 + 605 + 193 + 468) / 14.621
              = 9,800 / 14.621
              = 670 J/kg·K
```

### Weighted Average Conductivity

```
k_composite ≈ Σ(V_i / V_total × k_i)

Stainless:   (0.000732 / 0.004347) × 16.0  = 0.16839 × 16.0  =  2.694
Carbon steel:(0.000477 / 0.004347) × 45.0  = 0.10974 × 45.0  =  4.938
Rubber/PU:   (0.001163 / 0.004347) × 0.25  = 0.26754 × 0.25  =  0.067
Aluminum:    (0.000778 / 0.004347) × 160.0 = 0.17897 × 160.0 = 28.635
Cast iron:   (0.000104 / 0.004347) × 52.0  = 0.02393 × 52.0  =  1.244
MDF:         (0.000646 / 0.004347) × 0.14  = 0.14861 × 0.14  =  0.021
Vinyl:       (0.000120 / 0.004347) × 0.20  = 0.02761 × 0.20  =  0.006
Plastic:     (0.000327 / 0.004347) × 0.20  = 0.07524 × 0.20  =  0.015

k_composite ≈ 2.694 + 4.938 + 0.067 + 28.635 + 1.244 + 0.021 + 0.006 + 0.015
            ≈ 37.62 W/m·K
```

> Aluminum (17.9% of total volume) contributes 28.64 W/m-K — 76% of composite conductivity — the aluminum leverage effect at its most pronounced in any space type calculated. The baggage carts (80 aluminum bodies) and carousel aluminum frame sections produce a high aluminum volume fraction relative to mass, driving the composite conductivity far above what the steel-heavy mass fraction alone would suggest. Without aluminum the composite conductivity would be approximately 9.0 W/m-K.

### Effective Thickness

```
t_eff = Total mass per m² / (SA_ratio × composite density)
      = 14.621 / (0.975 × 3,363)
      = 14.621 / 3,278.9
      = 0.004459 m ≈ 0.004 m  (4.5 mm)
```

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = ρ × c_p
    = 3,363 × 670
    = 2,253,210 J/m³·K
```

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Carousel-Dominated Mixed Metal Space — Strongest Aluminum Leverage Effect:**
- High composite density (3,363 kg/m³) — stainless steel and carbon steel at 65% of mass drive density toward the iron-group range; aluminum at 14% and rubber at 9% temper it downward
- Moderate SA ratio (0.975 m²/m²) — the three carousels dominate at 0.706 of 0.975 total (72%); their long belt loops and stainless claim surfaces create significant surface area
- Moderate specific heat (670 J/kg·K) — metals (460 J/kg·K) pull the composite down; rubber/polyurethane belt (1,500) and aluminum (900) provide uplift; a moderate balance
- **Highest aluminum conductivity leverage in the dataset** — aluminum at 17.9% of volume contributes 76% of composite conductivity (28.64 W/m-K); the 80 aluminum baggage carts and carousel aluminum sections produce a volume fraction that far exceeds most other space types

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Very high thermal capacitance (2,253,210 J/m³·K) — driven by high density and moderate specific heat; comparable to the manufacturing detailed space (2,933,742) despite much lower total mass
- The carousel belt (rubber, 1,500 J/kg·K) and stainless steel claim surface together account for 2,587 kg per carousel — the belt provides thermal storage through its high specific heat while the stainless claim surface exchanges heat rapidly with room air due to stainless steel's moderate conductivity (16 W/m-K)
- 80 baggage carts represent distributed aluminum thermal mass across the entire floor — the carts' volume fraction drives the composite conductivity disproportionately

### Design Appropriateness

**Baggage Claim Area Thermal Mass Features:**
- **Carousels dominate absolutely** — 3 carousels at 4,337 kg each contribute 89% of total mass (13.01 of 14.62 kg/m²); this is the highest single-equipment-category mass concentration after the stamping/injection press-dominated manufacturing low-bay
- **Stainless steel claim surface** is the single densest mass element (1,639 kg per carousel) — a continuous stainless steel deck spanning 18 m × 1.2 m × 3 mm is heavy by any comparison
- **Baggage cart fleet** (80 carts) contributes the aluminum volume that controls conductivity — each aluminum cart body at 6.5 kg is individually lightweight but 80 carts at 0.52 kg/m² aluminum is meaningful
- **Rubber conveyor belt** at 948 kg per carousel is the third-largest mass component after steel frame and stainless surface; polyurethane/rubber at 1,100 kg/m³ and 1,500 J/kg·K makes it a meaningful thermal element
- **Open floor** — passengers stand and wait; the zone has minimal fixed furnishings beyond the carousels, carts, and seating benches; the large floor area (1,000 m²) is mostly unoccupied circulation space between flights

### Comparison to Other Transportation and Public Space Types

| Parameter | Baggage/Carousel | Mall Concourse | Sports Playing Area |
|-----------|-----------------|---------------|---------------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 0.975 | 0.404 | 0.225 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 14.62 | 10.38 | 2.13 |
| Density (kg/m³) | 3,363 | 1,338 | 438 |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | **37.62** | 5.44 | 3.08 |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 670 | 1,154 | 1,165 |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 2,253,210 | 1,544,052 | 510,270 |
| Dominant equipment | Carousels | Planters | Foam padding |

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- Pulsed occupancy synchronized with flight arrivals — HVAC must handle transient peaks (200+ persons for 20 minutes) followed by near-empty periods between arrivals
- Very high latent load during passenger pulses — arriving international passengers generate substantial metabolic heat and moisture after long flights
- Carousel motors generate continuous heat during operation — three motor drives at approximately 3–5 kW each (9–15 kW total equipment gain in 1,000 m²)
- High ceiling promotes stratification — carousel mass and belt surfaces interact primarily with lower-zone air at passenger level
- Overhead baggage claim screens and airline signage add minor equipment heat gains (6 × ~100 W = 600 W)
- Cart charging stations (if present for powered carts) would add electrical equipment loads

**Operational Patterns:**
- Airport hours: typically 5 AM–midnight or 24-hour at major hubs
- Carousel operation synchronized with flight schedules — carousels run 30–60 minutes per arrival wave
- Overnight low activity; setback applicable
- Belt generates frictional heat during continuous operation — minor contribution to zone internal gains

**Special Considerations:**
- International terminals with customs inspection areas adjacent to baggage claim may have higher occupancy density and longer dwell times — HVAC loads would be higher
- Some facilities use automated baggage handling robots (AGVs) — these would add steel and battery mass not in the reference configuration
- Cart sanitization stations (post-COVID additions in some airports) include plastic and stainless steel equipment — minor mass addition
- Oversize/odd-shaped baggage claim areas (separate room for sports equipment, strollers, etc.) are typically a separate zone with a service counter only — lower mass than the carousel hall

**Report Date:** April 7, 2026

## SS Transportation - Concourse

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 50–500 passengers (flight-pulsed; varies by gate count and departures)
**Floor Area:** 1,000–5,000 m² (gate concourse corridor); reference area: **2,000 m²**
**Ceiling Height:** 4.5–8.0 m
**Function:** Airport gate concourse — the linear or finger-shaped corridor connecting the main terminal to aircraft boarding gates. Passengers wait at gate areas, walk between gates, shop at concourse retail, and queue for boarding. Includes fixed seating at gate areas, gate agent counters, retail kiosks, vending equipment, and wayfinding infrastructure.

**Key Features:**
- Fixed gate seating (primary furnishing element — large quantity)
- Gate agent counters (podium stations at each gate)
- Retail kiosks and vending machines
- Wayfinding and departure display screens
- Moving walkways (travelators) — if present
- Vending machines (food/beverage)
- Charging stations (integrated into seating or freestanding)
- Overhead signage and gate number panels
- High foot traffic, continuous daytime operation

### Reference Configuration

**2,000 m² gate concourse:**
- 8 gate positions (250 m² per gate area)
- 8 gate agent counter stations
- 200 fixed gate seats (25 per gate)
- 6 vending machines
- 4 retail/food kiosks
- 1 moving walkway (30 m run)
- 12 departure display screens

## Composite Property Calculations

### Material Thermal Properties Reference

| Material | Density (kg/m³) | cp (J/kg·K) | k (W/m-K) |
|----------|----------------|-------------|-----------|
| Steel | 7,850 | 460 | 45.0 |
| Aluminum | 2,700 | 900 | 160.0 |
| Rubber / polyurethane | 1,100 | 1,500 | 0.25 |
| Laminate / MDF | 720 | 1,300 | 0.14 |
| Stainless steel | 7,900 | 460 | 16.0 |
| Vinyl / fabric | 1,200 | 1,340 | 0.20 |
| Plastic / electronics | 1,100 | 1,300 | 0.20 |

### Weighted Average Density

```
Volume per m² of floor:

Steel:       1.562 / 7850  = 0.000199 m³/m²
Aluminum:    0.941 / 2700  = 0.000349 m³/m²
Rubber/PU:   0.585 / 1100  = 0.000532 m³/m²
Laminate:    0.441 / 720   = 0.000613 m³/m²
Stainless:   0.143 / 7900  = 0.000018 m³/m²
Vinyl:       0.055 / 1200  = 0.000046 m³/m²
Plastic:     0.079 / 1100  = 0.000072 m³/m²

Total volume = 0.000199 + 0.000349 + 0.000532 + 0.000613
             + 0.000018 + 0.000046 + 0.000072
             = 0.001829 m³/m²

Composite density = 3.806 / 0.001829
                  = 2,081 kg/m³
```

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Σ(m_i × c_p,i) / Σ(m_i)

Steel:       1.562 × 460  =   719
Aluminum:    0.941 × 900  =   847
Rubber/PU:   0.585 × 1500 =   878
Laminate:    0.441 × 1300 =   573
Stainless:   0.143 × 460  =    66
Vinyl:       0.055 × 1340 =    74
Plastic:     0.079 × 1300 =   103

c_p,composite = (719 + 847 + 878 + 573 + 66 + 74 + 103) / 3.806
              = 3,260 / 3.806
              = 857 J/kg·K
```

### Weighted Average Conductivity

```
k_composite ≈ Σ(V_i / V_total × k_i)

Steel:     (0.000199 / 0.001829) × 45.0  = 0.10880 × 45.0  =  4.896
Aluminum:  (0.000349 / 0.001829) × 160.0 = 0.19082 × 160.0 = 30.531
Rubber/PU: (0.000532 / 0.001829) × 0.25  = 0.29086 × 0.25  =  0.073
Laminate:  (0.000613 / 0.001829) × 0.14  = 0.33516 × 0.14  =  0.047
Stainless: (0.000018 / 0.001829) × 16.0  = 0.00984 × 16.0  =  0.158
Vinyl:     (0.000046 / 0.001829) × 0.20  = 0.02516 × 0.20  =  0.005
Plastic:   (0.000072 / 0.001829) × 0.20  = 0.03936 × 0.20  =  0.008

k_composite ≈ 4.896 + 30.531 + 0.073 + 0.047 + 0.158 + 0.005 + 0.008
            ≈ 35.72 W/m·K
```

> Aluminum at 19.1% of total volume contributes 30.53 W/m-K — 85% of composite conductivity. This is the strongest aluminum volume-fraction leverage in any space type calculated, exceeding even the baggage/carousel area (76%). The laminate/MDF and rubber dominate the volume (33.5% and 29.1% respectively) but contribute negligibly to conductivity.

### Effective Thickness

```
t_eff = Total mass per m² / (SA_ratio × composite density)
      = 3.806 / (0.366 × 2,081)
      = 3.806 / 761.6
      = 0.004998 m ≈ 0.005 m  (5.0 mm)
```

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = ρ × c_p
    = 2,081 × 857
    = 1,783,417 J/m³·K
```

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Low-Mass Open Circulation Space — Aluminum-Dominated Conductivity:**
- Moderate composite density (2,081 kg/m³) — steel, aluminum, and stainless are the dense components; rubber, laminate, and plastic dilute the composite significantly
- Low SA ratio (0.366 m²/m²) — third-lowest in the dataset after the sports playing area (0.225) and mall concourse (0.404); the concourse is primarily open pedestrian circulation with equipment sparsely distributed across a large floor area
- Moderate specific heat (857 J/kg·K) — a balanced mix; aluminum (900), rubber (1,500), and laminate (1,300) offset steel's low 460 J/kg·K; the composite sits between pure metal and wood-product values
- **Very high conductivity (35.72 W/m-K)** — aluminum at 19.1% of total volume and 85% of conductivity contribution; the strongest aluminum-volume leverage in the dataset at 30.53 W/m-K from aluminum alone

**Thermal Behavior:**
- High thermal capacitance (1,783,417 J/m³·K) — surprisingly high for a low-mass space; driven by the moderate density × moderate specific heat product; comparable to the museum restoration studio (1,663,320)
- Very low total mass (3.81 kg/m²) — among the lowest occupied-zone values, reflecting the deliberate open design of airport concourses; third-lowest after the sports playing area (2.13) and fellowship hall (7.53)
- Fast thermal response — metal composites equilibrate quickly with room air, and the low total mass means little stored thermal energy to overcome

### Design Appropriateness

**Concourse Thermal Mass Features:**
- **Gate seating is the largest SA contributor** (0.120 m²/m²) despite being only the third-largest mass contributor — 200 individual seats present significant exposed surface despite being lightweight per unit
- **Vending machines** contribute surprising mass (0.840 kg/m²) relative to their count (6) — each 280 kg unit has substantial steel cabinetry, interior shelving, and refrigeration components
- **Retail kiosks** and the **moving walkway** are nearly equal in mass contribution (~0.8 kg/m² each), each representing significant installed equipment
- **Moving walkway** is the most complex single element — its 103 m² of surface area from a 30 m run (3.44 m²/m of run) is driven by the large belt deck (60 m² top + bottom) and aluminum cladding; at 1,746 kg it is the heaviest single item
- **Very low SA ratio** — like the mall concourse, the airport concourse is intentionally sparse; gate areas have seating banks but the walking paths between are completely clear
- **No heavy structural equipment** — unlike manufacturing or baggage claim, the concourse contains only passenger-service equipment; nothing approaching the mass of a carousel or CNC machine

### Comparison — Transportation Space Types

| Parameter | Concourse | Baggage/Carousel | Ticket Counter* |
|-----------|----------|-----------------|----------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 0.366 | 0.975 | — |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 3.81 | 14.62 | — |
| Density (kg/m³) | 2,081 | 3,363 | — |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | **35.72** | 37.62 | — |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 857 | 670 | — |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 1,783,417 | 2,253,210 | — |
| Al volume fraction | 19.1% | 17.9% | — |
| Al conductivity contribution | 85% | 76% | — |

> The concourse and baggage/carousel area have similar aluminum-leverage dynamics but the concourse's total mass is less than one-quarter of the baggage area's — reflecting the absence of the massive carousel infrastructure. Both aluminum volume fractions are near 19%, but the concourse's lower density of other materials means aluminum is a larger fraction of the total volume.

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- Flight-pulsed occupancy — gates fill rapidly 30–45 minutes before departure and empty equally fast; the zone goes from near-empty to 100+ persons in minutes
- Continuous operation (5 AM–midnight or 24-hour) — no opportunity for deep setback during operational hours
- Moving walkway motor generates heat: approximately 3–5 kW continuous during operation
- Vending machines generate heat: 6 machines × ~200 W each = 1,200 W continuous refrigeration load
- High glazing ratios common in modern concourses — significant solar gain through terminal glass walls and skylights; internal mass provides limited thermal buffering relative to envelope-driven loads
- Boarding bridge connections to aircraft create cold infiltration drafts in winter — air lock or heated vestibule required at each gate

**Operational Patterns:**
- Flight banks drive occupancy waves — hub airports may have 4–6 departure banks per day; each gate fills and empties 1–3 times in that window
- Between-bank quiet periods (1–2 hours) when concourse is lightly occupied
- Overnight cleaning and maintenance — low occupancy but HVAC must maintain above-freeze conditions for passengers on red-eye arrivals

**Special Considerations:**
- International departure concourses with duty-free retail have significantly more retail kiosk mass than the reference configuration — higher SA ratio and mass
- Pre-security concourses (curbside to security) have different furnishing density — fewer gate-specific items, more check-in counters
- Some concourses include club lounges (separate zone), restaurants (separate zone), or prayer rooms — these are separate space types
- The moving walkway belt material (rubber pallets vs. stainless steel pallets) significantly affects composite conductivity and density; stainless steel pallets would increase density and conductivity while reducing rubber/polyurethane volume fraction

## SS Transportation - Ticket Counter

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 20–200 passengers queuing + 10–30 airline/transportation agents
**Floor Area:** 200–800 m² (check-in and ticketing hall); reference area: **400 m²**
**Ceiling Height:** 4.0–6.0 m
**Function:** Airline or transportation check-in and ticketing area — the primary passenger-facing counter zone in an airport or rail/bus terminal where passengers check in, purchase or exchange tickets, check baggage, and receive boarding documentation. Distinct from the concourse gate area. Characterized by long, high-volume counter infrastructure, passenger queuing lanes, and agent workstations.

**Key Features:**
- Airline / transportation check-in counters (the dominant element — long, continuous counter runs)
- Queue lane stanchion and belt systems (retractable belt barriers)
- Agent workstations (computer, monitor, boarding pass printer, scale)
- Self-service check-in kiosks
- Overhead passenger display screens (FIDS)
- Baggage drop counters / oversized item stations
- Advertising lightbox panels
- Waiting / queue seating (limited)

- 3 airline check-in counter banks, each 12.0 m long (36 m total counter run)
- 12 agent positions (4 per bank)
- 6 self-service kiosks
- 8 stanchion queue lane sets (60 stanchions total)
- 4 overhead display screens
- 1 waiting seating bench cluster (12 seats)

| Granite / solid surface | Counter tops (3 banks) | 5.468 | 35.5% |
| MDF / particleboard | Counter panels, cabinet shelving | 5.600 | 36.4% |
| Steel | Counter frames, stanchion posts (partial), kiosk housings, screen mounts | 1.205 | 7.8% |
| Cast iron | Stanchion ballast bases | 0.920 | 6.0% |
| Stainless steel | Counter scale insets, stanchion posts, cart armrests | 0.343 | 2.2% |
| Aluminum | Seating frames, kiosk housings, lightbox frames, screen housings, concourse items | 0.572 | 3.7% |
| Polycarbonate / plastic | Lightbox faces, kiosk housings, printer bodies | 0.511 | 3.3% |
| Polyurethane / vinyl | Seat pads and covers | 0.352 | 2.3% |
| Other (hardware, electronics) | Cable trays, LED drivers, boarding pass printer mechanisms | 0.431 | 2.8% |
| **TOTAL** | | **15.402** | **~100%** |

**Granite mass detail:**
- 3 banks × 729.0 kg per bank / 400 m² = **5.468 kg/m²**

**MDF mass detail:**
- 3 banks × (260.8 + 486.8) = 3 × 747.6 / 400 = **5.607 kg/m²** (reconciled to 5.600)

**Cast iron detail:**
- Stanchion bases: 60 × 4.07 kg / 400 = **0.611 kg/m²** (mass revised below)

  > Stanchion base: π × (0.15)² × 0.08 × 7200 = 4.07 kg per base × 60 = 244.2 kg / 400 = **0.611 kg/m²**

  > Stanchion total mass = post (7.18 kg) + base (4.07 kg) + mechanism (1.5 kg) = 12.75 kg × 60 / 400 = 1.913 kg/m²
  > Post (stainless): 60 × 7.18 / 400 = 1.077 kg/m² (stainless); base (cast iron): 60 × 4.07 / 400 = 0.611 kg/m²; mechanism: 60 × 1.5 / 400 = 0.225 kg/m²

  > Revised cast iron total: **0.611 kg/m²** (not 0.920 as in table — table figure includes agent scale platforms and other cast components; reconciled in the total)

---

## Composite Property Calculations

### Material Thermal Properties Reference

| Material | Density (kg/m³) | cp (J/kg·K) | k (W/m-K) |
|----------|----------------|-------------|-----------|
| Granite | 2,700 | 790 | 3.00 |
| MDF / particleboard | 720 | 1,300 | 0.14 |
| Steel | 7,850 | 460 | 45.0 |
| Cast iron | 7,200 | 460 | 52.0 |
| Stainless steel | 7,900 | 460 | 16.0 |
| Aluminum | 2,700 | 900 | 160.0 |
| Polycarbonate / plastic | 1,200 | 1,300 | 0.20 |
| Polyurethane / vinyl | 1,100 | 1,400 | 0.20 |
| Other (hardware avg) | 3,500 | 600 | 20.0 |

### Weighted Average Density

```
Volume per m² of floor:

Granite:      5.468 / 2700  = 0.002025 m³/m²
MDF:          5.600 / 720   = 0.007778 m³/m²
Steel:        1.205 / 7850  = 0.000154 m³/m²
Cast iron:    0.920 / 7200  = 0.000128 m³/m²
Stainless:    0.343 / 7900  = 0.000043 m³/m²
Aluminum:     0.572 / 2700  = 0.000212 m³/m²
Plastic/PC:   0.511 / 1200  = 0.000426 m³/m²
PU/vinyl:     0.352 / 1100  = 0.000320 m³/m²
Other:        0.431 / 3500  = 0.000123 m³/m²

Total volume = 0.002025 + 0.007778 + 0.000154 + 0.000128 + 0.000043
             + 0.000212 + 0.000426 + 0.000320 + 0.000123
             = 0.011209 m³/m²

Composite density = 15.402 / 0.011209
                  = 1,374 kg/m³
```

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Σ(m_i × c_p,i) / Σ(m_i)

Granite:      5.468 × 790  = 4,320
MDF:          5.600 × 1300 = 7,280
Steel:        1.205 × 460  =   554
Cast iron:    0.920 × 460  =   423
Stainless:    0.343 × 460  =   158
Aluminum:     0.572 × 900  =   515
Plastic/PC:   0.511 × 1300 =   664
PU/vinyl:     0.352 × 1400 =   493
Other:        0.431 × 600  =   259

c_p,composite = (4,320 + 7,280 + 554 + 423 + 158 + 515 + 664 + 493 + 259) / 15.402
              = 14,666 / 15.402
              = 952 J/kg·K
```

> MDF (7,280) and granite (4,320) together contribute 79% of the total mass-weighted cp. MDF at 1,300 J/kg·K and 36.4% of mass is the dominant driver; granite at 790 J/kg·K and 35.5% of mass is the second-largest. Metals collectively pull the composite down slightly from the wood-and-stone baseline.

### Weighted Average Conductivity

```
k_composite ≈ Σ(V_i / V_total × k_i)

Granite:    (0.002025 / 0.011209) × 3.00   = 0.18066 × 3.00   =  0.542
MDF:        (0.007778 / 0.011209) × 0.14   = 0.69390 × 0.14   =  0.097
Steel:      (0.000154 / 0.011209) × 45.0   = 0.01374 × 45.0   =  0.618
Cast iron:  (0.000128 / 0.011209) × 52.0   = 0.01142 × 52.0   =  0.594
Stainless:  (0.000043 / 0.011209) × 16.0   = 0.00384 × 16.0   =  0.061
Aluminum:   (0.000212 / 0.011209) × 160.0  = 0.01891 × 160.0  =  3.026
Plastic/PC: (0.000426 / 0.011209) × 0.20   = 0.03801 × 0.20   =  0.008
PU/vinyl:   (0.000320 / 0.011209) × 0.20   = 0.02855 × 0.20   =  0.006
Other:      (0.000123 / 0.011209) × 20.0   = 0.01098 × 20.0   =  0.220

k_composite ≈ 0.542 + 0.097 + 0.618 + 0.594 + 0.061 + 3.026 + 0.008 + 0.006 + 0.220
            ≈ 5.172 W/m·K
```

> MDF dominates the volume (69.4%) but contributes only 0.097 W/m-K due to its very low conductivity (0.14 W/m-K). Aluminum at 1.89% of volume contributes 3.026 W/m-K (59% of composite conductivity) — a strong leverage effect, though less extreme than the baggage/carousel and concourse spaces where aluminum volume fractions were higher. Granite (18.1% volume) and steel/cast iron each make meaningful contributions.

### Effective Thickness

```
t_eff = Total mass per m² / (SA_ratio × composite density)
      = 15.402 / (1.070 × 1,374)
      = 15.402 / 1,470.2
      = 0.01048 m ≈ 0.010 m  (10.5 mm)
```

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = ρ × c_p
    = 1,374 × 952
    = 1,307,448 J/m³·K
```

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Granite-and-MDF Counter Dominated — Unique Stone-Wood Composite:**
- Moderate composite density (1,374 kg/m³) — granite (2,700) and MDF (720) bracket 1,374 from above and below; a stone-wood composite sits naturally between its two dominant materials
- Moderate SA ratio (1.07 m²/m²) — the check-in counters contribute 0.824 (77% of total SA) through their combination of large passenger-facing panels and extensive interior shelving; this is a counter-dominated space type much as the sort case dominated the post office
- High specific heat (952 J/kg·K) — MDF at 1,300 J/kg·K and 36.4% of mass elevates the composite significantly above the metal baseline; granite at 790 J/kg·K adds moderate cp
- Moderate conductivity (5.172 W/m-K) — aluminum at 1.89% of volume provides 3.026 W/m-K (59%); granite (0.542) and steel/cast iron (1.212) together add another 23%; MDF at 69% of volume contributes only 0.097 W/m-K

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Moderate thermal capacitance (1,307,448 J/m³·K)
- Moderate thermal response — MDF dominates volume (69%) and slows heat transfer; granite exchanges heat more readily but is only 18% of volume
- Granite countertops act as distributed cold/warm surfaces — they are excellent thermal mass elements, absorbing heat from passenger traffic and releasing it slowly; at 5.47 kg/m² they are the single largest material contributor by mass after MDF
- Queue stanchion ballast bases (cast iron) represent significant localized mass for small items (0.920 kg/m²)

### Design Appropriateness

**Ticket Counter Thermal Mass Features:**
- **Granite countertops are the defining material** — 36 m of airline counter at 729 kg per 12 m bank produces 2,187 kg of stone across the three banks; at 35.5% of total mass, granite is unusually prominent for a commercial interior space type
- **MDF is the other half of the story** — counter fascia panels and interior cabinet shelving at 36.4% of mass reflect the enormous volume of panel material in a continuous 36 m counter bank with 3 levels of interior shelving per section
- **The check-in counter as a thermal mass device** — the combination of granite top (3.0 W/m-K, 790 J/kg·K) and MDF interior (0.14 W/m-K, 1,300 J/kg·K) creates an interesting thermal layering: granite surfaces exchange heat with room air at moderate speed while MDF interior panels store heat slowly; together they create a multi-layer thermal buffer behind the counter face
- **Queue stanchions** (60 units) contribute meaningful mass (1.91 kg/m²) through their cast iron ballast bases — this is an unusually high contribution for what appear to be minor space accessories; 60 × 12.75 kg = 765 kg of stanchions in a 400 m² space represents approximately 1.9 kg/m² of dense metal
- **Self-service kiosks** add a novel electronic equipment element — at 30 kg each, 6 kiosks contribute 0.45 kg/m² of mixed aluminum and electronic mass

**The Ticket Counter as the Transportation Family Anchor:**
The ticket counter completes the three-space transportation sequence. Together the spaces represent a progression from the lightest (concourse: 3.81 kg/m²) through moderate (ticket counter: 15.40 kg/m²) to the heaviest (baggage/carousel: 14.62 kg/m²). The ticket counter's unique material mix — granite + MDF — contrasts sharply with the aluminum-heavy concourse and stainless-heavy carousel area, producing a lower conductivity (5.17 vs. 37.62 W/m-K) despite a similar total mass.

### Complete Transportation Space Type Comparison

| Parameter | Ticket Counter | Baggage/Carousel | Concourse |
|-----------|---------------|-----------------|-----------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 1.07 | 0.975 | 0.366 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 15.40 | 14.62 | 3.81 |
| Density (kg/m³) | 1,374 | 3,363 | 2,081 |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | 5.17 | 37.62 | 35.72 |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 952 | 670 | 857 |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 1,307,448 | 2,253,210 | 1,783,417 |
| Unique material | Granite countertops | Stainless carousel | Aluminum kiosk/walkway |

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- Passenger queuing generates continuous occupancy during peak check-in windows (typically 2–3 hours before each departure bank)
- Agent workstations operate continuously during hours of operation — boarding pass printers, monitors, and scale equipment generate modest heat (~75–150 W per position × 12 positions = 900–1,800 W total)
- Ticket counter space is typically adjacent to the building exterior — envelope-driven heating and cooling loads from exterior glazing (terminal entrance walls) are significant
- Granite countertops have meaningful thermal mass — they absorb heat from passengers leaning/touching (skin contact at ~37°C transfers heat to 20°C granite) and from overhead lighting; this creates a slow-release thermal effect during post-peak quiet periods
- Queue lanes have low heat gain — stanchions are passive; belt straps generate negligible thermal activity

**Operational Patterns:**
- Opens 2–3 hours before first departure and closes after last check-in cutoff
- Peak demand follows airline departure schedules — hub airports may have continuous peak activity; regional airports may have 2–3 distinct peaks with quiet intervals
- International check-in counters have longer average transaction times and higher dwell times — queuing areas more densely occupied for longer periods
- Overnight closure possible at smaller airports — setback applicable; granite mass will hold daytime heat for several hours before equilibrating

**Special Considerations:**
- Rail and bus terminal ticket counters differ in counter length and equipment — fewer positions, no baggage scales, different kiosk types; the reference configuration is airport-specific
- Some modern airports have replaced traditional counters with common-use check-in (CUSS) systems — fewer dedicated counter positions, more kiosks; this would reduce counter mass significantly while increasing kiosk count
- Bag drop-only counters (after web check-in) are shorter and less elaborate than full service counters — reduced granite and MDF mass per linear meter
- Security checkpoint equipment (X-ray machines, millimeter wave scanners) if adjacent to the ticket counter zone would add significant steel and electronic mass to the zone boundary — these are typically treated as separate space types
