# Internal Mass Calculations: SS Warehouse - Medium/Bulky Items on Pallets

**Report Date:** April 7, 2026
**Scope:** Warehouse - Medium/Bulky Items on Pallets Space Type
**Purpose:** Calculate OpenStudio InternalMass properties for thermal modeling

---

## SS Warehouse - Medium/Bulky Items on Pallets

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 2–20 workers (forklift operators, pickers, receivers; low density)
**Floor Area:** 2,000–20,000 m² (bulk storage warehouse); reference area: **5,000 m²**
**Ceiling Height:** 6.0–12.0 m (high-bay storage); reference height: **9.0 m** (approx. 30 ft)
**Function:** Storage and retrieval of medium-to-large packaged goods on pallets — consumer goods, industrial supplies, building materials, appliances, food and beverage (non-refrigerated), automotive parts. Goods are stored on pallet rack systems and handled by forklifts. This space type is defined by pallet-based storage, distinguishing it from the hand-carried items warehouse.

**Key Features:**
- Selective pallet racking systems (the defining structural element)
- Stored inventory on pallets (the dominant thermal mass)
- Forklifts (electric and propane; parked between shifts)
- Pallet staging and receiving dock area
- Wire-guided aisle systems or open forklift aisles
- Dock levelers and dock doors (perimeter — excluded)
- Minimal office or worker amenity furniture
- Limited lighting (vapor-tight fluorescent or LED high-bay)
- Unheated or minimally conditioned environments typical (not always energy-code-regulated interior zone)

### Reference Configuration

**5,000 m² pallet warehouse floor:**
- Selective pallet racking: 50 rack bays, each 3.66 m wide × 1.07 m deep per face × 9.14 m high (6 pallet levels)
- Rack arrangement: double-deep (two-pallet deep per face), 25 rack rows of double-sided racks
- Pallet loading: 75% fill rate (conservative operating assumption)
- Forklifts parked: 4 electric counterbalanced forklifts
- Pallet receiving / staging area: 20 pallets staged on floor at any time

---

## Component Inventory

### 1. Selective Pallet Racking — Structure (50 bays per 5,000 m²)

**Standard Selective Pallet Rack Bay:**
- Bay dimensions: 3.66 m wide × 1.07 m deep per face × 9.14 m high
- Upright frames: 2 per bay (each frame is 1.07 m × 9.14 m, two uprights + horizontal braces)
- Beam levels: 6 load beams per bay level × 6 levels = 36 beams per bay
- Each beam: 3.66 m long × 0.10 m high × 0.05 m deep (roll-formed steel channel)
- Upright post cross-section: 100 mm × 65 mm lipped channel, 2 mm wall

**Surface Area per Bay — Uprights:**
- Each upright post (2 per frame, 2 frames per bay = 4 total posts): 4 × [(0.10 + 0.065) × 2 + lipped edges] × 9.14 ≈ 4 × 0.33 × 9.14 = 12.065 m²
- Horizontal braces (4 per frame × 2 frames): 8 × 2 × 1.07 × 0.04 = 0.686 m²
- Diagonal braces (3 per frame × 2 frames): 6 × 2 × 1.20 × 0.04 = 0.576 m²
- **Upright SA: 12.065 + 0.686 + 0.576 = 13.327 m²**

**Surface Area per Bay — Beams:**
- Each beam (3.66 m × 0.10 m, 3 faces exposed — top, front, bottom; back against uprights): 3 × 3.66 × 0.10 = 1.098 m²
- 36 beams per bay: 36 × 1.098 = 39.528 m²
- **Beam SA: 39.528 m²**

**Total Structural SA per Bay: 13.327 + 39.528 = 52.855 m²**

**Mass per Bay — Structure:**
- Upright frames (roll-formed steel lipped channel): each post 0.33 m/m × 9.14 m × 0.002 m × 7850 = 47.1 kg per post × 4 posts = 188.4 kg
- Bracing: 6 members × 1.20 × 0.04 × 0.002 × 7850 = 4.5 kg each × 6 = 27.0 kg + horizontal: 8 × 1.07 × 0.03 × 0.002 × 7850 = 4.1 kg; total bracing = **31.1 kg**

  > Upright frame mass simplified: typical selective pallet rack upright frame (1.07 m × 9.14 m, heavy-duty) weighs approximately 80–100 kg per frame pair; 2 frames per bay: **180 kg**

- Beams (36 beams, 3.66 m × 100 mm × 50 mm channel, 2 mm wall):
  - Beam cross-section area: approximately 2 × (0.10 + 0.05) × 0.002 = 0.00060 m² per meter
  - Each beam: 0.00060 × 3.66 × 7850 = 17.2 kg; 36 beams: **620 kg**

  > Industry reference: 4,000 lb capacity beam pair at 3.66 m ≈ 11–14 kg per beam; 36 × 12.5 = **450 kg**

- Beam safety clips (36 × 2 clips × 0.05 kg): 3.6 kg
- **Total Structural Mass per Bay: 180 + 450 + 3.6 = 633.6 kg**

**Per Floor Area (50 bays in 5,000 m²):**
- Surface Area: (50 × 52.855) / 5,000 = **0.529 m²/m²**
- Mass: (50 × 633.6) / 5,000 = **6.336 kg/m²**

---

### 2. Stored Pallet Inventory (per 5,000 m²)

**Pallet Count:**
- Rack positions: 50 bays × 6 levels × 2 pallets per level (double-deep) = 600 pallet positions
- Fill rate: 75% → 450 loaded pallets in racks
- Floor-staged pallets: 20
- **Total pallets in space: 470 loaded pallets**

**Wood Pallet (GMA Standard, 48" × 40" / 1.22 m × 1.02 m):**
- Construction: 9 boards (deck boards 4 on top, 3 on bottom) + 3 stringers; white wood (pine/spruce)
- Standard pallet: 1.22 m × 1.02 m × 0.14 m high
- Mass: **18.0 kg** (standard GMA wood pallet, new)
- Surface Area: top deck (3 × 4 board gaps): 3 top deck boards exposed: 3 × 1.22 × 0.14 = 0.513 m²; top face: 1.22 × 1.02 = 1.244 m²; bottom deck boards (3): 3 × 1.22 × 0.09 = 0.329 m²; stringers (3, sides): 3 × 2 × 1.02 × 0.09 = 0.551 m²; edges/ends: 2 × 1.22 × 0.09 × 3 = 0.659 m²

  > Simplified pallet SA (exposed surfaces — most faces covered by goods or adjacent pallets; effective exposed SA ≈ top + edges): 1.244 + 0.659 = 1.903 m²; bottom (on floor or resting on beams): 0.50 × 1.22 × 1.02 = 0.622 m² (50% exposure). **Effective SA per pallet: 2.525 m²**

**Pallet Mass per Floor Area (470 pallets):**
- Pallet wood: 470 × 18.0 / 5,000 = **1.692 kg/m²**

**Pallet SA per Floor Area:**
- (470 × 2.525) / 5,000 = **0.237 m²/m²**

---

**Stored Goods on Pallets:**
- Average loaded pallet weight (medium/bulky consumer goods): **500 kg** per pallet
  - Typical: 40 cases × 12.5 kg per case; or 8 appliance cartons × 60 kg; or industrial hardware
- Average pallet load footprint: 1.22 m × 1.02 m × 1.20 m high (standard 48" load height)
- Goods material: mixed packaged goods — approximately:
  - 40% cardboard/paper packaging (outer cartons)
  - 30% plastic products and packaging
  - 20% metal products / steel hardware
  - 10% other (wood, glass, textile)
- Total goods mass (470 pallets × 500 kg): 235,000 kg / 5,000 m² = **47.000 kg/m²**

**Goods Surface Area:**
- Exposed goods surfaces — primarily outer carton faces visible in rack:
  - Front face of pallet load: 1.22 m × 1.20 m = 1.464 m² per pallet
  - Top: 1.22 × 1.02 = 1.244 m² (exposed in upper rack positions)
  - Sides (partially visible through rack): 0.50 × 2 × 1.02 × 1.20 = 1.224 m²
  - **Effective SA per pallet load: 1.464 + 1.244 + 1.224 = 3.932 m²**
- Total goods SA: (470 × 3.932) / 5,000 = **0.370 m²/m²**

### 3. Forklifts — Parked (4 per 5,000 m²)

**Electric Counterbalanced Forklift (parked between shifts):**
- Same specification as post office sorting area: 3,500 kg; SA: 11.100 m²

**Per Floor Area (4 forklifts in 5,000 m²):**

## Composite Property Calculations

### Material Thermal Properties Reference

| Material | Density (kg/m³) | cp (J/kg·K) | k (W/m-K) |
|----------|----------------|-------------|-----------|
| Cardboard / paper | 700 | 1,300 | 0.06 |
| Steel | 7,850 | 460 | 45.0 |
| Mixed plastics | 950 | 1,800 | 0.30 |
| Mixed metals (Al/steel avg) | 4,000 | 480 | 35.0 |
| Wood (pine/spruce pallet) | 500 | 1,700 | 0.12 |
| Cast iron | 7,200 | 460 | 52.0 |
| Other goods (avg) | 1,200 | 1,000 | 0.50 |
| Rubber | 1,100 | 1,100 | 0.25 |

### Weighted Average Density

```
Volume per m² of floor:

Cardboard:    18.800 / 700  = 0.026857 m³/m²
Steel:         7.924 / 7850 = 0.001010 m³/m²
Plastics:     14.100 / 950  = 0.014842 m³/m²
Mixed metals:  9.400 / 4000 = 0.002350 m³/m²
Wood:          1.764 / 500  = 0.003528 m³/m²
Cast iron:     1.680 / 7200 = 0.000233 m³/m²
Other goods:   4.700 / 1200 = 0.003917 m³/m²
Rubber:        0.532 / 1100 = 0.000484 m³/m²

Total volume = 0.026857 + 0.001010 + 0.014842 + 0.002350
             + 0.003528 + 0.000233 + 0.003917 + 0.000484
             = 0.053221 m³/m²

Composite density = 57.900 / 0.053221
                  = 1,088 kg/m³
```

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Σ(m_i × c_p,i) / Σ(m_i)

Cardboard:    18.800 × 1300 = 24,440
Steel:         7.924 × 460  =  3,645
Plastics:     14.100 × 1800 = 25,380
Mixed metals:  9.400 × 480  =  4,512
Wood:          1.764 × 1700 =  2,999
Cast iron:     1.680 × 460  =    773
Other goods:   4.700 × 1000 =  4,700
Rubber:        0.532 × 1100 =    585

c_p,composite = (24,440 + 3,645 + 25,380 + 4,512 + 2,999 + 773 + 4,700 + 585) / 57.900
              = 67,034 / 57.900
              = 1,158 J/kg·K
```

> Cardboard (24,440) and plastics (25,380) together contribute 74% of the total mass-weighted cp. Both materials have high specific heat relative to metals. The composite of 1,158 J/kg·K reflects a warehouse stocked primarily with consumer goods packaging rather than dense metal products.

### Weighted Average Conductivity

```
k_composite ≈ Σ(V_i / V_total × k_i)

Cardboard:    (0.026857 / 0.053221) × 0.06  = 0.50464 × 0.06  = 0.030
Steel:        (0.001010 / 0.053221) × 45.0  = 0.01898 × 45.0  = 0.854
Plastics:     (0.014842 / 0.053221) × 0.30  = 0.27888 × 0.30  = 0.084
Mixed metals: (0.002350 / 0.053221) × 35.0  = 0.04416 × 35.0  = 1.546
Wood:         (0.003528 / 0.053221) × 0.12  = 0.06630 × 0.12  = 0.008
Cast iron:    (0.000233 / 0.053221) × 52.0  = 0.00438 × 52.0  = 0.228
Other goods:  (0.003917 / 0.053221) × 0.50  = 0.07361 × 0.50  = 0.037
Rubber:       (0.000484 / 0.053221) × 0.25  = 0.00910 × 0.25  = 0.002

k_composite ≈ 0.030 + 0.854 + 0.084 + 1.546 + 0.008 + 0.228 + 0.037 + 0.002
            ≈ 2.789 W/m·K
```

> Mixed metals on pallets (Al/steel hardware at avg k = 35 W/m-K) contribute 1.546 W/m-K — the largest single conductivity contribution despite being only 4.4% of total volume, again illustrating metal leverage. Steel rack structure contributes 0.854 W/m-K. Cardboard at 50.5% of volume contributes only 0.030 W/m-K — it is nearly a thermal insulator.

### Effective Thickness

```
t_eff = Total mass per m² / (SA_ratio × composite density)
      = 57.900 / (1.148 × 1,088)
      = 57.900 / 1,249.0
      = 0.04636 m ≈ 0.046 m  (46 mm)
```

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = ρ × c_p
    = 1,088 × 1,158
    = 1,259,904 J/m³·K
```

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Inventory-Dominated — Cardboard and Plastic Goods Drive the Composite:**
- Moderate composite density (1,088 kg/m³) — cardboard (700 kg/m³) and plastics (950 kg/m³) dominate volume; steel rack and metals raise the composite above the organic material baseline
- Moderate SA ratio (1.15 m²/m²) — rack beams contribute the largest share (0.529 m²/m²); goods faces contribute 0.370 m²/m²; pallets add 0.237 m²/m²
- High specific heat (1,158 J/kg·K) — cardboard at 1,300 J/kg·K and plastics at 1,800 J/kg·K together represent 57% of total mass; their high cp values pull the composite well above steel
- Low-moderate conductivity (2.789 W/m-K) — mixed metal goods provide the largest conductivity contribution; steel rack structure contributes meaningfully; cardboard and plastic dominate the volume but conduct poorly

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Moderate thermal capacitance (1,259,904 J/m³·K)
- Slow thermal response — cardboard dominates volume (50%) and insulates the stored goods; heat penetrates pallet loads slowly
- Very high total mass (57.90 kg/m²) — second only to the library stacks (146 kg/m²) among all space types, driven by the 47 kg/m² of stored goods; this is more than twice the mass of any other comparable space type
- Stored goods act as distributed thermal mass reservoirs throughout the rack system — each pallet at 500 kg of goods is effectively a localized heat sink or source

### Design Appropriateness

**Pallet Warehouse Thermal Mass Features:**
- **Stored goods massively dominate** — 47.0 of 57.9 kg/m² (81%) is stored inventory, not the building fixtures; this is the highest inventory-to-structure mass ratio of any space type in the dataset
- **Pallet rack structure** contributes meaningfully (6.34 kg/m²) but is secondary to the goods; the rack beams generate the most surface area through their multiple levels
- **Forklifts** (4 at 3,500 kg each) account for 2.8 kg/m² — the cast iron ballast at 1.68 kg/m² is disproportionately heavy for equipment that occupies minimal space; same dynamic noted in the post office sorting area
- **The 75% fill rate assumption is critical** — at 100% fill the goods mass would increase to 62.7 kg/m²; at 50% fill it drops to 38.7 kg/m²; the thermal mass of a warehouse is fundamentally variable by inventory level

**Inventory as Thermal Mass:**
The warehouse is the only space type in the dataset where the internal mass calculation primarily captures stored product rather than furnishings or equipment. This creates unique modeling challenges:
- Inventory level varies daily and seasonally
- Product mix changes (different goods have very different thermal properties)
- The 75% fill rate and mixed-goods assumption represent a reasonable mid-cycle average for a general merchandise warehouse
- A steel products warehouse would have dramatically higher density and conductivity; a paper products warehouse would have much lower density and higher specific heat

### Comparison to Other High-Mass Space Types

| Parameter | Warehouse (Pallets) | Library Stacks | Detailed Manufacturing |
|-----------|--------------------|--------------|-----------------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 1.15 | 8.85 | 1.04 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | **57.90** | 146.0 | 73.3 |
| Density (kg/m³) | 1,088 | 1,346 | 6,074 |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | 2.789 | 1.707 | 40.35 |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 1,158 | 1,140 | 483 |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 1,259,904 | 1,534,440 | 2,933,742 |
| Dominant mass | Stored goods (81%) | Books (78%) | CNC machines (92%) |

> The warehouse and library stacks are strikingly analogous in structure: both are primarily inventory (goods or books) stored on steel shelving, both have the shelving structure as a secondary mass contributor, and both have specific heats near 1,150 J/kg·K. The warehouse has lower SA ratio (shelving geometry is different — pallet loads are larger units than books) but similar material character.

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- Most large warehouses are semi-conditioned or unconditioned — energy code applicability depends on jurisdiction and use; This space type applies to conditioned warehouses
- Where conditioned, the enormous thermal mass (57.9 kg/m²) means very long thermal time constants — temperature setback recovery can take 8–24 hours
- Dock doors cause significant infiltration during receiving operations — this dominates the thermal load during peak receiving hours
- Forklift propane (if used) generates combustion heat and CO₂; electric forklifts generate battery heat gain during charging
- Rack-level temperature stratification is significant in 9 m high spaces — top rack levels may be 5–8°C warmer than floor level

**Operational Patterns:**
- Receiving operations typically daytime (shift-aligned with trucking schedules)
- Shipping typically overnight or early morning at major distribution centers
- Inventory levels cycle with business activity — lowest at fiscal month-end, highest pre-peak seasons (retail pre-holiday)
- Temperature requirements vary by product: ambient goods (15–25°C); some pharmaceutical products require tighter control

**Special Considerations:**
- Cold-storage or refrigerated warehouses are thermally distinct — the refrigeration load dominates and the internal mass interacts with a cooled environment; these are beyond the scope of this standard space type
- High-cube pallet warehouses (>12 m) would have more rack levels and proportionally higher inventory mass per floor area
- Automated storage and retrieval systems (AS/RS) replace forklifts with steel automated cranes — these would add significant additional steel mass to the overhead zone
- Variable inventory assumption: modeling warehouses with a seasonal peak fill scenario (100% fill at peak) and a low-season scenario (40% fill) would bracket the thermal mass range for energy simulation sensitivity analysis

# Internal Mass Calculations: SS Warehouse - Smaller Hand Carried Items

**Report Date:** April 7, 2026
**Scope:** Warehouse - Smaller Hand Carried Items Space Type
**Purpose:** Calculate OpenStudio InternalMass properties for thermal modeling

---

## SS Warehouse - Smaller Hand Carried Items

### Space Characteristics

**Typical Occupancy:** 5–30 workers (order pickers, stock clerks, receivers)
**Floor Area:** 500–5,000 m² (pick/pack or retail backstock warehouse); reference area: **1,500 m²**
**Ceiling Height:** 3.5–6.0 m (lower than pallet warehouse; hand-pick accessible)
**Function:** Storage and retrieval of small-to-medium items handled individually by workers without forklift assistance — pharmaceutical products, hardware, spare parts, retail backstock, archive documents, small electronics, medical supplies. Items are stored on open shelving, bin shelving, or mobile shelving units and picked by hand. Distinct from the pallet warehouse by the absence of pallet rack and forklift infrastructure; access is by worker on foot or rolling ladder.

**Key Features:**
- Open steel shelving (boltless or rivet-type; the dominant structural element)
- Bin storage inserts and dividers (plastic or steel)
- Stored inventory (small packaged goods, parts, documents)
- Rolling ladders or step stools
- Order picking carts and hand trucks
- Labeling and barcode scanning stations
- No forklifts — hand trucks and dollies only
- Moderate ceiling height (hand-pick accessible shelving up to ~2.4 m)
- Higher shelving density than pallet warehouse (tighter aisle spacing)

### Reference Configuration

**1,500 m² hand-carry warehouse:**
- 120 boltless steel shelving units (6-shelf, 4-foot wide)
- 60% inventory fill rate (conservative average)
- 8 order picking carts
- 4 rolling ladders
- 2 hand trucks / dollies
- 1 packing / labeling workbench station

---

## Component Inventory

### 1. Boltless Steel Shelving Units (120 per 1,500 m²)

**Standard 4-Post Boltless Shelving Unit:**
- Dimensions: 1.22 m wide × 0.46 m deep × 1.98 m high (6-shelf unit)
- Construction: Cold-rolled steel uprights (4-post design), steel or particleboard shelf decks
- Shelf decks: steel wire or solid steel; 6 shelves per unit

**Surface Area per Unit:**
- Uprights (4 posts, 4 faces each): 4 × 4 × 0.05 × 1.98 = 1.584 m²
- Upright side faces (4 posts × 2 sides): 4 × 2 × 0.46 × 1.98 = 7.286 m²
- Shelf decks (6, top + bottom): 6 × 2 × 1.22 × 0.46 = 6.730 m²
- Shelf edges (6 shelves, front + back edge): 6 × 2 × 1.22 × 0.025 = 0.366 m²
- **Total per Unit: 1.584 + 7.286 + 6.730 + 0.366 = 15.966 m²**

**Mass per Unit:**
- Uprights (4 posts × cold-rolled steel, approx. 6 kg each): 4 × 6.0 = 24.0 kg
- Shelf decks (6 × solid steel deck, 1.22 × 0.46 × 0.00159 × 7850): 6 × 7.0 = 42.0 kg

  > Steel deck: 1.22 × 0.46 × 0.00159 × 7850 = 7.02 kg per shelf; 6 shelves = 42.1 kg

- Shelf supports (12 steel clips + cross-bracing): 3.5 kg
- **Total Mass per Unit: 24.0 + 42.1 + 3.5 = 69.6 kg**

**Per Floor Area (120 units in 1,500 m²):**
- Surface Area: (120 × 15.966) / 1,500 = **1.277 m²/m²**
- Mass: (120 × 69.6) / 1,500 = **5.568 kg/m²**

- Average goods: mixed small items — spare parts, hardware, electronics, pharmaceutical packaging, retail backstock

- For hand-carry items: average load weight = 40 kg per shelf (60% fill of ~70 kg capacity)
- Total goods mass: 720 × 40 = 28,800 kg / 1,500 m² = **19.200 kg/m²**

- 25% small metal parts (hardware, spare parts): 19.2 × 0.25 = 4.80 kg/m²

## Composite Property Calculations

### Material Thermal Properties Reference

| Material | Density (kg/m³) | cp (J/kg·K) | k (W/m-K) |
|----------|----------------|-------------|-----------|
| Steel | 7,850 | 460 | 45.0 |
| Paper / cardboard | 700 | 1,300 | 0.06 |
| Mixed metals (Al/steel avg) | 4,000 | 480 | 35.0 |
| Plastic (PP, ABS, mixed) | 950 | 1,800 | 0.25 |
| Electronics (mixed) | 1,200 | 1,000 | 0.30 |
| Other goods (avg) | 1,200 | 1,000 | 0.50 |
| Rubber | 1,100 | 1,100 | 0.25 |

### Weighted Average Density

```
Volume per m² of floor:

Steel:        6.007 / 7850  = 0.000765 m³/m²
Paper:        6.720 / 700   = 0.009600 m³/m²
Mixed metals: 4.800 / 4000  = 0.001200 m³/m²
Plastic:      5.146 / 950   = 0.005417 m³/m²
Electronics:  1.920 / 1200  = 0.001600 m³/m²
Other:        0.960 / 1200  = 0.000800 m³/m²
Rubber:       0.092 / 1100  = 0.000084 m³/m²

Total volume = 0.000765 + 0.009600 + 0.001200 + 0.005417
             + 0.001600 + 0.000800 + 0.000084
             = 0.019466 m³/m²

Composite density = 25.358 / 0.019466
                  = 1,303 kg/m³
```

### Weighted Average Specific Heat

```
c_p,composite = Σ(m_i × c_p,i) / Σ(m_i)

Steel:        6.007 × 460  =  2,763
Paper:        6.720 × 1300 =  8,736
Mixed metals: 4.800 × 480  =  2,304
Plastic:      5.146 × 1800 =  9,263
Electronics:  1.920 × 1000 =  1,920
Other:        0.960 × 1000 =    960
Rubber:       0.092 × 1100 =    101

c_p,composite = (2,763 + 8,736 + 2,304 + 9,263 + 1,920 + 960 + 101) / 25.358
              = 26,047 / 25.358
              = 1,027 J/kg·K
```

### Weighted Average Conductivity

```
k_composite ≈ Σ(V_i / V_total × k_i)

Steel:        (0.000765 / 0.019466) × 45.0  = 0.03931 × 45.0  = 1.769
Paper:        (0.009600 / 0.019466) × 0.06  = 0.49317 × 0.06  = 0.030
Mixed metals: (0.001200 / 0.019466) × 35.0  = 0.06164 × 35.0  = 2.157
Plastic:      (0.005417 / 0.019466) × 0.25  = 0.27828 × 0.25  = 0.070
Electronics:  (0.001600 / 0.019466) × 0.30  = 0.08222 × 0.30  = 0.025
Other:        (0.000800 / 0.019466) × 0.50  = 0.04111 × 0.50  = 0.021
Rubber:       (0.000084 / 0.019466) × 0.25  = 0.00432 × 0.25  = 0.001

k_composite ≈ 1.769 + 0.030 + 2.157 + 0.070 + 0.025 + 0.021 + 0.001
            ≈ 4.073 W/m·K
```

> Mixed metal goods (hardware, spare parts) provide the largest single conductivity contribution (2.157 W/m-K) despite being only 6.16% of total volume — the metal leverage effect at moderate scale. Steel shelving contributes 1.769 W/m-K from 3.93% of volume. Paper at 49.3% of volume contributes just 0.030 W/m-K — nearly pure insulation by conductivity.

### Effective Thickness

```
t_eff = Total mass per m² / (SA_ratio × composite density)
      = 25.358 / (1.921 × 1,303)
      = 25.358 / 2,502.9
      = 0.01013 m ≈ 0.010 m  (10 mm)
```

### Thermal Capacitance

```
C_v = ρ × c_p
    = 1,303 × 1,027
    = 1,338,181 J/m³·K
```

## Key Observations

### Thermal Mass Characteristics

**Shelving-and-Goods Mixed Composition — Highest SA Ratio of the Warehouse Types:**
- Moderate composite density (1,303 kg/m³) — steel shelving pulls density up; paper and plastic goods pull it back toward 700–950 kg/m³; mixed metal goods provide an intermediate contribution
- Higher SA ratio (1.921 m²/m²) than the pallet warehouse (1.148) — the hand-carry warehouse achieves more surface area per floor area because the 120 smaller shelving units with six levels each present far more shelf-face area than the pallet rack geometry; additionally, the 2,880 individual plastic bins contribute 0.340 m²/m² that has no parallel in the pallet warehouse
- High specific heat (1,027 J/kg·K) — paper/cardboard at 1,300 J/kg·K and plastics at 1,800 J/kg·K together represent 47% of total mass; their high cp values raise the composite significantly above steel
- Moderate conductivity (4.073 W/m-K) — metal goods (2.157) and steel shelving (1.769) dominate conductivity; paper and plastic at 72% of volume contribute minimally

**Thermal Behavior:**
- Moderate thermal capacitance (1,338,181 J/m³·K) — similar to the ticket counter and library reading area
- Slower thermal response than the pallet warehouse — more shelf surface area means more air-mass heat exchange at the shelf level; but lower total mass than the pallet warehouse means less total thermal storage
- Individual plastic bins (2,880 units) are a distributed thermal feature unique to this space type — each bin at 0.18 kg of polypropylene is individually trivial, but collectively they add 519 kg of plastic with 1,800 J/kg·K specific heat throughout the shelving system

### Comparison — Warehouse Space Type Family

| Parameter | Hand Carry | Pallet (Bulky) |
|-----------|-----------|---------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | **1.921** | 1.148 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 25.36 | **57.90** |
| Density (kg/m³) | 1,303 | 1,088 |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | 4.073 | 2.789 |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 1,027 | 1,158 |
| Thermal Capacitance (J/m³·K) | 1,338,181 | 1,259,904 |
| Dominant structure | Boltless shelving | Pallet racking |
| Ceiling height | 3.5–6.0 m | 6.0–12.0 m |
| Goods density | ~40 kg/shelf | ~500 kg/pallet |
| Inventory fraction | 76% of mass | 81% of mass |

> The hand-carry warehouse has a higher SA ratio than the pallet warehouse because its smaller, denser shelving units create more surface per floor area, and the individual plastic bins add a SA term with no pallet warehouse equivalent. However, it has less than half the total mass per floor area — a direct consequence of loading individual hand-carry items (40 kg/shelf average) versus palletized bulk goods (500 kg/pallet). Both space types share a similar specific heat profile driven by paper and plastic packaging.

### Comparison to Analogous Space Types

| Parameter | Hand Carry Warehouse | Library Stacks | Post Office Sorting |
|-----------|---------------------|---------------|---------------------|
| SA Ratio (m²/m²) | 1.921 | 8.85 | 3.09 |
| Mass (kg/m²) | 25.36 | 146.0 | 31.79 |
| Density (kg/m³) | 1,303 | 1,346 | 6,314 |
| Conductivity (W/m-K) | 4.073 | 1.707 | 42.18 |
| Specific Heat (J/kg·K) | 1,027 | 1,140 | 491 |
| Primary driver | Steel shelving + mixed goods | Books on steel shelves | Steel sort cases |

> The hand-carry warehouse shares structural DNA with both the library stacks (steel shelving with stored items) and the post office sorting area (organized retrieval spaces with high unit counts). Its material profile — predominantly paper and plastic goods on steel shelving — produces composite properties between the insulating library stacks and the conductive sort area.

### Modeling Implications

**HVAC Considerations:**
- Lower ceiling height (3.5–6 m) means less thermal stratification than the pallet warehouse — the zone is closer to well-mixed conditions
- Hand-pick operations generate moderate worker activity (~2 MET for order picking); 20 workers in 1,500 m² provides meaningful latent gain
- No forklift propane combustion loads — electric hand trucks if any
- High density of shelving creates turbulent airflow patterns in aisles — mixing is better than in pallet warehouse, supporting convective heat exchange between goods and room air
- Fire suppression system (ESFR or standard wet pipe) runs steel pipe overhead — not modeled as internal mass per convention, but adds distributed steel mass

**Operational Patterns:**
- Typically daytime operation aligned with order fulfillment schedules; overnight pick operations in some e-commerce distribution centers
- Inventory levels vary by business cycle; pharmaceutical warehouses may maintain strict inventory levels while retail backstock fluctuates seasonally
- Temperature requirements: pharmaceutical warehouses often 15–25°C with tight control (±2°C); retail backstock may be uncontrolled or minimally conditioned

**Special Considerations:**
- Archive and document storage warehouses are a variant of this space type — if the goods were entirely paper/cardboard documents, the composite density drops to ~700 kg/m³ and specific heat rises toward 1,300 J/kg·K; conductivity drops to near the pure cardboard value of 0.06 W/m-K
- Mobile shelving systems (Spacesaver-type) achieve 40–60% more shelf density per floor area — SA ratio would rise to approximately 2.7–3.1 m²/m²; mass proportionally higher
- Pharmaceutical or food-grade warehouses may have stainless steel shelving rather than carbon steel — this increases mass and reduces conductivity slightly but does not dramatically change composite properties
- The fill-rate assumption (60%) is a modeling midpoint; actual modeling for a specific facility should reflect the actual average inventory level
